16. During the course of discussion on Demands for Grants (2020-21) pertaining to the Ministry 
of MSME, the Committee also heard the views of the Representatives of some  Associations from 
Industrial and MSME Sectors like FICCI and FISME. However, ASSOCHAM could not participate 
in the discussion but submitted its written response to the Committee. The Committee appreciates 
and is thankful to the Industry and MSME Associati ons.  Some important and meaningful 
points/suggestions were also shared by the Industry Associations.  
17. The Committee was apprised that the Budget does take a few steps towards addressing the 
decelerating growth rate, specifically in the areas of Govern ance, Export -Import Promotion, and 
Ease of Doing Business etc. for the Industry and Business. The Associations also acclaimed the 
Vivad se Viswas  tax facilitation scheme, increasing audit limits to five crore rupees, allowing 
NBFCs to participate in Bill discounting over the TReDS platform and financing working capital 
requirements through quasi-equity subordinate debts. 
18. The Committee was also apprised by the Associations that even after the government 
issuing policy guidelines, the guidelines are not followed. Most of the Banks do not give the benefit 
of CGTMSE to the MSMEs and insist on collateral security and harassment of the small 
entrepreneurs is a common thing without even giving opportunity and also with no justification. 
Accordingly, they suggested that officers dealing with financial matters and regulatory affairs be 
made more accountable and be allowed to support the MSMEs.  
19. It was also informed by the representatives of MSME Associations that the GST Act need to 
be simplified further for easy application, improvement and allow corrections of genuine mistakes 
and rate rationalization should be applied by the Government. MSMEs always  run on short of 
resources and GST and its maintenance have made MSMEs completely occupied with its processes 
and the returns. Besides, the Committee was also informed that MSMEs need to have separate GST 
registration in each state. As a result, even if th ey have limited or nil business in that State, they 
need to file return which is in totality a very tedious task for a unit who already lack resources. It 
was accordingly suggested that MSMEs should be allowed to have only one unified GST 
registration which is applicable in all states.  
20. Further, the Committee was informed by the representatives of the MSME Associations that 
though the products of Indian MSMEs have the immense potential in global markets,  the Indian 

6 
 
MSMEs are not able to export their go ods as per their true potential due to lack of resources and 
knowledge. Besides, they also do not have enough resources to have a dedicated research team to 
develop the products as per the demand of a certain region or country. In this regard, the 
representatives of MSME Associations suggested to set up an exclusive „Export Facilitation Centre‟ 
for MSMEs to promote exports of products and services from MSME sector. The centre can be 
established in each State with the cooperation of the State government, whi ch could be One Point 
Contact for export facilitation. 
Demands for Grants (2020-21) 
21. The Ministry of MSME informed the Committee while making presentation on the DFG 
(2020-21) that MSMEs provide employment to about 11.10 crore people and contribute around 
28.9% to the country‟s GDP. The Committee was also apprised that under PMEGP (till 15.02.2020) 
around 43,426 micro enterprises have been assisted and about 3.47 lakh employment opportunities 
have been created. Further, the Ministry apprised that the one -time cap of Rs. 200 lakh is removed 
and the borrower can avail incremental credit facil ities now under CGTMSE and so far 39.28 lakh 
guarantees have been approved with coverage of Rs.2.06 lakh crores under the Scheme. To add, it 
was apprised that the corpus to the Credit Guarantee Fund has been enhanced to Rs. 7,500 crores to 
ensure payment to the Banks in case the loan amount becomes NPA.  
22. The Committee was informed by the representatives of MSME Associations that many 
of the MSMEs were unable to meet the fixed deadline of 90 days in repaying their loan 
installments, due to the unique sys tem of their working cycle, which is much longer, due to 
their inability to meet the stipulated timeline for repayment, the MSMEs units are declared 
NPAs. To avoid such difficulties being faced by MSMEs, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry should en deavor to see to it that time limit for declaring a MSME as NPA due to 
non-payment of loan amount should be enhanced from the current 90 days to 180 days. 
Dream of Five Trillion Dollar Economy and the MSME Sector 
23. The Economic Survey 2018 -19 and the Uni on Budget 2019 -20 have indicated the goal of 
making India a US$ 5 trillion economy by 2024 -25. MSMEs are widely spread across the country 
in all the sectors and the current size of Indian Economy is around $3 trillion in which MSMEs ‟ 
share is estimated to be around $0.9 trillion based on its share of around 30% in the GDP.   
24. In order to increase the contribution of MSMEs in India‟s GDP and to achieve the target of 
$2 trillion mark for MSME sector by 2024 -25, Government is focusing on the key factors of 

7 
 
economic growth i.e. Investment and Productivity (efficiency) and the main parameters of the 
MSME Strategy is:  
(i) investment in all the vertical of MSME Ecosystem viz. human capital, knowledge 
dissemination, access to finance, technology, infrastructure, mar kets, policy, governance 
and ease of doing business. 
(ii) consolidation and convergence of all the MSME related activities under Central/ State 
management 
(iii)exploring the possibility of crowd sourcing of knowledge services and capital to 
supplement the efforts of the Government.  
(iv) implementing projects with external aid from World Bank, ADB etc. to supplement the 
investment of Government of India.  
(v) strengthening linkages of large manufacturing and services sector with micro, small and 
medium enterprises (MSMEs) and  developing a firm value chain within and across the 
sectors.  
(vi) upgrading the rural and urban livelihoods into enterprises by providing them with access 
to capital and market. This will not only lead to formalization of these sectors but also 
capture their contribution in the GDP which is at present either remains unreported or 
underreported.     
25. The Committee welcomes the Government’s goal of making India a $5 trillion 
economy by 2024 -25. The Committee is however of the considered view that the target o f 
becoming $5 trillion economy by 2024 can be achieved by exponential growth of MSME 
sector. This sector has the capacity of building up at a low cost and utilizing the modern 
innovative technology can be made commercially productive at lower cost. This se ctor has 
also the capacity to generate employment and multiplication of production is far easy than the 
big industries.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that Government need to play a 
proactive and constructive role in promoting MSME S ector. More than ease of doing 
business, there is need of creating ease of running business. More information dissemination 
regarding the export requirements should be taken care of. Financial institutions should be 
proactive, friendly and forthcoming. Gov ernment regulators should do handholding and play 
the role of mentors. Besides, change in the attitude of the Government regulators will 
immensely help the MSME S ector. Together with the industry, skilled manpower and the 
support of government authorities, the desired target can be achieved.   
26. Artificial Intelligence is a rapidly emerging concept in the market across the globe , 
which has great potential for enterprises. Most of the entrepreneurs are making use of this 
concept for their benefit and to in crease their outreach.  The Committee recommends that 
Ministry of MSME should also explore th e concept of AI for strengthening and betterment of 
MSME Sector in the country.    

8 
 
27. Market Intelligence plays a crucial role in strengthening and improving the e nterprises. A 
dedicated market intelligence cell is very essential to gather information about latest trends, taste 
and other aspects of the market. It is imperative to keep an eye on International markets and 
MSMEs of developed countries for knowledge of latest technology and developments and to adopt 
good practices prevailing in the developed markets across the globe for benefit of indigenous 
MSMEs. The Committee, therefore, recommends  that a Market Intelligence Cell for MSMEs 
should be set up that would regularly map specific markets, foreign as well as domestic, for 
meeting the requirement of specific MSME clusters and accordingly provide information and 
training to them about consumer preferences, product specifications, technological 
developments and trade agreements. 
28. Taking into consideration the views expressed by some of MSME Associations during 
the course of examination of DFG (2020 -21), the Committee also perceives that a lot of 
reforms on the Tax front too need to be taken to promote and encou rage the MSMEs. The 
Committee accordingly, is of the view that tax rates for proprietary and partnership firms 
should be reduced from 30% to at least 22% on the lines of reduction in Corporate Tax. 
Likewise, exemption and relief under Capital Gain should b e accorded to MSMEs for 
investment in expansion of the existing MSME or for fulfilling their working capital 
requirements. The Committee accordingly, desires that Ministry of MSME may take up these 
issues with the Ministry of Finance and apprise the Committee of the outcome thereof. 
29. The Committee recommends that MSMEs should be allowed to have only one unified 
GST registration , which is applicable in all states. With respect to the sharing of Taxes 
between Central and State Governments, it should be don e at the back end as the 
Government already has all the information in this regard.  
30. The Committee recommends that multiple registrations with multiple government 
agencies for various purposes should be done away with for MSMEs. Inter -Ministries 
coordination should be improved to bring out one registration to carry out all business 
activities including exports, tax and day -to-day business activities to improve ease of doing 
business for MSMEs.  
31. The Committee recommends that Ministry should play a pr oactive role in promoting 
MSMEs abroad and the foreign entrepreneurs should have profiles of Indian MSMEs so that 
they could promote them at appropriate level amongst companies of their respective country. 

9 
 
There should be an exclusive ‘Export Facilitation Centre’ for MSMEs in PPP mode in each 
State to promote exports of products and services from MSME sector.  
32. The Committee observes that there have been instances of inadequate credit 
disbursement by banks to MSMEs vis-à-vis large industries whereas the case should have 
been opposite. In Economic Survey 2018 -19, it has been stated that MSME sector has vast 
potential and it should be nurtured fully to convert dwarfs into the giants. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry s hould take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance and 
RBI to ensure that there is no inadequacy of funds to MSMEs.                             
Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) 
33. The KVIC is entrusted with the functions to plan, promote organize and assist in the 
implementation of the programme by financing the eligible units in Khadi and Village Industries 
sector, imparting training for the employment, ensuring supply of raw materials to the 
units/entrepreneurs, promotion of sales of Kha di and Village Industries products and undertaking 
research and development activities for the growth and spread of Khadi and Village Industries to 
promote the sale and marketing of Khadi or products of Village Industries or handicrafts by forging 
links wi th established marketing agencies wherever possible; and to encourage and promote 
research in technology used in Khadi and VI, including use of non -conventional energy and electric 
power with a view to increasing productivity. The programmes of the KVIC ar e implemented 
through its Regional/States level Offices and State Boards (KVIBs).  The KVIBs implement about 
90% of VI programmes and receive funds from both KVIC and State Governments.  Khadi Sector 
programme in its entirety and a small part of Village In dustries programmes are being implemented 
by KVIC directly.  Both the KVIC and KVIB are promotional bodies which extend a network of 
institutional, infrastructural and financial support to Khadi and Village Industries units/institution.  
34. In response to  a query regarding the future plans of the Ministry for the Khadi Sector and the 
suggestions for the betterment of Khadi Sector, the  Ministry informed that the Khadi Gramodyog Vikas 
Yojana (KGVY) has been implemented during 2019-20 and assistance is provided under various components 
viz., Modified Market Development Assistance (MMDA) to the Khadi Institutions and Khadi Artisans, 
Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme, ensuring availability of working capital to Khadi 
Institutions, Work-shed Scheme for providing sufficient space and congenial environment to Khadi artisans, 
Strengthening of Weak Khadi Institutions, assistance for modernization of sales outlets of Khadi 
Institutions, marketing component for promoting sales and marketing, assista nce under science & 
technology for developing new technologies, and training to the artisans. The Ministry also informed that 

10 
 
the social welfare schemes like Janashree Bima Yojana etc., are implemented for the artisans. Also, to make 
Khadi a youthful and g lobal brand, it is proposed to set up design houses to introduce new and vibrant 
designs.  
35. Regarding the export performance of KVIC/Coir Board, the Committee was apprised that  KVIC do 
not involve directly in the export activities of KVI products. The K VI products are being exported by KVIs 
directly or through merchant/agencies. Moreover, the targets for export are not fixed because export is 
demand driven. However, KVIC participates with Khadi and Village Industry Institutions/units in the 
International Exhibitions organized by different organizations like ITPO, FIEO, TEXPROCIL and other 
Government bodies in different countries. On the other hand, Coir Board has an exclusive export market 
promotion wing for promotion of coir exports. It facilitates coir entrepreneurs to register as coir exporter, 
participation in exhibitions abroad, availing assistance under International co -operation scheme and other 
trade-related matters. Recent research and development activities of Coir Board have made some 
remarkable breakthrough in the development of new products and end user applications of coir. The coir 
pith products are now widely used abroad for agriculture/horticulture applications due to the R&D efforts 
of Coir Board.  
36. It was informed that considering the new trend of e -commerce, new initiatives have been 
undertaken by the KVIC by signing Agreement with Paytm Mall and Aarmart Ecommerce for the 
promotion and marketing support of products produced by the KVI Institutions/Units. Recently 
KVIC had taken the ini tiative for launching exclusive e-commerce platform for marketing the 
products of Khadi and Village Industries through PPP model. 
37. The Committee notes that the constraints faced by KVIC/KVIB are mainly due to 
procedural delays, inadequate technology up-gradation, under utilization of funds etc. Despite 
providing technical guidance to the units in KVI, the problems of the units remain 
inadequately addressed, as a result there is suboptimal functioning of institutions/units and 
high drop outs among new entrants and low employment generation.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that KVIC, in view of the expansion of its area of operation in every 
nook and corner of the country, should come forward with a more holistic and unified policy 
in co-ordination with all the stakeholders. Proper planning, monitoring and implementation 
in each scheme are required to meet the primary objective of employment generation.  
38. The Committee feels that in face of stiff competition in the market from organized 
industries, KVIs should concentrate more on adoption of newer technology and upgradation of 
existing technology for products upgradation.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that 

11 
 
regular training by efficient staff having experience and expertise should be imparted  to the 
artisans through its network of training institutions.   
39. The Committee was apprised about the availability of Khadi Fabrics in private retail 
stores at competitive price.  The Committee observes that opening up of Khadi retailing to 
private players is a good initiative in this regard for enhancing and expanding the market of 
Khadi fabrics among the customers. Further, the recent innovative step to bring in fashion 
designers of repute to design Khadi fabrics is a welcome move and it needs to be c ontinued by 
bringing in more such steps.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that good market 
techniques like frequent awareness campaigns among the youth and introduction of Khadi in 
Schools, Hospitals, Railways and other Government Organizations could b e good recourse , 
which will surely increase the demand for Khadi products. Besides, premier showrooms 
known as Khadi Lounge should be opened in all the State capitals and Airports to market 
designer Khadi products and attract the younger generations towards Khadi products. In this 
direction opening up of Designer Houses in each state capitals would be a welcome step.  
40. The Committee observes that the rural as well as urban youths are not  inclined to work in 
KVI sector due to low wages and the hardships i nvolved in it. Therefore, the Committee is of the 
view that the economic empowerment of the poor artisans can be enhanced by allowing the 
potential spinners and weavers to work with the private designers of national and 
international reputation without the  approval of KVIC so that they could earn more wages 
from them directly.  Further, the issue of low wages of unskilled and semi -skilled artisans 
needs to be addressed properly so that more willing workers will bring in more quality output 
in Khadi sector.  
41. It was observed by the Committee that opportunities of export of products of Khadi and 
Village Industries are not yet exploited optimally and the government has to lay emphasis upon the

organised to  educate KVIs/MSMEs about opportunities of their products in global market 
and benefits of exports. Besides an e-portal can be designed where the MSME exporters can 
post their applications for clearance or for export facilitation like stuffing/de -stuffing and the

Scheme of Funds for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) 
64. The Committee was informed that KVIC is implementing centrally sponsored scheme 
known as Revamped Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) to make 
the traditional industries more productive, competitive and to facilitate for their sustainable 
development. It is basically a cluster development programme, designed to pr otect and preserve the 
arts and crafts of rural traditional artisans, in a cluster-based manner. The objective of the scheme is 
to organize traditional industries and artisans into clusters to make them competitive and provide 
support for their long -term s ustainability, sustained employment to enhance marketability of 
products of such clusters, to equip traditional artisans of the associated clusters with the improved 
skills, to make provision for common facilities and improved tools and equipment for artis ans, to 
strengthen the cluster governance systems with the active participation of the stakeholders and to 

19 
 
build up innovative products, improved technologies, advanced processes, market intelligence and 
new models of public-private partnerships. 
65. The Scheme covers three types of interventions: 
(i)   Soft interventions - Activities to build general awareness, counseling, skill   
      development & capacity building, exposure visits, market development initiatives, design 
and product development, etc. 
 (ii)  Hard interventions - Creation of common facility centers, raw material banks,    
        upgradation of production infrastructure, warehousing facilities, tools and     
        technological upgradation, etc. 
   (iii) Thematic interventions - Interventions on a cross-cutting basis for brand building,    
          new media marketing, e-commerce initiatives, research and development, etc. 
 
66. The financial assistance provided for any specific project shall be subject to a maximum of 
Rs. 5 crore to support Soft, Hard and Thematic interventions. 
67. The scheme is implemented through registered implementing agencies. Financial assistance 
is given for Khadi and Village Industries Institutions to create Common Facility Centres (CFCs) 
and new infrastructure, to purchase machinery, equipment, Charkha, Looms and tools, to construct 
Workshed, renovate sales outlets, to ensure Skill development of artisans and also to facilitate 
computer and computer related design, etc. Till December, 2019, 63 clusters were assisted and an 
additional 50 clusters are likely to be approved by March, 2020.  Further, 54 are functional 
benefitting 38970 artisans. The Ministry has so far approved 191 proposals for setting up clusters 
and approved an amount of Rs. 408.19 crores  as grant for implementation of clusters since 2015 -16 
to 2019-20 (till December, 2019). 
68. As per revised guidelines pattern of financial assistance, Rs. 2.50 crore is granted for regular 
Clusters (up to 500 artisans) and Rs. 5.00 crore is granted for ma jor Clusters (more than 500 
artisans). The financial assistance provided for any specific project shall be subject to a maximum 
of Rs. 5 crore.

Micro & Small Enterprises - Cluster Development Programme (MSE-CDP) 
105. The Ministry of MSME has adopted the Cluster Development approach as a key strategy for 
enhancing the productivity and competitiveness as well as capacity building of Micro and Small 
Enterprises (MSEs) and their collectives in the country. A cluster is a group of enterprises located 
within an identifiable and as far as practicable, contiguous ar ea or a value chain that goes beyond a 
geographical area and producing same/similar products/complementary products/services, which 
can be linked together by common physical infrastructure facilities that help address their common 
challenges.  
106. The mai n objective is to support the sustainability and growth of MSEs by addressing 
common issues such as improvement of technology, skills & quality, market access etc.; to build 
capacity of MSEs for common supportive action through formation of self help group s, consortia, 
upgradation of associations etc.; to create/upgrade infrastructural facilities in the new/existing 
Industrial Areas/Clusters of MSEs; to set up Common Facility Centres (for testing, training, raw 
material depot, effluent treatment, complement ing production processes, etc); and promotion of 
green & sustainable manufacturing technology for the clusters so as to enable units switch to 
sustainable and green production processes and products. 
107. The scheme supports financial assistance for establishment of common facility centres 
(CFCs) and to create/upgrade infrastructural facilities (IDs) in the new/existing industrial 
areas/clusters of MSEs. As far as the government grant is concerned CFCs, it is restricted to 70% of 
the cost of Project o f maximum Rs. 20.00 crore.  However, the grant will be 90% for CFCs in 
North-East & Hilly States, Island territories; Aspirational Districts/LWE affected Districts; Clusters 
with more than 50% micro/ village, women owned, and SC/ST units. 
108. Further, the Ministry informed that u nder the MSE-CDP, 1421 potential clusters have been 
identified by field establishments of Office of DC (MSME) namely MSME - Development 
Institutes, across the country. The project proposals along with the Detailed Project Reports (D PRs) 
are required to be forwarded by respective State Governments in respect of these identified clusters 
to office of DC (MSME). Ministry of MSME would accord necessary approvals for the submitted 
proposals and provide financial assistance for setting up of Common Facility Centres (CFCs) under 
the MSE -CDP subject to availability of budgetary provision. The Steering Committee under the 

30 
 
Chairmanship of Secretary, MSME is the Apex Body to sanction and monitor progress of MSE -
CDP. 
109. The Committee is of the view that Micro & Small Enterprises - Cluster Development 
Programme is quite important for the growth and development of Micro and Small 
Enterprises in the country for employment generation and economic development. The 
Scheme, therefore, should never ever  suffer due to paucity of funds. The Committee 
recommends that more budgetary provisions should be made under the scheme so that its 
objectives are achieved. Further, for development of Clusters, state governments should be 
sensitized for timely clearance of procedural matters so that target is achieved.

mandated that every Central Ministry/Department/PSU shall set an annual goal for procurement 
from the MSE sector at the beginning of the year, with the objective of achi eving an overall 
procurement goal of minimum 25 per cent of the total annual purchases from the products or 
services produced or rendered by MSEs, with sub-targets of 4 per cent for SC/ST-owned MSEs, and 
3 per cent for women -owned MSEs. The SAMBANDH portal  shows the procurement from the 
MSEs by the CPSEs as per the PPP-MSE Order, 2012 provisions.  
141. Further, it was informed by the Ministry that there is provision of Tender sets free of cost 
and exemption from payment of earnest money to registered MSEs. MSEs quoting price within 
price band L -1 + 15%, when L1 is from someone other than MSE, shall be allowed to supply at 
least 25% of tendered value at L -1 subject to lowering of price by MSEs to L -1. 358 items are 
reserved for exclusive procurement from MSEs . For enhancing participation of MSEs in 
government procurement, Ministry/Department/CPSUs shall conduct Vendor Development 
Programmes or Buyer Seller Meets for MSEs especially for SC/ST entrepreneurs. 
142. On the effectiveness of the MSME “SAMBANDH PORTAL” in monitoring the settlement 
of payments to MSEs under the Public Procurement Policy, the Ministry of MSME apprised that 
SAMADHAAN PORTAL was launched on 30 th October, 2017 to enable Micro & Small 
Enterprises (MSEs) across the country to directly register their cases online on the portal relating to 
delayed payments by Central Ministries/Departments/CPSEs/State Government etc. The 
information about the pending payments from Central Ministries/Departments/CP SEs/State 

38 
 
Government etc., and other buyers are available in public domain and can be viewed by the MSEs 
or any member of the public.  Further, it was informed that since inception till date , around 8028 
disputes have been registered and out of that 459 di sputes have been disposed off through the 
portal. 
143. In a visit of the Committee  to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in January, 2020 , it 
came to the notice that although the CPSEs have made payments to the MSEs but still the 
portal showed pendency against the concerned CPSEs due to lack of updation of information 
on the Portal . The Committee recommends that a proper monitoring mechanism should be 
put in place to check such type of information on the SAMADHAAN portal and data about 
the payments made should be regularly updated and errors must be rectified immediately. 
144. The Committee also observes that the procurements by the CPSEs from the SC/ST and 
Women entrepreneurs, as mandated under the Public Procurement Policy, are much below 
than the sub-quota of 4% and 3% respectively. Even many of the CPSEs have not organized 
Vendor Development Programmes (VDPs) to sensitize the SC/ST entrepreneurs. The 
Committee recommends that sufficient number of VDPs be organized along with buyer -seller 
meets for the benefit of SC/ST and Women entrepreneurs. 
145. Since delayed payments to MSEs have been a longstanding issue, the  Committee also 
recommends that more MSEFC should be constituted in all the states to resolve the problem 
of delayed payments expeditiously. Besides, the MSEs should be made aware of the benefits of 
the newly introduced TReDS Platform, wherein bills are paid on a fast track basis. 
146. The Committee is of the view that the Government Purchase scheme may be amended 
so as to reduce the PBG/secur ity deposit requirement to 10% for Micro Enterprises, 20% for 
Small Enterprises and 30% for Medium Enterprises compared to the PBG required from 
non-MSMEs. It is also suggested that Medium Industry should also be granted the 
preferential procurement facility and to pay 25% of the EMD/Bid Bond & tender charges as 
specified in the tenders. Besides, priority sector lending target for micro enterprises from 
current 7.5% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit may be enhanced to at least 12%.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE – AT A GLANCE 
1. The present classification of MSMEs based on investment in plant and machinery has 
been effective since the adoption of the MSMED Act, 2006.  However, the extant financial 
limits fixed in 2006 for MSMEs are no longer relevant given the impact of inflation.  Mo st of 
the Industry Associations and stakeholders have, therefore, expressed the need for changing 
the present criteria of investment in plant and machinery to annual turnover as criterion for 
classification of MSMEs. 
 (Para 8) 
 
2.  The Committee is of the view that the present classification based on investment in 
plant and machinery also has a number of disadvantages as it prevents MSMEs to become 
competitive in the market, inhibits investment to modernize, upscale, improve productivity 
and technology upgradation due to rigor of investment thresholds. On the other hand, taking 
turnover as a criteria shall overcome the said shortcomings as it can be pegged with reliable 
data available in GST Network and other methods of ascertaining, which will help in having a 
non-discretionary, transparent and objective criteria and will eliminate the need for 
inspections and make the classification system progressive and evolutionary. 
(Para 9) 
 
3. It is observed by the Committee that the growth of MSMEs is concentrated mos tly in a 
few States only, which induces the people to migrate to those areas in search of employment 
and livelihood. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should work in the 
direction of removing all the existing geographical imbalances and  ensuring that equitable 
presence of MSMEs is there in all the States so that there is industrialization and employment 
generation in all the States. 
(Para 10) 
 
4.  The Committee was informed by the representatives of MSME Associations that 
many of the MSMEs were unable to meet the fixed deadline of 90 days in repaying their loan 
installments, due to the unique system of their working cycle, which is much longer, due to 
their inability to meet the stipulated timeline for repayment, the MSME units are declar ed 
NPAs. To avoid such difficulties being faced by MSMEs, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry should endeavor to see to it that time limit for declaring a MSME as NPA due to 
non-payment of loan amount should be enhanced from the current 90 days to 180 days. 
(Para 22) 
 
5.  The Committee welcomes the Government’s goal of making India a $5 trillion 
economy by 2024 -25. The Committee is however of the considered view that the target of 
becoming $5 trillion economy by 2024 can be achieved by exponential growth of MSME 
Sector. Thi s sector has the capacity of building up at a low cost and utilizing the modern 
innovative technology can be made commercially productive at lower cost. This sector has 
also the capacity to generate employment and multiplication of production is far easy than the 
big industries.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that Government need to play a 
proactive and constructive role in promoting MSME S ector. More than ease of doing 
business, there is need of creating ease of running business. More information dis semination 

50 
 
regarding the export requirements should be taken care of. Financial institutions should be 
proactive, friendly and forthcoming. Government regulators should do handholding and play 
the role of mentors. Besides, change in the attitude of the Gov ernment regulators will 
immensely help the MSME S ector. Together with the industry, skilled manpower and the 
support of government authorities, the desired target can be achieved.   
(Para 25) 
6. Artificial Intelligence is a rapidly emerging concept in the market across the globe , 
which has great potential for enterprises. Most of the entrepreneurs are making use of this 
concept for their benefit and to increase their outreach.  The Committee recommends that 
Ministry of MSME should also explore th e concept of AI for strengthening and betterment of 
MSME Sector in the country.     
(Para 26) 
 
7. Market Intelligence plays a crucial role in strengthening and improving the enterprises. A 
dedicated market intelligence cell is very essential to gather information abou t latest trends, taste 
and other aspects of the market. It is imperative to keep an eye on International markets and 
MSMEs of developed countries for knowledge of latest technology and developments and to adopt 
good practices prevailing in the developed ma rkets across the globe for benefit of indigenous 
MSMEs. The Committee, therefore, recommends  that a Market Intelligence Cell for MSMEs 
should be set up that would regularly map specific markets, foreign as well as domestic, for 
meeting the requirement of s pecific MSME clusters and accordingly provide information and 
training to them about consumer preferences, product specifications, technological 
developments and trade agreements. 
(Para 27) 
 
8. Taking into consideration the views expressed by some of MSME Associations during 
the course of examination of DFG (2020 -21), the Committee also perceives that a lot of 
reforms on the Tax front too need to be taken to promote and encourage the MSMEs. The 
Committee accordingly, is of the view that tax rates for propri ety and partnership firms 
should be reduced from 30% to at least 22% on the lines of reduction in Corporate Tax. 
Likewise, exemption and relief under Capital Gain should be accorded to MSMEs for 
investment in expansion of the existing MSME or for fulfillin g their working capital 
requirements. The Committee accordingly desires that Ministry of MSME may take up these 
issues with the Ministry of Finance and apprise the Committee of the outcome thereof. 
(Para 28) 
9. The Committee recommends that MSMEs should be  allowed to have only one unified 
GST registration , which is applicable in all states. With respect to the sharing of Taxes 
between Central and State Governments, it should be done at the back end as the 
Government already has all the information in this regard. 
(Para 29) 
 
10. The Committee recommends that multiple registrations with multiple government 
agencies for various purposes should be done away with for MSMEs. Inter -Ministries 
coordination should be improved to bring out one registration to carry ou t all business 

51 
 
activities including exports, tax and day -to-day business activities to improve ease of doing 
business for MSMEs. 
(Para 30) 
 
11. The Committee recommends that Ministry should play a proactive role in promoting 
MSMEs abroad and the foreign entrepreneurs should have profiles of Indian MSMEs so that 
they could promote them at appropriate level amongst companies of their respective country. 
There should be an exclusive ‘Export Facilitation Centre’ for MSMEs in PPP mode in each 
State to promote exports of products and services from MSME sector. 
(Para 31) 
 
 12. The Committee observes that there have been instances of inadequate credit 
disbursement by banks to MSMEs vis-à-vis large industries whereas the case should have 
been opposite. In Economic Survey 2018 -19, it has been stated that MSME sector has vast 
potential and it should be nurtured fully to convert dwarfs into the giants. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance and 
RBI to ensure that there is no inadequacy of funds to MSMEs. 
(Para 32) 
 
13.  The Committee notes that the constraints faced by KVIC/KVIB are mainly due to 
procedural delays, inadequate technology up-gradation, under utilization of funds etc. Despite 
providing technical guidance to the units in KVI, the problems of the units remain 
inadequately addressed as a result there is sub optimal functioning of institutions/units and 
high drop outs among new entrants and low employment generation.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that KVIC, in view of the expansion of its area of operation in every 
nook and corner of the country, should come forward with a more holistic and unified policy 
in co-ordination with all the stakeholders. Proper planning, monitoring and implementation 
in each scheme are required to meet the primary objective of employment generation.  
(Para 37) 
14. The Committee feels that in face of stiff competition in the market from organized 
industries, KVIs should concentrate more on adoption of newer technology a nd upgradation of 
existing technology for products upgradation.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that 
regular training by efficient staff having experience and expertise should be imparted to the 
artisans through its network of training institutions.   
(Para 38) 
15. The Committee was apprised about the availability of Khadi Fabrics in private retail 
stores at competitive price.  The Committee observes that opening up of Khadi retailing to 
private players is a good initiative in this regard for enhancing  and expanding the market of 
Khadi fabrics among the customers. Further, the recent innovative step to bring in fashion 
designers of repute to design Khadi fabrics is a welcome move and it needs to be continued by 
bringing in more such steps.  The Committee , therefore, recommends that good market 
techniques like frequent awareness campaigns among the youth and introduction of Khadi in 

52 
 
Schools, Hospitals, Railways and other Government Organizations could be good recourse , 
which will surely increase the demand  for Khadi products. Besides, premier showrooms 
known as Khadi Lounge should be opened in all the State capitals and Airports to market 
designer Khadi products and attract the younger generations towards Khadi products. In this 
direction opening up of Designer Houses in each state capitals would be a welcome step. 
 
(Para 39) 
 
16.  The Committee observes that the rural as well as urban youths are not  inclined to work in 
KVI sector due to low wages and the hardships involved in it.  Therefore, the Committee is of the 
view that the economic empowerment of the poor artisans can be enhanced by allowing the 
potential spinners and weavers to work with the private designers of national and 
international reputation without the approval of K VIC so that they could earn more wages 
from them directly. Further, the issue of low wages of unskilled and semi -skilled artisans 
needs to be addressed properly so that more willing workers will bring in more quality output 
in Khadi sector. 
(Para 40) 
 
17. It was observed by the Committee that opportunities of export of products of Khadi and 
Village Industries are not yet exploited optimally and the government has to lay emphasis upon the 
exports of KVI products . The Committee recommends that ample facilitat ion, incentives, less 
compliances, easy and cheaper funds etc. should be adopted by the Government to encourage 
KVIs/MSMEs to go for exports. Besides, seminars and workshops in clusters should be 
organized to educate KVIs/MSMEs about opportunities of their  products in global market 
and benefits of exports. Besides an e-portal can be designed where the MSME exporters can 
post their applications for clearance or for export facilitation like stuffing/de -stuffing and the 
exporter should also post the date when the actual work will be undertaken. 
(Para 41) 
 
18. The Committee is of the view that because of complicated pattern of project reports, 
PMEGP could not be implemented successfully. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the long-drawn process of selection of beneficiaries and banks should be further reduced and 
evaluation of Entrepreneur Development training programme before issue of certificate and 
cost reducing process should be adopted. 
(Para 51) 
 
19. The Committee observes that only half of the targeted projects set up by KVIC have 
been approved/disbursed by the Banks , which does not portray a rosy scenario.  The 
Committee desires that the Ministry may step in to resolve the problems in consultation with 
KVIC and financial institutions so that targets set forth are achieved. 
 
(Para 52) 
 

53 
 
20. The Committee observes that P MEGP mainly focuses on generating self -employment 
opportunities through Micro enterprises in the non -farm sector by helping unemployed youth 
and traditional artisans. However, there are a few hiccups in the guidelines such as minimum 
educational qualifications, negative list etc. that hampers the efficacy of the programme. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should look into the matter and revise 
the negative list in order to bring in more new industries/projects like floriculture etc. un der 
the ambit of PMEGP to make it more employment oriented. 
(Para 53) 
 
21.  In its recent study visit to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in January, 2020 , the 
Committee was apprised that subsidies under the PMEGP are not claimed by the l ending 
institutions/banks from the KVIC timely as a result of which the Micro enterprises face 
financial crunch and shortage of working capital. The Committee , therefore, recommends 
that necessary steps should be taken in this regard so that the subsidy mon ey is 
claimed/released timely by the Banks to the beneficiaries. 
(Para 54) 
 
22. The Committee observes that the actual ISEC issued and funds released by Banks is 
not very encouraging and creates gap in working capital requirement and actual fund 
availability as a result of which the KIs fails to achieve the desired level performance.  It also 
feels that norms for turnover formula on one working cycle differs both at KVIC and Bank 
level, which appears to be one of the lacuna s for the gap existing between ISE C issued and 
Bank finance, which needs to be addressed at the appropriate level.   
(Para 59) 
23. The Committee observes that the number of ISEC issued under Khadi and Polyvastra is almost 
negligible in North Eastern Region except in Assam and Manipur. The Committee desires that 
appropriate steps should be taken to address the issue. 
(Para 60) 
 
24.  The KVIC, as a social security measure to artisans engaged in the Khadi activity, 
introduced the Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyothi Bima Yojana  (PMJJBY)/Pradhan Mantri  
Suraksha Bima Yojana  (PMSBY) and Modified Aam Admi Bima Yojana (AABY) Schemes for 
the Khadi artisans, mostly workers. The Committee , however, observes that less number of 
artisans are covered and the benefits provided under these schemes are very meager. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that more artisans should be covered under these schemes 
and the monetary benefits may be revised for the benefit of Khadi artisans. Awareness 
generation programmes may also be organized in rural areas regarding the ben efits of 
insurance schemes among Khadi artisans. 
(Para 63) 
 
25. The SFURTI Scheme , which was introduced with an objective to encourage 
Traditional Industries and Artisan clusters of the country, is about to complete 10 years of 
operation and  by now every d istrict of the country should  have had at least one project. 

54 
 
However, the Committee notes with dismay  that the scheme could not make its presence felt 
even in 10 per cent districts of the country. The Ministry of MSME as well as KVIC and Coir 
Board appear to have not made much headway  on this front. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry should come out with the specific targets so that each district of the country 
will have at least one SFURTI project. 
(Para 73) 
 
26. The Committee is of the view that the Mission Solar Charkha has huge potential to 
provide employment to a large number of potential professionals like stitchers, weavers, 
tailors and other skilled artisans in rural areas along with generation of Green ener gy for 
controlling pollution in the country. Also, the Scheme further aims to provide employment to 
youths including at least 50 women artisans, will go in long way to boost rural economy. 
Moreover, Solar Charkha Mission is proposed to be set up with a corpus of Rs. 951.43 crores 
to set up 500 exclusive solar charka based clusters (250 during 2018 -19 and 250 during 2019 -
20) by the end of 2020 . The Committee, therefore, recommends that setting up of more solar 
charkha clusters under the Mission Solar Charkha  should be given priority in areas of high 
solar insolation across the country. Besides, the Committee also recommends that the 
Ministry should provide timely interventions so that the Solar Charkha Clusters so set up are 
operationalized in an expeditious manner. 
(Para 79) 
 
27. Since ancient times, honey has been used as both a food and medicine. It is very high in 
beneficial compounds and offers several health benefits. In order to popularize use of honey, 
the Committee recommends that, like sugar pouches, initiatives should be taken to encourage 
production of honey pouches for ready consumption especi ally in organizations like Indian 
Railways, Air India, Hospitals , Hotels and other organizations in view of its health benefits. 
Besides, production of honey pouches would encourage the Village Industries artisans and 
generate employment in the urban areas under the Honey Bee Mission in the country. 
(Para 82) 
 
28. During the last couple of years, the Village Industries have witnessed a growth 
parameter in respect of production, sales and employment generation due to various strategic 
initiatives undertaken by the KVIC/Ministry of MSME. However, there remains much more 
to be done in this regard. The Committee is of the view that concentration of pottery fam ilies 
may be identified in the States and training to them may be imparted in modern techniques of 
pottery for employment generation and creation of market linkages through Village 
Industries even in the remotest of locations in the country with the support of state 
governments. Besides, cheap loan facility  may be provided for expanding business using 
technology so that they can sustain because the art of pottery is also on the verge of extinction. 
Moreover, now there is a rising demand for pottery items. 
(Para 84) 

55 
 
29.  The Committee notes that  organizations like Coir Board are providing training on 
various aspects of production and development of new/innovative products.  One of the most 
important objectives of the implementation of various Schemes under Coir Board is the 
employment generation , especially in rural areas. The Committee , therefore, recommends 
that Ministry of MSME should give a consideration for recognition of such training 
courses/training institutions so that younger generation will be attracted to such training for 
gainful employment. 
(Para 101) 
 
30. Deforestation is one of the major threats for the maintenance of ecological balance. 
The Committee, in order to avoid grave threats , which are endangering the climatic 
conditions and human life, recommends that the production of subs titutes for wood, such as 
coir wood, has to be encouraged and more coir clusters under SFURTI have to be established 
to meet the demands of coir -based furnishings and building materials from the domestic as 
well as international market. To achieve this, mo re funds should be allocated by the Ministry 
of MSME to the Coir Board. 
(Para 102) 
 
31. The Committee is of the firm opinion that in order to have a better co -ordination for 
export promotion of coir and its by -products for aiding in multifarious activities  such as soil 
erosion control, landscaping, river embankment etc., tie ups with Indian Missions abroad may 
be explored. 
(Para 103) 
 
32. The Committee is aware that, there are various schemes implemented by the 
Government under which technology developed is transferred to the beneficiaries without any 
charges. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the technology developed by the Coir 
Board should be transferred to entrepreneurs, traders, clusters etc. free of cost to encourage 
potential entrepreneurs to get into the coir sector business.  Besides, steps should also be taken 
to explore the potential overseas markets for export of coir products particularly innovative 
coir products. The Committee is also of the opinion that Buyer -Seller meets and Vendor 
Development Programmes may be organized overseas to popularize Indian coir products and 
to tap the virgin overseas markets. 
 
(Para 104) 
33. The Committee is of the view that Micro & Small Enterprises - Cluster Development 
Programme is quite important for the growth and development of Micro and Small 
Enterprises in the country for emp loyment generation and economic development. The 
Scheme, therefore, should never ever  suffer due to paucity of funds. The Committee 
recommends that more budgetary provisions should be made under the scheme so that its 
objectives are achieved. Further, for development of Clusters, state governments should be 
sensitized for timely clearance of procedural matters so that target is achieved. 
(Para 109) 
 

56 
 
34. For a successful business, a successful  marketing strategy  from market research is required for 
making profit and achieving the overall objectives of the organization  in the present scenario. However, 
the Committee observes that the budgetary allocations made under the Marketing Promotion Scheme 
for the FY 2020 -21 is Rs. 103.63 crores , which is less than what  was allocated for the previous year. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that more funds be allocated for the purpose at the Revised 
Estimates stage so that marketing promotion aspect does not suffer due to lack of funds.  
  
(Para 113) 
 
35. Today‟s age is the age of Science & Technology.  Science & Technology has become an 
integral part of our life and life without it is unimaginable now.  The Committee recommends that 
with changing time and scenario, the Science & Technology aspect should be focused upon  
more in order to benefit the Khadi and Village Industries Sector.  The Ministry may ensure 
that suitable technology and research being practiced in the other developed MSME Sector s 
across the world be incorporated suitably for indigenous MSMEs. 
(Para 115) 
 
36. The Committee recommends that Ministry must encourage MSMEs for innovation 
and R&D, provide adequate institutional support for encouraging innovation, provide special 
support, both technical & financial, to innovators to set up enterprises for scient ific & 
technological R&D  purposes to make indigenous MSMEs more competitive in the world 
market vis-a-vis MSMEs of the developed countries. The Ministry must also ensure that 
budgetary allocations are fully utilized for the intended purposes. 
(Para 116) 
 
37. The Committee recommends that Ministry may tie up with different research 
organizations, both in government as well as private sector, for R&D of scientific & 
technological activities of KVIC and Coir Board. Besides, exhibitions, Seminars, Workshops, 
Awareness programmes/road shows all over India may be organized. Incubation & intensive 
training on the latest technologies developed should be imparted to the industry/beneficiaries 
free of cost or on nominal fee. The Committee desires that the Ministry may pursue with right 
earnest to put in place a network of incubators in the entire length & breadth of the country 
to enhance the competitiveness of the MSMEs. 
(Para 117) 
 
38. R&D is an important aspect of any enterprise. In developed countries, proper and 
dedicated R&D is undertaken to improve the quality of products and performance of the 
enterprises. However, for 2020-21, a meager amount of Rs. 2.00 crore has been earmarked for 
R&D purposes. The Committee recommends that more funds should be allocated for R&D 
and Technology related support facilities in order to match the quality of international 
products. 
(Para 118) 
 

57 
 
39. The Committee notes with satisfaction that an amount of R s. 973.16 crores was 
provided in 2018-19 towards subsidy claims settlement. However, the Committee recommends 
that the Ministry of MSME should strive to get sufficient allocation from the Ministry of 
Finance for clearance of subsidy claims and liquidate all pending subsidy claims. 
(Para 131) 
 
40. Presently, benefits under CLCS-TUS are extended to the beneficiaries only through 11 
Banks. The Committee recommends that more Banks should be added to the list of banks.  
Moreover, the list of 51 subsectors should  be increased in consultation with Industry 
Associations so as to bring more and more activities under CLCS-TUS. 
 
(Para 132) 
 
41.  The Committee further recommends that steps should be taken so that the MSEs 
could obtain collateral free loans from designated Banks under the CLCS -TU Scheme in the 
same lines as given under CGTMSE Scheme to encourage more and more entrepreneurs to 
avail the benefits of the scheme and upgrade their technology for quality products. 
(Para 133) 
 
42. During examination of DFG 2020 -21, the Committee was apprised of the fact that 
partial collateral had been introduced under CGTMSE Scheme and that a portal is likely to 
be developed by  April 2020, which would appraise loan proposal upfront, and give a rating. 
This rating would bring down the risk perception level of the lending Bank Branch Manager. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may launch the proposed Portal expeditiously 
and also apprise the Committee of the enhancement in the off -take in the Scheme, if any, post 
the launch of the Portal. 
(Para 134) 
 
43.  During its study visit to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai during January 2020, the 
Committee was informed by the MSME Asso ciations that the subsidy limit under the CLCS -TUS 
may be enhanced to 25% as provided under other Schemes under the Ministry to SC/ST 
entrepreneurs. Thus, in order to increase the participation of SC/ST/Women entrepreneurs under the 
CLCS-TU Scheme, the percentage of subsidy may be increased under the scheme. The Committee 
recommends that the subsidy amount should be raised to 25% for  SC/ST/Women 
entrepreneurs as provided under the Special Credit Linked Subsidy Schemes to attract more 
SC/ST/Women entrepreneurs for making it a meaningful scheme for these categories. 
 (Para 135) 
  
44. The Committee observes that there is constant decline in the number of beneficiaries 
benefitted in the last three years i.e. year 2016-17, 2017-18 and 2018-19 Workshed Scheme for 
Khadi Artisans. Even in the year 2018 -19, the figure is less than half of the figure that was in 
2016-17. The Committee desires to know the reason behind this decline. The Committee , 
therefore, recommends that necessary steps should be taken to construct sufficient number of 
Workshed for improving the working conditions of Khadi Artisans of the BPL Group. 
Moreover, the disbursements  for the construction of Worksheds should be made in a very 
transparent and time-bound manner. 

58 
 
(Para 139) 
 
45. In a visit of the Committee  to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in January, 2020 , it 
came to the notice that although the CPSEs have made payments to the MSEs but still the 
portal showed pendency against the concerned CPSEs  due to lack of updation of information 
on the Portal . The Committee recommends that a proper monitoring mechanism should be 
put in place to check such type of information on the SAMADHAAN portal and data about 
the payments made should be regularly updated and errors must be rectified immediately. 
(Para 143) 
 
46. The Committee also observes that the procurements by the CPSEs from the SC/ST and 
Women entrepreneurs, as mandated under the Public Procurement Policy, are much below 
than the sub-quota of 4% and 3% respectively. Even many of the CPSEs have not organized 
Vendor Development Programmes (VDPs) to sensitize the SC/ST entrepreneurs. The 
Committee recommends that sufficient number of VDPs be organized along with buyer -seller 
meets for the benefit of SC/ST and Women entrepreneurs. 
(Para 144) 
47. Since delayed payments to MSEs have been a longstanding issue, the  Committee also 
recommends that more MSEFC should be constituted in all the states to resolve the problem 
of delayed payments expeditiously. Besides, the MSEs should be made aware of the benefits of 
the newly introduced TReDS Platform, wherein bills are paid on a fast track basis. 
(Para 145) 
 
48. The Committee is of the view that the Government Purchase scheme may be amended 
so as to reduce the PBG/security deposit requirement to 10% for Micro Enterprises, 20% for 
Small Enterprises and 30% for Medium Enterprises compared to the PBG required from 
non-MSMEs. It is also suggested that Medium Industry should also be granted the 
preferential procurement facility and to pay 25% of the EMD/Bid Bond & tender charges as 
specified in the tenders. Besides, priority sector lending target for micro enterprises from 
current 7.5% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit may be enhanced to at least 12%. 
(Para 146) 
 
49. The Committee is very concerned about this under utilization of budget repeatedly. 
Also, the BE of Rs. 30.00 crore seems significantly reduced against BE of Rs. 232.00 crore in 
year 2018 -19. To consider ASPIRE an important and crucial scheme for i nnovative 
entrepreneurship in agro-industry, the Committee is , however disappointed to note that only 
an amount of Rs. 30 crore has been proposed for 2020 -21. The Committee , therefore, 
recommends that more budgetary provisions should be made for such an im portant scheme. 
Apart from, steps may be taken to restructure the Scheme to make it more attractive for 
potential entrepreneurs with proper assessment and planning to implement the scheme 
successfully and meaningfully. 
(Para 148) 
 
50. The Committee is of t he opinion that Ministry needs to improve employability of 
incubates if the schemes are to succeed. The Committee is also of the opinion that it would be 

59 
 
better if ASPIRE is closely linked up with MUDRA, Stand Up and Start Up schemes to 
provide financial a ssistance to the entrepreneurs. Further, the LBIs should tie up with S elf 
Help Groups and women organizations, ITIs and skill development institutions. 
(Para 149) 
 
51. The Committee recommends that more LBIs/TBIs should be set up by the Ministry to 
overcome the problems of unemployment, poverty, drudgery and migration , which are still 
rampant in rural areas of the country.  The Committee also recommends that Ministry of 
MSME should expedite the sanctioning and setting up of the targeted number of LBI s and 
TBIs across the country and also simplify the technical and procedural formalities , which are 
hindering the whole process. 
(Para 150) 
52. The Committee recommends that awareness camps should also be 
organized/undertaken by the Ministry in rural areas  to create awareness among rural 
population in general and among potential artisans in particular regarding these LBIs/TBIs 
and other useful schemes implemented by the Ministry. 
(Para 151) 
 
53. The Committee recommends that more technical institutes, acade mic institutes, R&D 
laboratories, Universities, both in  government as well private sectors, should be roped in set up 
new LBIs/TBIs for promotion of innovative technology based entrepreneurs in the agro -rural 
areas. 
 
(Para 153) 
 
54.  LBIs under NSIC servi ng single window system for new enterprises and has been a 
source of employment. Further, NSIC through its Incubation Centres provides training to the 
prospective entrepreneurs in the manufacturing as well as service sector for skill development 
and employment purposes. The Committee recommends that more Incubation Centres should 
be established in cooperation with State Governments so that training on conventional as well 
as  hi -tech trades are imparted to entrepreneurs for their skill development in areas of 
business operation for gainful employment. 
(Para 159) 
 
55. The Committee notes that despite hindrances , NSIC is trying hard to fulfil the 
objective to promote and facilitate small scale industries, NSIC is however facing problems 
such as uncertainty in timely availability of raw material; no allocation/preference of Raw 
Materials; no additional rebate/conce ssion; and no financial assistance being provided by the 
government to NSIC etc.  
(Para 160) 
 
56.  The Committee recommends that a robust procurement system should be evolved, 
which could ensure unhindered supply of raw materials to NSIC and monitor that a llocation 
order is released by the respective Ministries timely so that there is no scarcity of raw 

60 
 
material supply to MSME sector. The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry should 
also explore other available options for raw material supply to M SMEs instead of becoming 
solely dependant on NSIC in coordination with other concerned Ministries/Departments to 
meet the requirement of MSMEs. 
(Para 161) 
 
57. The Committee observes that under National SC/ST Hub, the Actual Expenditure has 
always been less than the BE. The Committee is concerned about the under -utilization of 
allocated funds for the marginalized communities. The Committee recommends that special 
efforts need to be made to improve the situation dili gently and the Ministry should set up a 
dedicated monitoring cell for this purpose under the supervision of  a Monitoring Committee. 
The Committee would also like to know the reasons for continuously projecting inflated 
demands and thereafter underutilizat ion of funds every year and why the SC/ST 
entrepreneurs are not able to reap the benefits of the scheme specifically designed for them.   
(Para 165) 
 
58. The Committee observes that NSIC through its Vendor Development Programme s 
sensitize and facilitate MSEs, including SC/ST  enterprises, to become qualified vendors to 
public sector enterprises and other Government Departments as per the provision of 25% 
mandatory procurement under Public Procurement Policy. Of this, 4% should be from 
SC/ST MSEs. Also, during its visit to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in January, 2020 , the 
Committee found that while the PSUs and Government procurement from MSEs has been 
gradually improving, procurement from SC/ST units is negligible. Therefore, the  Committee 
recommends that there should be more Vendor Development Programmes organized to 
popularize Public Procurement Policy among MSEs including SC/ST and Women 
entrepreneurs. 
(Para 167) 
 
59. The Committee also recommends that the Hub should create an All India Database of 
SC/ST entrepreneurs’ locations and vocations and share the same with PSEs so that PSEs can 
locate SC/ST units easily. Also, the SC/ST Hub should run NSQF compliant skill development 
programmes for SC/ST technicians who could take cont ract jobs and services that PSEs 
outsource. 
(Para 168) 
60. During 2019-20 (till December, 2019), 4548 units have availed testing services from these 
centers. However, the Committee was informed by the representatives of Associations during 
consideration of  DFG 2020 -21 that exorbitant rates are charged from MSMEs for testing 
their products for quality certification etc. which is difficult for them to pay as most of them 
face the problem of working capital shortage. The Committee , therefore, recommends that 
Testing & Certifications should be made convenient and cheaper for MSMEs. It is required 
that a mechanism/tie -up should be developed that testing can be done at Indian Centres 
whereas certificates for the same test could be issued from various global testin g centres , 
which are acceptable in respective countries/regions. Alternatively, Indian Testing 
Certificates should have global acceptance. Besides, MSMEs should be given subsidies for 
testing facilities in the country.  The Committee further recommends that  the setting up of 
Tool Rooms and Technology Centres can be explored under the Public -Private Partnership 
(PPP) model. 
(Para 170) 

61 
 
61. The under utilization of Budget Allocations and lack of performance of various 
important MSME S chemes viz. PMEGP, CLCS -TUS etc. in NER  has been a recurring 
concern for the Committee, which was communicated to the Ministry from time to time in its 
earlier Reports. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should make concerted efforts 
for industrialization in NER region, be it in the field of traditional art, craft and artisan work.   
(Para 174) 
62. The Committee observes that many schemes of the Ministry are not working 
satisfactorily in North Eastern Region and has a very negligible presence in these areas.  The 
number of ISEC issued under Khadi and Polyvastra are almost negligible except in the 
previous financial years. The Committee recommends that serious efforts should be made by 
the Government/Ministry to benefit the populace of NER through various scheme s run by 
them with the help of State Governments. Particularly potential women and SC/ST 
entrepreneurs be encouraged to participate in the growth process. 
(Para 175) 
63. The Committee notes the initiative taken by the Ministry for honoring MSMEs for 
quality production, exports, innovation, product development etc.  for the economic growth of 
the country. However, the Committee is of the view that the award distribution functions 
should be organized in and around areas where the award winning MSMEs are locate d or in 
areas where concentration of MSMEs is less like the North Eastern Region so as to generate 
awareness and to encourage the potential entrepreneurs to set up new MSMEs in those areas. 
(Para 178)

Report 
 
Government of India has leveraged Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) to achieve 
various socio-economic objectives.  The main objectives for setting up of the PSEs, as 
enumerated in the Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956 were to (i) help in the rapid 
economic growth and industrialisation of the country and create the necessary 
infrastructure for economic development; (ii) earn return on investment and thu s generate 
resources for development; (iii) promote redistribution of income and wealth; (iv)  create 
employment opportunities; (v)  promote balanced regional development;  (vi) assist in the 
development of small -scale and ancillary industries; and (vii) p romote import 
substitutions, save and earn foreign exchange for the economy.  
The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) in India 
2. The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) comprise enterprises established 
by the Government of India (GOI) as Gover nment companies under Section 617 of the 
Companies Act, and wherein the equity holding of the GOI is more than 50 per cent. It 
also includes statutory corporations constituted under specific statutes of the Parliament. 
However, the CPSEs do not, include de partmental undertakings, banking institutions and 
enterprises where equity holding of the GOI is 50% or less. 
3. Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) play an important role in the process of 
nation building through their contributions to various aspec ts like economic growth, 
infrastructure development, healthy market competition, balanced regional development 
and price stabilization etc besides fulfilling social objectives.  
4. There were only 5 CPSEs with a total investment of merely 29 crore at the time of 
1st Five Year Plan.  As per the Public Enterprises Survey (2018 -19),  the number of 
CPSEs has increased to 348 with a total investment of Rs. 16,40,628 crore as on 
31.03.2019.  Out of this 348 CPSEs,  249 were operational CPSEs,86 under construction  
and 13 were under closure or liquidation. Out of 249 operational CPSEs, 178 are profit 
making, 70 incurred losses and 1 CPSE(Food Corporation of India) registered no 
profit/no loss. As on 31.3.2019 the overall networth of all CPSEs was Rs 12.09 lakhs 
crores. The overall net profit of operating CPSEs was Rs 1.43 lakh crores during       
2018-19. CPSEs are functioning under various Ministries/Departments and decision with 
regard to major investments, expansion, diversification, joint ventures, modernisation,  
technology upgradation, etc. are taken by the CPSEs in consultation with their respective 
administrative Ministries/Departments. 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE).  
 5. In their 52 nd Report, the Estimates Committee of 3 rd Lok Sabha (1962-67) stressed 
the need for setting up a centralized c oordinating unit, which could also make continuous 
appraisal of the performance of public enterprises. This led to the setting up of the Bureau 
of Public Enterprises (BPE) in 1965 in the Ministry of Finance. Subsequently, as a result of 
the reorganization of the Ministries/Departments of the Union Government in September, 
1985, BPE was made part of the Ministry of Industry. In May, 1990, BPE was made a full -
fledged Department known as the DPE.  Presently, it is part o f the Ministry of Heavy 
Industries & Public Enterprises (Mo HI &PE). 
1 

6. The DPE is the nodal department for all the CPSEs and formulates policy pertaining 
to them. It lays down, in particular, policy guidelines on performance improvement and 
evaluation, autonomy and financial delegation and personnel management in CPSEs. It 
further, collects and maintains information in the form of a Public Enterprises Survey on 
several areas in respect of CPSEs.  
 7. In fulfilling its role, the Department c oordinates with other Ministries, CPSEs and 
concerned organizations. As per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government, the 
following subjects have been allocated to the DPE: 
 Residual work relating to erstwhile Bureau of Public Enterprises including 
Industrial Management Pool. 
 Coordination of matters of general policy affecting all Public -Sector 
Enterprises. 
 Evaluation and monitoring the performance of Public Sector Enterprises, 
including the Memorandum of Understanding mechanism. 
 Matters relating to Permanent Machinery of Arbitration for the Public-Sector 
Enterprises. 
 Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central Public 
Sector Undertakings under Voluntary Retirement Scheme. 
 Review of capital projects and expenditure in Central Public Sector 
Enterprises. 
 Measures aimed at improving performance of Central Public Sector 
Enterprises and other capacity building initiatives of Public Sector Enterprises. 
 Rendering advice relating to revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector 
Enterprises including the mechanisms therefore. 
 Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises. 
 Matters relating to International Center for Public Enterprises. 
 Categorization of Central Public Sector Enterprises including conferring 
‘Ratna’ status. 
 Survey of Public Enterprises. 
8. According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public 
Enterprises the Vision and Mission statements of DPE  are as follows: 
 Vision 
“Effective, Profitable and Globally Competitive Central Public Sector 
Enterprises” 
 Mission 
“To continuously improve management and performance of CPSEs through 
Corporate Governance, performance Evaluation, Human Resource Management, 
Research & Development so as to enhance their global competitiveness” 
 
2 

9. As a part of examinatio n of DFG, the Committee enquired from the Department of 
Public  Enterprises as  to  how  effectively  and through  adoption  of what mechanism does 
DPE as a nodal Department perform its role to achieve its Vision and Mission, apart from 
citing the fact tha t onus for enhancing global competitiveness of CPSEs vests primarily 
with the Administrative Ministry concerned. 
10. DPE clarified that it is primarily a policy formulation Department dealing with 
matters of general policy affecting all CPSEs. In complianc e of its mandate, DPE has 
formulated guidelines on important issues such as (i) performance improvement of CPSEs 
through MoU system, (ii) delegation of powers to CPSEs under ‘Ratna Scheme’ (iii) 
performance appraisal of top management incumbents of CPSEs, (iv) revival, restructuring 
or closure of PSEs, (v) counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees of CPSEs 
under VRS /VSS, (vi) Categorization of CPSEs, (vii) Corporate Governance for CPSEs, 
(viii) time bound closure of sick/loss making CPSEs and di sposal of assets, etc. DPE has 
also taken measures for capacity building of employees of CPSEs through organization of 
regular training programmes in the areas of corporate governance, Companies A ct 
provisions, Ind -As standard, Financial management, Contra ct management CSR etc. in 
association with IIMs, IICA, ICAI, ICSI etc.  
 
11. In order to expand their global operations, the Boards of Maharatna and Navratna 
CPSEs have been empowered to incur capital expenditure without any financial limits, 
make equity I nvestment in JVs/subsidiaries and acquisition of raw material assets abroad 
through merger and acquisition subject to prescribed limits, and enter into Technical 
JV/Strategic Alliances. CPSEs have also been encouraged to formulate action plans in the 
areas of enhancing their global outreach, minimizing the import bill, collaborative research 
with other CPSEs or similar agencies and benchmarking of efficiency/productivity related 
parameters and align their MoU targets with such action plans.  
12. In response  to a query regarding the steps taken by DPE under ‘Research & 
Development’ to formulate policy guidelines which are in tune with the rapid changes 
faced by CPSEs so as to improve their management and performance,  DPE, in the 
written submission informed the Committee that it has not issued any guidelines on the 
subject matter of ‘Research & Development’. However under the DPE plan scheme of 
RDC, DPE has been organizing orientation courses/workshop/ training programme in 
association with reputed Government institutions for capacity building of senior 
management and executives of CPSEs. Further, with a view to promote R&D in CPSEs 
in the MoU system, during target setting of CPSEs, result oriented parameters are given 
for Research & Development (R & D) on the recommendations of Administrative 
Ministries/ Departments. 
13. The Committee is aware that CPSEs in India are undergoing rapid changes 
and have to contribute towards the twin objective of economic development and social 
cause, within the rules and guidelin es framed by Government of India.  CPSEs are 
also expected to remain competitive and generate profit i n a highly globalised and 
market environment.  Under such circumstances, it is very challenging for CPSEs to 
show impressive performances.  The Committee is also aware of the fact that all 
CPSEs give utmost importance to critical performance indicators including R&D, 
technology upgradation etc. in order to improve their performance.  
 3 

The Committee also observes that as the Nodal Department for all CPSEs,  
DPE has been entrusted with a huge responsibility to fulfill.  The Committee , 
therefore, recommends that the guidelines be ing framed by the DPE should be in  
unison with the rapid changes the CPSEs are going through.  Further , the guidelines 
should enable CPSEs to stand on their own and prove their worth in the expanding 
globalised and market economy.  The Committee  further recommends that DPE 
being the formulator of general policy guidelines affecting CPSEs should have a full 
fledged the R&D wing of its ow n to aide and advise the CPSEs to achieve the desired 
goal as explained above. 
14. The information submitted by DPE regarding categorization and autonomy of 
CPSEs is as under:-   
Categorization of CPSEs 
15. CPSEs are categorized into four schedules namely ‘A’, ‘B’, ‘C’ & ‘D’ based 
on criteria such as quantitative factors like investment, capital employed, net sales, 
profit before tax, number of employees and units, capacity addition, revenue per 
employee, sales/capital employed, capacity utilization, value added per employee 
and qualitative factors such as national importance, complexities of problems being 
faced by the company, level of technology, prospects for expansion and 
diversification of activities and competition from other sectors, etc. 
 
Parameters for categorisation of CPSEs 
 
Quantitative Parameters Investment, Capital employed, Net sales, Profit before Tax, 
Number of employees and units, Capacity Addition, 
Revenue per employee, Sales/Capital Employed, Capacity 
utilization, Value added per employee 
 
Qualitative Parameters  National importance, Complexities of problems faced by 
them, Level of technology, Prospects for expansion and 
diversification of activities, Competition from other sectors 
 
Other Factors Critical strategic importance, Share pric e, MOU ratings, 
ISO certification, Maharatna/Navratna/ Miniratna status  
 
16. The categorization of CPSE s has implications on grant of Ratna status, pay 
scales of chief executives and full time functional Directors of CPSEs, number of 
levels allowed for b elow board level posts, etc . As on 31.3.2019, there are 65 
Schedule ‘A’, 66 Schedule ‘B’, 44 Schedule ‘C’ and 5 Schedule ‘D’ CPSEs, as 
given in Annexure-I. 
 
 
 
4 

Autonomy of CPSEs: 
 
17. The endeavour of the Government is to make Central Public Sector 
Enterprises (CPSEs) autonomous board managed companies. Government has 
granted enhanced powers to the Boards of the profit making enterprises under 
various schemes like Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna by delegating powers in 
the areas of (i) capital expenditure, (ii) investment in joint ventures/subsidiaries, (iii) 
mergers & acquisitions, (iv) human resources management, etc. Presently there are 
8Maharatna CPSEs, 16 Navratna CPSEs and 73 Miniratna CPSEs.  
18. Criteria for the grant of Maharatna, Navratna and Min iratna Status to CPSEs 
are as follows:- 
For Maharatna 
• Listed Navratna CPSE 
• Average Annual turnover of more than Rs. 25,000 crore for last 3 years 
• Average net worth of more than 15,000 crore for last 3 years 
• Average net profit of more than Rs. 5,000 crore for last 3 years. 
• Significant global / international operations. 
For Navratna 
• Miniratna category- I, Schedule ‘A’
