The committee observes that one of the main objectives  for setting up of PSEs was to 
create employment opportunities in the country.  However, the macro -view of the 249 
operating CPSEs for the last 3 years show  gradual  decline in number of regular 
employees. A s per the information furnished by DPE as part of  examination of 
Demands for Grants 2020 -21, there is a reduction of 55,560 employees from 2017 -18 
to 2018-19.   
 However, as per the Public Enterprises Survey 2018 -19 brought out by DPE, 
CPSEs across Sectors provided employment to 15,14,064 people as on 31 .03.2019, 
including casual workers and contract workers, as against 15,54,967 as on 31.03.2018.  
As per the Survey , there is a reduction of 40,903 employees (2.63%) in total no. of 
people employed by CPSEs including casual and contract employees.  
 The Committee notes that there is a mismatch in the figures regarding number 
of employees in CPSEs  as shown in the written submission made by DPE before the 
committee and the Public Enterprises Survey 2018-19.However,it is a fact that there is 
a gradual decline i n number of regular employees in CPSEs.   The Committee 
therefore recommends that CPSEs should be encouraged to fulfil their Social 
Objective and provide more permanent employment to people, instead of engaging 
personnel on casual and contract basis.  
 The Committee also observed during the course of examining the Demands for 
Grants that a number of PSUs, even the profit making Maharatnas fail to fill up 
vacancies of personnel and many a time, such vacancies are filled by hiring of 
superannuated employees on contractual basis, to fill up the vacancies, which is not a  
6 

healthy trend.  The Committee recommends that DPE should take steps to encourage 
CPSEs and Ministries concerned to desist from this practice and employ young minds 
in the vacancies, on regular  basis, so that CPSEs can gain from the new concepts and 
interests evinced by such young minds and become globally competitive.

Scheme of Research, Development and Consultancies (RDC) on Generic issues 
related to Public Sector Enterprises  
 
29. The Scheme of RDC on Generic issues of Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) was 
introduced in t he year 2007 -08 and is being implemented since 2008 -09. In view of 
instructions issued by the Ministry of Finance (MoF) with regard to rationalization of 
Schemes, the Scheme for Skill Development/Training programme to executives/employees 
of State Level Pu blic Enterprises (SLPEs)  was merged with the Scheme of RDC on 
Generic issues of Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) during the year 2016-17.  
 30. RDC scheme was modified so that activities could be spread round the year and its 
scope was expanded and diversi fied to include more activities. Some of the features of 
revised scheme are elaborated as under: 
 
(i) Thematic studies and consultancies on generic issues like corporate governance, 
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) system, professionalization, project 
management, risk management, human resource management, Corporate Social 
Responsibility (CSR) etc. related to Public Sector Enterprises are undertaken. In 
addition, benchmarking studies on selected sectors are also undertaken to enable 
enterprises to move towards  achieving those benchmarks and become nationally 
/internationally competitive. 
(ii) With objective to gain experience in many ways of learning and to keep engaged 
through learning activities s eminars, workshops, conferences, etc. on various 
generic issues are organized. After coming into force of the provisions of 
Companies Act, 2013 on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), frequent meets are 
held. 
(iii) Under RDC Scheme, MoU is very important instrument towards improving the 
performance of the CPSEs. Some modificat ions and improvements made in MoU 
mechanism since 2016 -17 include (i) proposed result oriented parameters (ii) 
Parameter included for monitoring CAPEX contracts/projects running/completed 
without time/cost overrun (iii) CAPEX parameter weightage has been increased;  
10 

and (iv) Procurement policy issued by Ministry of MSME has been given 
importance.  Efforts are being made for online system based on a single window  
concept for all MoU related matters for all stakeholders. Task force system has been 
dispensed with and now, Inter- Ministerial Committee of MoU has taken place. 
 (iv)   DPE supplements the efforts of CPSEs/ SLPEs in improving / upgrading    the skills 
of managers / executives / employees through capacity building Skill Development / 
Training Programmes for upgrading the skills and knowledge of their executives. To 
supplement the efforts of SLPEs/CPSEs, DPE conducts training programmes in 
collaboration with some of the premier management / training institutes IITs, IIMs, 
ASCI, IIPA etc. This enable s wider exposure and sharing of experience on pertinent 
issues.  
(v) The guidelines on Corporate Governance for CPSEs issued by DPE stipulate 
training to newly inducted Non Official Directors (NODs) in the business model of 
the company. Besides induction train ing by CPSEs with a view to familiarize with 
the rules and regulations, business module, risk profile etc., DPE also in 
collaboration with respective CPSEs, from time to time, organizes general short 
term training for NODs, official directors and other Dir ectors on the boards of 
CPSEs on relevant areas including model code of business ethics and conduct of the 
company. This enriches the board in suggesting the best solution for short/long term 
viability/ profitability of the enterprises. 
   (vi) The objective of International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE) 
Ljubljana, Slovenia is to promote and support enterprise development in developing 
countries in both private and public sector. ICPE is an intergovernmental 
organization. Being a founder member of ICPE, India has been taking active part in 
its activities by way of attending Council/Assembly Sessions regularly at the level 
of Secretary.

Counselling, Retraining & Redeployment (CRR) Scheme for Separated Employees of 
CPSEs. 
 
35. DPE is implementing CRR Scheme  since 2001-02, as a social safety net to pro vide 
opportunities of self/wage employment to the employees or dependents of CPSEs separated 
under Volu ntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)/ Voluntary Separation Scheme (VSS) or 
retrenched due to closure / restructuring of the enterprise s. The objectives of the Sc heme 
are as under:- 
(i) Separated employees of CPSEs to be brought into the mainstream economy and 
thereby contribute to national income. 
(ii) Reorientation of VRS/VSS optees/dependents to enable them to adjust to new 
environment and adopt new vocations. 
(iii) Skill development for VRS optees/dependents for their redeployment. 
(iv) Exposure to various industry associations, which is also a component of the CRR 
scheme, to help the trainees in product/service selection. 
(v) Awareness of various Central and St ate Government loan assistance/subsidized 
schemes.

Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) 
 
43. From the year 2016-17, the mandate of DPE had been augmented w ith the 
responsibility of CAPEX monitoring  among other things . During the examination of 
Demands for Grants, DPE informed the Committee that the following measures are being 
taken to monitor the Capital Expenditure:- 
 
(i)     Sensitization of CPSEs to leverage net-worth for CAPEX 
(ii)    For CPSEs taking CAPEX as parameter, achievement of CAPEX without              
time & cost overrun is also taken as MoU parameter for CPSEs with          
CAPEX of 100 crores or more. 
(iii)     Progress of achievement of CAPEX targets o f Rs. 500 crore and above is 
reviewed by DPE and a report is sent to PMO every month. 
 
44. The CAPEX increases productivity of PSEs thereby improving economic 
growth. CAPEX by PSEs also contribute to fixed assets creation in the economy. The 
Government has already directed Maharatna & Navratna companies to review and 
enhance their CAPEX. The Committee, therefore, desires that DPE may encourage 
CPSEs to increase their CAPEX through regular monitoring as it is also a parameter 
for MoU evaluation.  DPE may also conduct outreach programmes to sensitise CPSEs 
to leverage their networth for infusion into their CAPEX fund.    
 
 
MoU System for CPSEs 
 
45. The Government of India introduced the MoU system in the year 1986, based on 
the recommendations given by Arjun S en Gupta Committee Report (1984). The report 
recommended that the CPSEs should enter agreement with their administrative Ministries 
for five years, with progress to be reviewed annually. The MoU system was given broader 
thrust by the Governments after the announcement of the New Industrial Policy of 1991.   
 
46. DPE monitors and evaluates the profitability and efficacy of MoU signing CPSEs 
through their MoU targets & their evaluation to measure the performance of the 
management of the CPSEs on key selected parameters so as to improve the critical 
performance indicators of the organization. 
47. MoU guidelines are reviewed from time to time based on the feedback received 
from Administrative Ministries/ CPSEs and based on the changes occurred in the 
Regulations. 
 
16 

48. Some of the main points of the latest MoU Guideline issued by DPE on 17th 
January, 2019 are as under:- 
 
1. Memorandum of Understanding (MoU): MoU is a negotiated agreement and 
contract between the Administrative Ministry/ Department/ Holding CPSE i.e . 
majority shareholder and the Management of the Central Public Sector Enterprise 
(CPSE) on selected parameters having targets decided normally before the start of a 
new financial year and results evaluated after the end of the year to measure the 
performance.  For carrying out this exercise, CPSEs would provide brief  and trend 
analysis. 
 
2. Purpose of MoU :  The purpose of the MoU is to measure the performance of the 
management of the CPSEs on key selected parameters against the targets agreed 
upon so as to improve the critical performance indicators of the organisation. 
 
3. Scope: All CPSEs (Holding as well as Subsidiaries) are required to sign MoUs. The 
Apex/Holding companies will sign MoUs with their administrative Ministries/ 
Departments, while the Subsidiary  companies will sign MoUs with their respective 
Apex/ Holding companies. 
 
4. Exemption from MoU:    
4.1 High Powered Committee in its meeting held on 8 th March, 2017 had confirmed/ 
approved exemption to following CPSEs from signing of MoU:- 
i.  India Infrastructure Finance Co. Ltd., and its subsidiaries. 
4.2 Following CPSEs may be exempted from MoU system by the Inter -Ministerial 
Committee (IMC): 
i. CPSEs under liquidation where Liquidator has already been appointed. However 
administrative ministry would provide the list of  such CPSEs to DPE along -
with brief write-up. 
ii. CPSE which is not in operation or having no employees or on any other ground 
on the recommendation of administrative Ministry. 
 
5. Parameters:  CPSEs work in various sectors under different conditions.  In view of  
this, the following guidelines are laid down:- 
 
5.1 There would be uniform parameters for measuring financial performances such as 
revenue from operations, operating profit and return on investment (e.g. ratio of 
PAT/Net-worth). This would be applicable to al l CPSEs, except CPSEs which are 
dependent on government grant or performing functions of distribution of grant etc. 
e.g. Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC).  Hence, 3 
financial parameters have been prescribed for all CPSEs with total weightage of 50% 
except for CPSEs like BIRAC.   
5.2 For the remaining 50% weightage, a menu of parameters has been suggested for 
selection depending on the sector in which the CPSE is operating.  Separate Format 
has been given for Finance Sector and another Format for the remaining operating 
CPSEs. The parameters most appropriate and relevant for measuring performance 
shall be suggested by the Pre-Negotiation Committee (PNC) to the Inter-Ministerial  
 
17 

Committee (IMC).  In all the cases IMC shall take appro priate decision on the 
suggestions made by PNC. 
5.3 Chairman, IMC is authorised to modify the parameters or weightages of parameters 
in sector specific cases, if justified. 
 
5.4 For CPSEs under closure/ under construction/ under reconstruction, parameters have 
not been prescribed leaving it to the PNC to suggest the most appropriate parameters 
and targets for IMC to take decisions.  For such CPSEs, the emphasis should be to 
suggest parameters and fix targets for starting commercial operations as early as 
possible.  For CPSEs under closure, the targets would be for ensuring time bound 
closure.   
 
6. MoU Ranking:   
i. With a view to distinguish ‘excellent performance’ from ‘poor performance’, five 
different performance ratings have been fixed in the MoU, i.e., ‘Excellent’, 
‘Very Good’, ‘ Good’, ‘ Fair’ and ‘Poor’. 
ii. Apart from rating of CPSEs, MoU performance of all MoU signing CPSEs, 
there will be category -wise ranking of CPSEs (Maharatna, Navratna, 
Miniratna, others) and sector -wise ranking of CPSEs (Mining, Power, 
Petroleum, Finance, consultancy etc.) only for the purposes of acknowledging 
where they stand in their respective category/ sector.   
 
7. MoU Targets: 
i.  Targets fixed should be realistic, growth oriented and aspirational.Generally 
target for Excellent should not be low er than best achieved in last 5 years and 
Very Good should not be lower than the expected achievement of the current 
year (year immediately preceding the year for which targets are being fixed) 
unless there are specific reasons to fix lower targets and are  duly supported by 
the administrative ministry/ department. 
ii. Once MoUs are signed, any revision of targets would not be permissible. MoU 
targets are unconditional and non-provisional. 
 
8. Pre-negotiation Committee (PNC):   The role of the Pre -negotiation Commit tee 
(earlier known as Standing Committee on MoU) would be to assist IMC in 
determining the most appropriate and relevant parameters for measuring 
improvement in performance and for fixing targets.  Meetings of the Pre -negotiation 
Committee would be held in  each case b efore the meetings of IMC to look at the 
trends, discuss, negotiate and recommend MoU parameters and targets.  The 
composition of Pre -negotiation Committee would remain the same of erstwhile 
Standing Committee.  
 
9. Inter-Ministerial Committee (IM C):MoU targets would be decided by the IMC.  
There is no change in the composition of the Committee. Any change in the 
composition of the committee would be done with the approval of Cabinet Secretary. 
 
10. Time-lines for submission of MoU : The draft MoU with all documents/ Annexures 
should be submitted to administrative Ministry/ Department in respect of all CPSEs 
and their subsidiaries by 21st November of each year for the forthcoming year. The

draft MoU after the approval of administrative Ministry/ Depa rtment should be sent 
to DPE by 15 th December of each year for the forthcoming year with all 
documents/Annexures. Administrative Ministry/ Department would ensure that the 
targets are realistic, growth -oriented, aspirational and consistent with the latest 
Annual Plan, Budget and Corporate Plan of the CPSE.A copy of draft MoU may also 
be sent to IMC Members other than DPE.  Secretary, DPE is authorized to extend the 
dates.  
 
11. MoU Signing Process :MoUbased on the parameters, targets and weightage 
recommended by IMC without any deviation shall be signed between CMD/ MD of 
CPSE and Secretary of administrative Ministry/ Department in case of holding/ 
independent CPSEs and between CEO/ MD of subsidiary company and CMD/ MD 
of holding CPSE in case of subsidiary by 31 st March (i.e. before start of financial 
year in respect of which targets are fixed) or within 21 days from issue of IMC 
meeting minutes, whichever is later.  In case, deviation is detected, IMC minutes 
would prevail.  
 
12. MoU Evaluation: Evaluation of MoU of the CPSE is done after the end of the year 
on the basis of actual achievements vis -à-vis the MoU targets. CPSEs (Holding as 
well as Subsidiaries) are required to submit performance evaluation reports on the 
basis of audited accounts to Department of Public  Enterprises after approval of the 
Board of CPSE and through the administrative Ministries/Departments on or before 
30th September (in respect of immediately preceding year) or any other date 
communicated by DPE.  Figures and information in the MoU achievement which are 
not verifiable from audited accounts would be relied on the basis of certification by 
way of resolution of the Board given separately for each parameter. 
 
12.1 Pro-rata adjustment may be made in the targets in case of improvement in actual 
performance over the estimated performance in the base year informed at the time of 
target setting. 
 
12.2 If at the time of evaluation, it is observed that any CPSE may have under -pitched 
their projected performance for the year concerned to have soft targets fixed,  DPE/ 
IMC may call the CMD of such CPSE to clarify the matter for enabling the IMC to 
evaluate the performance and assign marks and rating based on justification given by 
the CMD.

Revival/Restructuring/Closure of CPSEs 
51. The Government of India has taken many steps to make the mechanism and process 
for revival/ r estructuring of CPSEs time bound, comprehensive, performance driven and 
efficient. The Government has decided to remove the multiple layers in the decision -
making process to ensure timely revival/ restructuring of CPSEs. It has been decided that 
revival/ r estructuring of sick /incipient sick CPSEs is to be merit based considering 
strategic, national and business concerns of the CPSEs. Accordingly, the Government has 
wound up BRPSE and administrative Ministries/Departments concerned are made 
responsible to m onitor sickness of CPSEs functioning under them and to take timely 
redressal measures with the approval of the competent authority. On these lines DPE first 
issued guidelines on 29 th October, 2015 and thereafter on 7 th September, 2016 for 
‘Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/ incipient sick and weak 
CPSEs: General principles and mechanism of restructuring’ to be followed by the 
administrative Ministries/ Departments. Further, DPE issued revised guidelines on 14 th 
June, 2018 rega rding ‘T ime bound closure of sick/ loss -making CPSEs and disposal of 
their movable and immovable assets’. These revised guidelines are intended to 
expeditiously complete the procedures for closure of CPSEs and lay down responsibilities 
of the concerned Min istries/Departments/CPSE etc., including the support required to be 
extended by nodal Departments/Organizations like, Ministry of Finance, NITI Aayog etc.  
The revised guidelines prescribe a matrix of timelines for step by step process to be 
completed in re spect of a CPSE under closure and about disposal of its assets.  The 
guidelines on time bound closure of sick/loss making CPSEs uniformly provide for 
payment of VRS/VSS at 2007 notional pay scale to employees of CPSEs under closure 
irrespective of the existing pay scales of the company.

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) 
62. As per the provisions on CSR in Section -135 of Compa nies Act, 2013, all 
corporates (including CPSEs) exceeding the threshold limits as specified in the Act, are 
mandated to allocate at least 2% of their average net profits (PBT) of three immediately 
preceding years to undertake CSR activities. Further, in p ursuance to the powers conferred 
in Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, CSR Rules were notified by Ministry of 
Corporate  Affairs  with effect  from 1st April, 2014.  The  Rules  issued  by Ministry  of  
26 

Corporate Affairs (MCA) provide that in case the company fails to spend 2%   of the 
average net profit of the last three financial years or any part thereof, the company shall 
provide reasons for not spending the amount in its Board’s Report made under Section 134 
of the Companies Act, 2013. List of CSR activities which are eligible to be undertaken are 
given in Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013. 
 
63. In order to ensure that the CPSEs undertake CSR activities in a focused manner, 
Department of Public Enterprises has issued guidelines on 10.12.20 18 (Annexure-IV) for 
theme-based utilization of CSR funds. The guidelines provide for 60% of annual CSR 
expenditure by a CPSE on thematic programme with preference to aspirational districts 
identified by NITI Aayog. The theme for 2018-19 was school education and healthcare and 
for 2019-20, the theme is School education, Healthcare and Nutrition.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE 
The Committee is aware that CPSEs in India are undergoing rapid changes 
and have to contribute towards the twin objective of economic development and social 
cause, within the rules and guidelines framed by Government of India.  CPSEs are 
also expected to remain competitive and generate profit i n a highly globalised and 
market environment.  Under such circumstances, it is very challenging for CPSEs to 
show impr essive performances.  The Committee is also aware of the fact that all 
CPSEs give utmost importance to critical performance indicators including R&D, 
technology upgradation etc. in order to improve their performance.  
 The Committee also observes that as t he Nodal Department for all CPSEs, 
DPE has been entrusted with a huge responsibility to fulfill.  The Committee , 
therefore, recommends that the guidelines being framed by the DPE should be  in 
unison  with the rapid changes the CPSEs are going through.  Fur ther, the guidelines 
should enable CPSEs to stand on their own and prove their worth in the expanding 
globalised and market economy.  The Committee  further recommends that DPE 
being the formulator of general policy guidelines affecting CPSEs should have a full 
fledged the R&D wing of its own to aide and advise the CPSEs to achieve the desired 
goal as explained above.

showing a decrease in growth by 3.49%.  Further most of the in dicators such as the 
paid-up Capital, Capital Employed, Networth, Investment, Reserves & Surplus total 
turnover, overall profit, Foreign Exchange Earnings etc. indicate a steady increase 
from 2016-17 to 2018-19. 
 However, indicators such as Dividend paid, regular employment in numbers, 
Market Capitalism etc. have shown a steady decline from the year 2016-17 to 2018-19.  
The committee observes that one of the main objectives for setting up of PSEs was to 
create employment opportunities in the country.  Howev er, the macro-view of the 249 
operating CPSEs for the last 3 years show  gradual  decline in number of regular 
employees. A s per the information furnished by DPE as part of examination of 
Demands for Grants 2020 -21, there is a reduction of 55,560 employees from 2017-18 
to 2018-19.   
 However, as per the Public Enterprises Survey 2018 -19 brought out by DPE, 
CPSEs across Sectors provided employment to 15,14,064 people as on 31.03.2019, 
including casual workers and contract workers, as against 15,54,967 as on 31.03.2018.  
As per the Survey , there is a reduction of 40,903 employees (2.63%) in total no. of 
people employed by CPSEs including casual and contract employees.  
 The Committee notes that there is a mismatch in the figures regarding number 
of employees in  CPSEs as shown in the written submission made by DPE before the 
committee and the Public Enterprises Survey 2018-19.However,it is a fact that there is 
29 

a gradual decline in number of regular employees in CPSEs.   The Committee 
therefore recommends that C PSEs should be encouraged to fulfil their Social 
Objective and provide more permanent employment to people, instead of engaging 
personnel on casual and contract basis.  
 The Committee also observed during the course of examining the Demands for 
Grants that  a number of PSUs, even the profit making Maharatnas fail to fill up 
vacancies of personnel and many a time, such vacancies are filled by hiring of 
superannuated employees on contractual basis, to fill up the vacancies, which is not a 
healthy trend.  The C ommittee recommends that DPE should take steps to encourage 
CPSEs and Ministries concerned to desist from this practice and employ young minds 
in the vacancies, on regular basis, so that CPSEs can gain from the new concepts and 
interests evinced by such young minds and become globally competitive.  
 
(Para 20) 
 The Committee finds that during 2018 -19, the total BE of Rs. 20.44 crore was 
increased to Rs. 21.44 crore in RE, whereas the AE stood at 21. 20 crore.  For the year 
2019-20, both BE & RE were 22.64 crore and the AE for the year till 31.1 2.2019 is Rs. 
15.96 crore. The Committee appreciates that the Department has managed almost 
100% fund utilisation of RE during 2018 -19 and 70.49% during 2019 -20 till 
31.12.2019.  The Committee hopes that the Department w ill optimally utilise the fund 
allocation in the remaining quarter of the year. 
 While examining the Head wise budgetary provisions for 2020 -21, the 
Committee observed  that the largest allocation has been made under the head 
„Secretariat Economic Services‟.  Out of the total allocated funds of 24.15 crore, 12.98 
crore has been given to this Non -Scheme head and the Scheme allocation is only 10.5 
crore.  The Committee notes that year after year, budget allocation under Non -
Scheme Head is higher than the Schem e Head.   The Committee recommends that 
allocation of funds should be more concentrated on the “Scheme Heads” which in 
fact, pertains to the flagship schemes of the DPE such as CRR and RDC and on the 
efficient running of which, the performance and result -orientation of CPSEs hinges 
on. 
 
(Para 28) 
 
 The Committee takes note with satisfaction that the objective of the RDC 
Scheme to keep senior management of CPSEs abreast of the latest developments in 
corporate governance, Corporate Social Responsibility Laws, financial matters, 
Accounting Standards, organization and management etc. is being met with the kind 
of training programmes and workshops being conducted by DPE. The Committee 
notes that utilization under RDC Scheme for 2017-18 is almost 100% & for 2018-19, it 
is 92%.  However, during 2019 -20, the actual utilization till 31.12.2019 stood at 41%.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that DPE should continue to make efforts to 
conduct more number of training programmes & workshops under RDC scheme in 
2020-21 so that the budget allocation can be used optimally. 
(Para 34) 
30 

 The Committee notes with satisfaction that there has been  the almost 100% 
utilisation of the budget allocation under CRR Scheme. The Committee is, however of 
the view that the real achieve ment of the scheme can be gauged from the number of 
VRS/VSS optees/dependants getting re -deployed after availing the skill training.   
DPE in their Annual Report has stated that during the year 2018 -19, an allocation of 
Rs. 3.96 crore (RE) was made availab le for the CRR Scheme. 2000 
VRS/VSS/dependants were trained and 924 were re -deployed (self/wage employment) 
which is 46.2%.   The same has been the trend in the previous years also.  Therefore, 
the Committee recommends that re -deployment of the trained VRS/ VSS 
optees/dependants should be given equal weightage along with their counselling and 
retraining.  The Committee also recommends that enhancement in the redeployment 
rate of VRS/VSS optees be perceived by DPE with the association of NSDC.  The 
Committee notes that „Job Fairs‟ have been held in the State of Jharkhand and West 
Bengal by the NSDC for the beneficiaries in order to enhance re -deployment. The 
Committee suggests that more job fairs may be organised in other States as well, 
especially the North Eastern States to promote re-deployment. 
(Para 39) 
 
 The Committee notes that  DPE has been able to use the budget 
allocation under RDC scheme optimally, in the North Eastern Region.  The 
Committee also notes that DPE periodically reviews the CRR scheme to make it more 
useful to VRS/VSS optees/dependants.  The scheme however, will be more meaningful 
when the trained VRS/VSS optees/dependants are re -deployed.  The Committee , 
therefore, reiterates that the beneficiaries of a particular area should be imparted 
training in such skills which are in demand and which can be made use for 
employment in that area. 
 The Committee can not fathom the fact that year after year, DPE has not been 
able to utilise the fund allocated under CRR in North Eastern Region, due to non -
availability of VRS/VSS optees/dependants in North Eastern Region.  Even though  
the unutilised funds do not lapse and gets transferred to Non Lapsable Pool, it does 
not reach the beneficiaries, thereby hampering the development of the North Eastern 
Region. 
 The Committee, therefore, recommends that DPE should re -visit the CRR 
scheme and find out ways and means to make it more attractive for the VRS/VSS 
optees/dependants of North Eastern Region, so that the desired results can be 
achieved.  Further, quarte rly/mid term review of the scheme may be undertaken to 
improve the utilisation of the scheme.   DPE should also sensitise the CPSEs in North 
Eastern Region which undertake downsizing of employees to use the data bank 
available with them to encourage VRS/VSS optees/dependants of such CPSEs to make 
use of the CRR scheme. 
(Para 42) 
 The CAPEX increases productivity of PSEs thereby improving economic 
growth. CAPEX by PSEs also contribute to fixed assets creation in the economy. The 
Government has already directe d Maharatna & Navratna companies to review and 
enhance their CAPEX. The Committee, therefore, desires that DPE may encourage  
31 

CPSEs to increase their CAPEX through regular monitoring as it is also a parameter 
for MoU evaluation.  DPE may also conduct ou treach programmes to sensitise CPSEs 
to leverage their networth for infusion into their CAPEX fund.    
 
(Para 44) 
 The Committee notes that MoU system is an important tool that enables DPE 
to evaluate the performance of the management of CPSEs on key selec ted parameters 
against targets agreed upon so as to improve critical performance indicators of the 
organisation.  The MoU system also helps CPSEs to upgrade their processes and 
systems, address corporate governance imperatives and improve accountability. 
During the year 2019 -20, 144 CPSEs have signed MoU with their respective 
Ministries/ Departments and their performance rating would be evaluated after 
completion of the financial year. Since Independent Directors of Boards of CPSEs 
play key role in ensuring  good corporate governance, the Committee recommends 
that MoU system may be reviewed  to incorporate a new evaluation parameter on 
„Non-filling up of vacant posts of Non -Official Directors on the Boards of CPSEs as a 
deterrent for CPSEs which do not take action timely to fill up such vacant posts. 
 
(Para 50) 
 The Committee notes that Government is keen on disinvestment of CPSEs 
except those belonging to high priority areas such as National Security, Sovereign 
function at arm‟s length & market imperfection a nd public purpose, as 
Government doesn‟t want to engage itself in Sectors where competitive markets 
have come of age. However, the Committee recommends that to support and 
strengthen the CPSEs operating in „Priority  Areas‟ of Business, as identified by 
Niti Aayog.  DPE should play a more pro -active role, especially in respect of those 
CPSEs, which are already doing business in the „Priority Areas‟, which need 
support to excel their performance.  In the case of sick, incipient sick and weak 
CPSEs, their con cerned Administrative Departments have been vested with the 
responsibility of monitoring their sickness and evolve measures for their 
revival/re-structuring. The Committee also observes that even though DPE is not 
mandated to deal with matters concerning d isinvestment of CPSEs, it issues broad 
policy guidelines of CPSEs. Therefore the Committee recommends that while 
disposing of the land of CPSEs identified for closure/strategic disinvestment, the  
applicable guidelines should be scrupulously followed. The Committee during the 
course of examination of the Demands for Grants desired to know whether in the 
„Net Worth‟ of a Company its total holding value, including land assets were taken 
into consideration as per its current market value or only its paid up cap ital and 
reserves made out of its profits were taken into consideration.  In case only the 
latter parameter is considered while assessing the networth of a company, then a 
policy intervention is the need of the hour, which was to be taken up by DPE with 
the concerned Ministry. Further, the Committee suggest that networth of the land 
of such CPSEs should be calculated as per the prevalent market rates.   
(Para 57) 
32 

 The Committee is aware that professionalisation of boards of CPSEs is 
extremely essential f or making CPSEs more competitive and viable in the emerging 
market economy.  It is also essential for ensuring good corporate governance. 
 In its 290th  Report the Committee had inter alia recommended that the process 
of filling  up the regular Board level  vacancies should be initiated by the CPSEs at 
least one year before vacancy actually occurs so that there is no gap between the 
anticipated vacancy and recruitment. Subsequently, the Department of PE in its ATR 
had informed that the said recommendation ha d been forwarded to Public Sector 
Enterprises Selection Board (PSEB) under the DOPT for necessary action, as it 
initiates the selection process for filling up of Board level posts in CPSEs one year in 
advance of occurrence of anticipated vacancies.  
 
 However, it is saddening to note that around 313 positions out of 701 positions 
of non -official Directors are at present vacant in various CPSEs.  The Committee 
therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that the process for filling up of  
vacant posts of regular non-official Directors in various CPSEs should be initiated one 
year before the actual occurrence of the vacancy to avoid delay in filling up of 
vacancies. The Committee also recommends that DPE should follow up the matter 
with PSEB and concerned administrative ministries and report the outcome to the 
Committee.  The Committee further recommends that the existing 313 vacant 
positions of Non -official Directors in various CPSEs should be filled up expeditiously 
to ensure good corporate governance.  
 
(Para 61) 
 The Committee notes that all CPSEs meeting the criteria specified in Section 
135 of Comp Act, 2013 are mandated to undertake CSR activities in project mode 
preferably, in the local area of the company‟s unit, plant or factory as far as possible . 
Wherever it is not possible, the CPSEs are at liberty to undertake the CSR activities 
in any part of the country. Further, as per the latest guidelines for CSR expenditure 
of CPSEs issued by DPE on 10th Dec.2018, a common theme will be identified for each 
year for undertaking CSR by CPSEs, which should cover 60% of annual CSR 
expenditure and Aspirational Districts have to be given preference. 
 
 However, during the recent study visit of the Committee to Hyderabad on 
8/01/2020 the Committee observed that th e CSR expenditure by most of the CPSEs 
were incurred on construction of toilets, contribution to Swachh Bharat Kosh, 
improving existing drinking water facility, health care facilities etc.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that DPE in co -ordination wit h administrative ministries 
should ensure that the CPSEs are aware of the new provisions in the revised 
guidelines such as theme based activity to be undertaken every year, preference  to be 
given to Aspirational Districts, etc. 
 
 The Committee also recomm ends that the CPSEs should desist from using 
CSR fund to supplement Government schemes as the objective of CSR fund is to 
involve corporates in discharging their social responsibility with their innovative ideas 
and management skills.  The Committee is als o of the considered opinion that the 
CSR expenditure in NER should be given more weightage. 
33 

 The Committee feels that the involvement of local representatives such as the 
area MLA/MLC and MP is of paramount importance in CSR related activities.  The 
Committee, accordingly, recommends that area MLA/MLC and MP should be 
consulted both at the time of selection of CSR projects as well as at their 
implementation stage.  This will go a long way to fulfil the aspirations of residents of 
these areas.  
 
(Para 67)

A sustained economic growth is broadly associated with the capacity of diversified 
domestic production, particularly Industrial production. Industrial growth and economic growth 
go hand in hand. Today Capital Goods, Heavy Electrical & Engineering I ndustry and Auto 
Sector play a pivotal role in nation building. Healthy industrial sector lead to vibrant & Robust 
economy. With this view, to boost industrial growth including infrastructure sector, the 
Government is taking steps such as putting in place a policy framework to create conducive 
business environment, strengthening infrastructure network, simplifying and liberalising Foreign 
Direct Investment (FDI) Policy and Procedures, and series of measures to improve Ease -of-
Doing business. 
   
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI)

basic industries such as Steel, Mining, Non-Ferrous metals, Power, Fertilizers , refineries, 
petrochemicals, shipping, paper, cement etc.

Overview of the Automotive Industry 
10. The automobile industry is one of the key drivers of the Indian economy. Since 
the liberalization of the sector in 1991 and allowing 100 percent FDI through automatic 
route, Indian automobile sector has come a long way. Today, there is a presence of 
almost every global auto manufacturer in the country. All categories of vehicles like two -
wheeler, three wheelers, passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, Trucks, Buses, 
Tractors, heavy Commercial vehicles etc. are produced in India. India is the largest 
manufacturer of two Wheeler and three Wheeler and 4 th largest manufacturer of 
passenger cars in the world. The manufacturing of automobiles including truck, buses, 
cars, th ree wheeler/two wheelers etc. in India , has risen at a very high pace. Indian 
Automobile Industry today is 119 Billion USD industry i.e. `8.2 lakh crore industry . 
Automobile industry turnover constitutes 7.1% of GDP, 27% of Industrial GDP and 49% 
of Manufacturing GDP and provides about 37 million direct and indirect jobs , 15% of 
total GST collection ( i.e. ,GST of 1.5 lakh crore) . The current annual sale of vehic les is 
about 26 million.

11. Department’s Initiatives in Automobile Sector 
o Automotive Mission Plan 2016-26. 
o National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP). 
o Promotion of Electric Mobility and FAME-2. 
  
Automotive Mission Plan (AMP)2026 
12. AMP set growth targets for the automotive industry and recommended 
interventions to make India a global automotive hub. The mission plan envisaged to make 
India emerge as the desti nation of choice in the world for design and manufacture of 
automobiles and auto components, with output reaching a level of US$ 145 billion 
(accounting for more than 10% of the GDP) . The idea is to bring Indian automotive 
industry among the top three of t he world in engineering, manufacturing and export of 
vehicles and auto components. Second part of the vision is to ensure that the automotive 
industry contributes to over 12% of the Indian GDP and generates an additional 65 
million jobs to fulfil a major part of its responsibility. 
13. AMP 2026 also seeks to define the trajectory of evolution of the automotive 
ecosystem in India including the specific regulations and policies that govern research, 
design, technology, testing, manufacturing, import/export, s ale, use, repair, and recycling 
of automotive vehicles, components and services. In terms of production and basic 
numbers, under the AMP 2026 , vehicle sales are expected to touch 66 million units by 
2026 with additional investment of 4.5 trillion  - 5.5 tri llion. A large share of the 
production is expected to be exported globally. This growth is expected to impact directly 
the auto component sector, providing it huge opportunities. Indian automotive industry 
has evolved very significantly and we are now the 4th largest market for passenger 
vehicles. 
14. A draft automotive policy, framed by DHI inter alia proposes to:- 
 Adopt a long -term road map for emission standards beyond BS -VI and 
harmonize the same with global standards by 2028. 
 Roll out CAFE norms till 2025 and beyond and setup incentives/ penalties and 
introduce banking, trading.  
 Adopt a composite criterion based on length and CO 2 emissions to classify  
vehicles for differential taxation purposes.  
 Harmonize automotive standards over the next 5 years in  line with                            
WP-29. 
 Improve the skill development and training eco -system, increase 
accountability of ASDC and implement a Labour Market Information System.  
 Retain tax exemption on different levels of R&D expenditure with  
strong audit control.  

 7 
 Scale-up of indigenous R&D with  commercially viable innovations.  
 Harmonize AIS and BIS standards on safety critical parts over next 3 years.  
 Fast track adoption of Bharat New Vehicle Safety Assessment Program. 
 
 
15. The core objectives of  AMP 2026 can be summarised under five themes as 
follows:  
 AMP 2026 aims to propel the Indian Automotive industry to be the engine of 
the "Make in India" programme, as it is amongst the foremost drivers of the  
Manufacturing sector: Over the next decade, t he Indian Automotive sector is  
likely to contribute in excess of 12% of the country's GDP and comprise more 
than 40% of its manufacturing sector. Around 13% of the excise duty 
collection of the  Government can be attributed to the Indian Automotive 
Industry. The Automotive  Industry can be termed as the mother of the 
manufacturing sector in an economy, as its fortunes directly impact the 
fortunes of several related manufacturing industries (e.g. Iron & Steel, 
Aluminium, Lead, Rubber, Plastics, Glass, Machi ne tools, Moulds & dies, 
Chemicals, and Capital Goods) and several in the Services sector (e.g. 
Logistics, Banking, Insurance, Sales & distribution, Service & repair, and 
Fuels). The rapid growth of the Indian Automotive industry will provide a 
strong fillip to the Micro, Small and Medium industries of the country across 
multiple sectors, the development of which is one of Government's principal 
objectives.  
 
 AMP 2026 aims to make the Indian Automotive Industry a significant 
contributor to the "Skill India"  programme and make it one of the largest job 
creating engines in the· Indian economy . The incremental number of jobs to 
be created by the Indian Automotive industry over the next decade is 65 
million. This is over and above the 25 million jobs created in the previous 
decade. The automotive industry has numerous backward and forward 
linkages with over two dozen industries across manufacturing and service 
sectors, across rural and urban India, and across the formal and informal 
sectors of the economy. Most o f the jobs in the Indian Automotive industry 
involve acquiring specialist skills, and confer to the person sufficient 
technical and soft skills to progress professionally within and outside the 
automotive sector. In addition to creating high skilled jobs,  
the industry also provides employment opportunity to a large number of semi-  
skilled and low-skilled workers.  
 
 

 8 
 AMP 2026 seeks enhancing mobility:   The focus of AMP 2026 is to promote 
safe, efficient and comfortable mobility for every person in the coun try, with an 
eye on environmental protection and affordability through both public and 
personal transport options. The objective is to provide a choice to the consumer to 
access multiple options for mobility. AMP 2026 aims to enhance mobility in the 
country while also addressing the need to minimize the negative externalities 
arising from the use of automobiles, such as, congestion, air pollution, global 
warming, and road accidents. AMP 2026 seeks to achieve a healthy balance 
between the human aspiration of  personal transport and efficiency of public 
transport in India.  
 AMP 2026 seeks to increase net exports of the Indian Automotive industry 
several fold: AMP 2026 recognises that the Indian Automotive industry (both 
vehicles and auto components) has the pot ential to scale up exports to the extent 
of 35 -40% of its overall output over the next ten years and become one of the 
major automotive export hubs of the world. In line with this, AMP 2026 makes 
several prescriptions to improve competitiveness, technologi cal advancement, 
infrastructure investment, and branding. On the flip side, the import intensity of 
automobiles is likely to increase in the coming years on account of the increasing 
use of electronics and the enhancement in the value of design and enginee ring in 
making of vehicles and components. At present, India is deficient in skills and 
capabilities in both these areas, namely, auto-electronics and design/ engineering. 
AMP 2 026 seeks to increase the share of local manufacture of vehicles and 
components, in particular, automotive electronics, light -weighting materials, 
moulds & dies, and machinery, which will save the country substantial foreign 
exchange and be a shot in the arm for the "Make in India" programme as well. 
AMP 2026 also aims to increase th e quantum of indigenously carried out 
research, design, engineering and manufacturing in both automotive vehicles and

in the country and the price anxiety for EVs can come down significantly.

a multiple percolating impact on other areas  also like employment etc. The 
Committee also finds merit in the suggestions made by the Auto Industry 
Associations.  The Committee therefore recommends that to revive the Auto Sector, 
the Department sho uld initiate immediate appropriate action with the Ministries 
concerned to either suspend or postpone the enhanced Registration charges and 
upfront insurance payment for 5 years, till the Auto Industry is back o n track.  The 

 10 
new BS-VI variant with upgraded Technology is going to roll out with a higher cost. 
Hence to mitigate such higher cost and create demand for purchases, the Committee 
recommends that GST rate may be reduced to a lowe r slab at least till the revival of 
the Auto Sector. The Committee also recommends that the DHI may pursue with 
the Ministry concerned for introducing incentive based scrappage policy for 
creating purchase demand for new vehicles, after scrapping the old vehicle.

Associations had put forth their views/suggestions for revival of the Auto Industry 
from the present slump that it is undergoing , by measures such as reduction in 
import duty for lithium ion cell battery which is used for operating the e -vehicles 
etc.  The Committee after hearing the Associations recommends that Ministry may 
take up the following issues with the concerned: 
 
(i) Import duty on lithium ion cells in Batteries on which e-vehicles are

Vehicles in India] to promote hybrid/electric technology in transportation so as to reduce  
dependence on fossi l fuels. The overall  scheme was proposed to be implemented  over a 
period of 6 years, till 2020, wherein it was intended to support the hybrid/electric vehicles 
market development and its manufacturing eco-system to achieve self -sustenance at the 

 13

FAME India Phase-I 
 
29. Phase-1 of the scheme was approved initially for a period of 2 years, commencing 
from 1st April 2015 i.e. FY 2015-16 and FY 2016-17, with an outlay of `795 crore. The 
duration of Phase-l of the schem e was extended from time to time and the last extension 
was allowed upto 31st March 2019, with enhancement of total outlay to `895 crore. 
 
30. The scheme had four focus areas i.e. Technology Development, Demand 
Creation, Pilot Proj ect and Charging Infrastructure.  Market creation through demand

Auto, Passenger 4-Wheeler vehicles, Light Commercial Vehicles and Buses. The scheme

private transportation/vehicular mobility for the masses. The demand incentive is

1. The Committee notes that there is huge variations in allocation of funds both 
at BE as well as RE stage.  An amount `2600 which was allocated at BE for the year 
2017-18 was cut down steeply to `1107.26 at RE stage. Likewise `1125.73 allotted as

years, DHI utilize d the allocated fund in a relatively optimal manner , the huge 
variations in BE & RE do not exhibit prudent financial practice. For the present 
financial year 2019-20, DHI could utilize only 80% of the RE upto 31.01.2020, with 
little time left for utilizing the remaining 20%. The Committee recommends that the 
Department of Heavy Industry which oversees important CPSEs, Engineering 
Industries and Auto Sector should ensure that the entire RE is fully utilized in the 
remaining period of the financial year, so t hat the important 
initiatives/schemes/projects do not suffer for lack of sufficient fund. Also in future 
the Department should rationalize the expenditure spreading all through the year to 
avoid uneven spending. 
(Para 8) 
2. From the above table as per information furnished by the DHI, it can be seen 
that only a sum of `1489.98 as BE is allocated for 2020 -21 which is less than 50% of 
the demanded amount. DHI’s flagship scheme like FAME-India has been given very 
less allocation than what was projected by the Department. The sectors under DHI 
viz. Capital goods sector, heavy Engineering & Electrical, Auto sector are very 
critical to economic growth and any shortfall in fund may adversely affect the 
successful implementation and efficient performance of various schemes/Projects as 
they have a huge bearing on the economy. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that DHI should convince the M/o Finance for enhanced allocation at RE stage, so 
that the schemes/Projects/Initiatives could be implemented to its fullest cap acity, so 
that the purpose & objective of the new initiatives are not defeated.

3. The Committee notes that as Automobile Industry constitutes 27% of 
Industrial GDP and 49% of Manufacturing GDP, any strain in this sector will have 
a multiple percolating impact on other areas also like employment etc. The 
Committee also finds merit in the suggestions made by the Auto Industry 
Associations.  The Committee therefore recommends that to revive the Auto Sector, 
the Department should initiate immediate a ppropriate action with the Ministries 

 34 
concerned to either suspend or postpone the enhanced Registration charges and 
upfront insurance payment for 5 years, till the Auto Industry is back on track.  The 
new BS-VI variant with upgraded Technology is going to roll out with a higher cost. 
Hence to mitigate such higher cost and create demand for purchases, the Committee 
recommends that GST rate may be reduced to a lower slab at least till the revival of 
the Auto Sector. The Committee also recommends that the DHI may pursue with 
the Ministry concerned for introducing incentive based scrappage policy for 
creating purchase demand for new vehicles, after scrapping the old vehicle. 
(Para 18)

Department utilized only `0.20 crores out of the allocated fund of `0.50 crore in FY 
2019-20, compelling the MoF to allot only a meagre amount of `0.20 crore for the 
financial year 2020-21. The Committee notes that a sum of `0.20 crore is a miniscule 
amount to meet the important aspect of promotional activities for creating 
awareness of the benefits of manufacturing and technology related aspects for the 
Capital Goods sector. The Department’s explanation that during the year 2018 -19, 
no suitable proposals were received from the Industry Association/PSUs for 
providing financial support is not well received by the Committees. The Committee 
recommends that the  Department should pro -actively interact with the 
Industry/PSUs for arranging effective promotional activities in large numbers to 
create vast awareness of the benefits of Capital Goods Sector. The Committee also 
recommends that the DHI should seek more fu nds in RE 2020 -21 for carrying out 
promotional activities. 
(Para 65) 
 
 
15. The Committee notes that the allocated BE 2020 -21 is only `6 crores as 
Grants in Aid for salaries support to CMTI as against the Projected Budget of 
`22.00 crores. As the fund allot ted is just sufficient to meet the salaries of the 
faculty, the R&D programmes are likely to be badly affected. The Committee 
recommends that the DHI should seek sufficient funds in the RE 2020 -21 for the 
purpose of R&D Programme, for developing high tech core manufacturing 
technologies. 
(Para 70) 
 

 38 
16. Further, in reply to a query, it was brought to the notice of the Committee 
that out of an allocated amount of `19 crores, the actual release under this h ead is 
only `14 crore and the balance of `5 crore will  be released before the close of the 
financial year.  As per provisions of GFR, not more than 20% expenditure is to be 
expended in the last quarter of a financial year and such rush of spending in the last 
quarter is likely to attract audit objections.  He nce the Committee recommends that 
Ministry may avoid such rush of expenditure in the last quarter and keep the 
spending pattern uniform throughout the year. 
 (Para 71) 
 
17. The Committee observes that a sum of `95 crores and `90 crores have been 
allocated at BE 2017-18 and 2018-19 respectively. However, the entire BE amount in 
both the years have been taken away at RE Stage. The Committee is not convinced 
with the explanation given by DHI for fund exemption.  The Committee is cognizant 
of the fact that the government is giving impetus for developing North Eastern 
Regions and that many of the Aspirational Districts have been selected in NER. The 
Committee recommends that the Department should seek funds in the RE stage for 
development of North Eastern Areas.  
(Para 74) 
 
18. The Committee observes that the number of CPSEs under the administrative 
control of DHI i.e., 31 CPSEs in 2016-17 has dwindled to 22 as on date, out of which 
only 10 are profit making and 12 are making loss. 7 CPSE are under closure. The 
Committee is concerned about the large rate of attrition of CPSEs under DHI. The 
Committee recommends that DHI should undertake a thorough appraisal of each 
loss making CPSEs and explore all possibiliti es to revive or restructure the CPSEs 
with a view  to bri ng about a turnaround in its performance with Government 
support in the first instance. 
 (Para 77) 
 
19. The Committee notes that there is lackadaisical approach on the part of DHI 
in implementing the recommendations of the Report for  modernization of the plant 
by Dr. V. K. Saraswat, Member, NITI Aayog way back in January 2017 which is 

 39 
still pending with the DHI. The Committee is left with no option but to express its 
displeasure on the callous  and nonchalant approach of the Department in taking 
remedial measures for reviving HEC. The Committee desires that the department in 
consultation with the Govt. of India should implement the recommendation of Dr. 
Saraswat Committee, without any further delay. 
(Para 82) 
20. From the above facts it is seen that the ent ire amount of `469.41 crore for 
undergoing the Revival and Mill Development Plan has been sanctioned/released. 
Though the RMDP was supposed to be completed by December, 2019, the deadline 
has missed. The DHI in their submission has assured that it is likel y to take some 
more time for completion. The Committee therefore, expect the RMDP of NEPA to 
be completed soon by fast track monitoring by the Department and report 
compliance to the Committee.  
(Para 85) 
 
21. The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction on  the lethargic attitude of DHI 
towards these CPSEs for their final closure . The Committee is of the opinion that 
after final disposal of these Unit, DHI would be able to concentrate and dedicate 
their time and money on the other CPSE, particularly the sick  and incipient for 
their restructuring for a turnaround. 
 (Para 87) 
 
22. The Committee observes that some irregularity has been done by BHEL by 
misusing the funds towards extending undue benefits to its employees on account of 
payment of Late Night Snacks Allowance in gross violation to the extant 
rules/guidelines of DPE.  The Committee would like to know the present status of 
the Audit observation and action taken by BHEL and DHI for its settlement.  The 
Committee also desire s that DHI should issue instruc tions to all CPSEs under its 
domain to strictly adhere to the guidelines of DPE and maintain financial propriety 
in accordance with the laid-down policy. 
(Para 89)

THIRD REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman, Department- Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, 
having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this 
Third Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants for 1993-94 of the Ministry of 
Mines. 
2. In pursuance of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Rajya Sabha 
pertaining to Department-Related Standing Committees, Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha 
and Hon'ble Speaker , Lok Sabha nominated 42 members of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha to 
the Committee on Industry for the functions assigned to it under the Rules. Further 
Chairman, Rajya Sabha and Speaker, Lok Sabha decided that all provisions of Rule 270 of 
the Rules relating to the functions of the Committee shall become operative with effect from 
30th March, 1993. 
3. The Committee on Industry deals with the subjects falling in the jurisdiction of the 
Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Steel and Ministry of Mines. 
4. The Committee accordingly held its first meeting on the 22nd April, 1993 and 
considered relevant documents and papers received from the Ministry of Mines on the 
Demands for Grants for the year 1993-94. 
5. The Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretary of the Ministry of Mines 
on the performance budget in the context of Demands for Grants of that Ministry. 
6. The Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in three sittings and 
considered and adopted the Report at its sitting held on 4th May, 1993 (Annexure consisting 
of the minutes of the First, Fourth and Fifth sittings of the Committee). 
7. Demands for Grants as presented for the Ministry as under:-

Total Voted 209.41 crores 
8. The Committee had no time to consider in depth and arialyse the Demands for Grants 
of the Ministry and the other documents. The Committee is conscious of the fact that the 
Demands for Grants of various Ministries and Departments are to be put for vote of the 
Lok Sabha on the 4th May, 1993. We, therefore, offer general comments. We propose to 
consider the detailed expenditure at a later stage and will present our views in subsequent 
reports so as to enable the Government to recaste their expenditure priorities in the revised 
estimates. 
9. Taken into account the documents and other material made available to it, the 
Committee concludes as under:-

9.2(ii) Bharat Aluminium Company Ltd. (BALCO): It is a company under the Ministry to 
produce primary aluminium metal. In the Korba Plant , technology used in the smelter had 
become outdated and the cost of production was going high and high. The modernisation of 
the existing smelter was accordingly approved and limited tender enquiries from interna­
tional technological suppliers were floated. Finally, the price bids were opened in December, 
1992 as per the following details:-

Aluminium and Alesa Alusuisse respectively. It was also found that in terms of the

Ales a Alusuisse. The Committee was also informed that the parties offered financial 
packages through commercial ban~s~financial institutions. In addition, Alesa Alusuisse 
informed BALCO that mixed Swiss Credit with 40% grant-in-aid would be available for the 
project as part of the financial offer. Accordingly, BALCO requested Alesa Alusuisse to 
produce a confirmatory letter from the Swiss Government to this effect. Alesa Alusuisse, 
however. could not furnish the confirmatory letter. On a reference from BALCO the 
Ministry of Mines enquired from the Department of Economic Affairs if the Swiss mixed . 
credit with 40% grant-in-aid, would be available to the company. That Department informed 
that subject to its availability and approval such assistance whether in grant or loan would be 

passed on to BALCO as a loan through Government of India at the usual rates of interest. 
The Committee understands that BALCO with the approval of their Board of Directors 
accepted the offer of the Kaiser Aluminium of USA on the basis of the delegated powers 
enjoyed by the company in this type of investments with the approval of the Ministry. The 
Committee would observe that with the Budgetary support of Rs. 4 crores in the Budget 
Estimates for 1993-94 the modernisation of Korba Plant Smelter is undertaken. The 
Financial delegation of powers to be enjoyed by the Board of Directors of the Company in 
awarding such contracts should therefore be precisely laid down. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that it should be clearly defined and indicated in appropriate chapter in the 
Performance Budget for correct appraisal of financial relations between the Ministry and the 
Undertakings functioning under its administrative control. The Committee do not intend to 
go into the merits and demerits and award of the content at this point of time. The 
Budgetary figures and the memorandum relating thereto should be self-explanatory in this 
behalf. 
9.3 Mineral exploration: One of the important functions of the Ministry is the exploration 
of minerals and their utilisation for the economic development of the country. The activities 
relating to minerals are being looked after by the Mineral Exploration Corporation Limited. 
The Budget allocation for the year 1993-94 with corresponding figures of 1992-93 are as

promotional fund for exploration and Rs. 35.93 crores was made for capital outlay. The 
Mineral Exploration was therefore , able to undertake drilling of 18.39 lacs mtrs. and 54.600 
mtrs. of mining resulting in a reserve of 17,750.73 million tonnes of different minerals in 
roughly 140 projects. The Committee finds that against this background, an amount of 
Rs. 13 crores for the promotional work and one crore for capital outlay for the current 
financial year has been made. Contractual drilling and promotional activities are basic 
functions of the Corporation. The Committee feels that the reduced allocation for this item 
in the Budget estimates is likely to decrease the net profit and will hamper its growth. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should re-examine the allocation and 
submit the revised re-appropriation for the consideration of the Lok Sabha. 
9.4 Zinc: Another area in production of non-ferrous metals falling under the jurisdiction of 
the Ministry is the Production of Zinc. The Committee has noticed that in the matter of 
purchasing metallurgical grade of Coke required for use in the smelter· of Hindustan Zinc 
Limited at Chanderiya in Chittorgarh District of Rajasthan the HZL ha~ not taken any note · 
of the indigenous metallurgical coke available with indigenous companies with the requisite 
grade and quality of Coke. It has come to the notice of the Committee that ten thousand 
tonnes of Coke of the required grade and quality was purchased by HZL after verifying the 
technical suitability of the Coke. The quality purchased from indigenous resources was 
however not even given a trial in the actual production in the smelter and instead the 
foreign-based companies in Singapore and Japan were awarded the contract for supplying 
the coke afresh. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the entire transaction needed 
to be thoroughly probed to identify and fix responsibility for purchasing coke from abroad. 

9.5 Bharat Gold Mines Ltd.: The Committee notes that a sum of Rs. 20 crores have been 
earmarked for restructuring/diversifying the activities of Bharat Gold Mines Ltd. (BGML) 
and out of Rs. 20 crores Rs. 8.5 crores have been earmarked for the year 1992-93. The 
Committee also had an overall view of the financial position of BGML. The Committee is 
given to understand that the Company is under heavy losses and has also beeh referred to 
BIFR. The Committee has been informed that some of the units of BGML have acquired 
optimum expertise in their respective fields of operation . The Committee proposes to study 
the subject in depth taking into account various factors and will submit its report -at -a later 
stage. However, the Committee like to observe that efforts should be made to experiment 
shallow mining and reduce establishment expenditure on the maintenance of township of the 
factory. Proceedings before BIFR may be kept in suspension or deferred till the Committee 
has studied the problem in greater detail. Based on these observations, the Committee 
recommends required Budgetary support for shallow mining of BGML on experimental 
basis. 
9.6 The Committee finds that Geological Survey of India is a premier organisation under 
the Ministry. The Committee finds that only Rs. 42 crores out of a total of Rs. 112.10 crores 
have been .earmarked as a plan expenditure for the GSI while the non-plan expenditure is 
Rs. 70.10 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommends that more funds for plan 
expenditure for different activities of the GSI like survey, mapping, mineral exploration, etc . 
may be provided. 
9.7 In regard to Mining, the Committee regrets to note that large scale closure of mines in 
.different States and Union Territories has become a normal feature. The Committee , 
therefore, recommends that every step should be taken by Government to ensure that this 
trend is immediately reversed and effective measures are taken to halt the deterioration in 
the operation of mines and for revitalising and rejuvenating the mines for better mineral use 
for our economic development. The Committee do not find any specific monetary allocation 
in the Budget for the purpose.

consideration for implementation.

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises on the recommendations contained in 
the Committee’s Two Hundred Ninety Seventh Report on Demands for Grants (20 20-
21) pertaining to the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
2.  Action Taken Notes received from the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises in respect of the recommendations contained in  the 297th Report have been 
categorized as follows:- 
 
Chapter –I  The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the 
Ministry. The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry has 
accepted its recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter -I of the 
Report. 
 
Chapter -II The recommendations/observations , which the Committee does not 
desire to pursue  further in view of the Government’s replies. In respect 
of these recommendations, the Committee is convinced with the logic 
and explanations adva nced by the Ministry and therefore does not want 
to pursue them further for the present. 
 
Chapter -III The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee 
has not accepted the replies of the Ministry and desires the Ministry to 
review their reply. The Committee is not convinced with the replies of 
the Ministry in respect of recommendations contained in Chapter -III and 
desires that the Ministry, in the light of further 
recommendations/observations of the Committee, furnish explanations 
thereof. 
 
Chapter -IV   The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee 
desire further comments of the Ministry . In respect of recommendations 
placed in Chapter -IV, the Ministry has either furnished the interim 
replies, therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry may furnish 
Action Taken Notes in respect of recommendations categorized in 
Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the 
recommendations of the Committee. 
 
The details of the ATR of the Ministry and recommendations/observations of the  
Committee thereon are given in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
1 

CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1. The present classification of MSMEs based on investment in plant and machinery has 
been effective since the adoption of the MSMED Act, 2006.  However, the extant financial 
limits fixed in 2006 for MSMEs are no longer relevant given the impact of inflation.  Most of 
the Industry Associations and stakeholders have, therefore, expressed the need for changing 
the present criteria of investment in plant and machinery to annual turnover as criterion for 
classification of MSMEs. 
 (Para 8) 
 
Action Taken 
 
Definition of MSMEs has changed vide S.O. 1702  dated 01/06/2020 (Annexure-I) and 
then vide S.O. 2119 dated 26/06/2020 (Annexure -II), by superseding the one dated 
01/06/2020. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
2. The Committee is of the view that the present classification based on investment in 
plant and ma chinery also has a number of disadvantages as it prevents MSMEs to become 
competitive in the market, inhibits investment to modernize, upscale, improve productivity and 
technology upgradation due to rigor of investment thresholds. On the other hand, taking  
turnover as a criteria shall overcome the said shortcomings as it can be pegged with reliable 
data available in GST Network and other methods of ascertaining, which will help in having a 
non discretionary, transparent and objective criteria and will elimi nate the need for 
inspections and make the classification system progressive and evolutionary. 
           (Para 9) 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
Definition of MSMEs has changed vide S.O. 1702 dated 01/06/2020 and then vide 
S.O. 2119 dated 26/06/2020, by superseding the one dated 01/06/2020. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3. Artificial Intelligence is a rapidly emerging concept in the market across the globe 
which has great potential for enterprises. Most of the entrepreneurs are making use of this 
concept for their benefit  and to increase their outreach. The Committee recommends that 
Ministry of MSME should also explore the concept of AI for strengthening and betterment of 
MSME Sector in the country. 
       (Para 26) 
 
2 

Action Taken 
 
Looking at the importance of Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Augmented Reality (AR) and 
Virtual Reality (VR) in the era of Industry 4.0, these technologies have already been 
included/will be included as one of the essential feature in all Technology Centres/Extension 
Centres. The Ministry is active ly working in this direction to ensure utilization of the AI 
framework to enhance the outreach. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4. Market Intelligence plays a crucial role in strengthening and improving the 
enterprises. A dedicated market intelligence cell is  very essential to gather information about 
latest trends, taste and other aspects of the market. It is imperative to keep an eye on 
International markets and MSMEs of developed countries for knowledge of latest technology 
and developments and to adopt goo d practices prevailing in the developed markets across the 
globe for benefit of indigenous MSMEs. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a Market 
Intelligence Cell for MSMEs should be set up that would regularly map specific markets, 
foreign as well as domestic, for meeting the requirement of specific MSME clusters and 
accordingly provide information and training to them about consumer preferences, product 
specifications, technological developments and trade agreements. 
         (Para 27) 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
The Ministry will take all necessary steps to ensure access to Market Intelligence to 
gather all requisite information from the international markets.

19. The Committee was informed by the representatives of MSME Associations that many 
of the MSMEs were unable to meet the fixed deadline of 90 days in repaying their loan 
installments, due to the unique system of their working cycle, which is much longer, due to 
their inability  to meet the stipulated timeline for repayment, the MSME units are declared 
NPAs. To avoid such difficulties being faced by MSMEs, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry should endeavour to see to it that time limit for declaring a MSME as NPA due to 
non-payment of loan amount should be enhanced from the current 90 days to 180 days. 
         (Para 22) 
Action Taken 
 
 
 
 
In this regard, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has stated that banks are free to take credit 
decisions, including designing of appropriate repayment schedules of the MSME borrowers 
based on the expected cash flows. Once the repayment schedule has been arrived at, any 
default risk on account of delay in repayment has to be suitably recognized. Accordingly, the 
classification of assets has to b e done on the basis of objective criteria of record of recovery, 
which in turn ensures a uniform and consistent application of the norms. 
 
In this context, 90 days delinquency norm was brought in through a calibrated manner 
to benchmark the prudential regu lation to the international standards after extensive 
consultations and was based on the report of the Committee on Banking Sector Reforms 
chaired by Shri M Narasimhan. It may also be mentioned here that default in payment is a 
lagging, not leading, indica tor of financial stress of a borrower and the 90 days delinquency 
norm is considered appropriate as it will facilitate the implementation of a resolution plan by 
lenders in respect of stressed borrowers. As such, increasing the delinquency norm for NPA 
classification for MSMEs may not be desirable. 
 
Recommendation/Observation

economy by 2024 -25. The Committee is however of the considered view that the target of 
becoming $5 trillion economy by 2024 can be achieved by exponential growth of MSME

innovative technology can be made commercially productive at lower cost. This sector has 
also the capacity to generate employment and multiplication of production is far easy than the

proactive and constructive role in promoting MSME Sector. More than ease of doing 
business, there is need of creating ease of running business. More information dis semination

proactive, friendly and forthcoming. Government regulators should do handholding and play 
the role of mentors. Besides, change in the attitude of the Gov ernment regulators will 
immensely help the MSME Sector.

Together with the industry, skilled manpower and the support of government authorities, the 
desired target can be achieved.

The Micro, Small & Medium Enterp rises (MSMEs) have been contributing 
significantly to the expansion of entrepreneurial endeavors through business innovations. The 
MSMEs are widening their domain across sectors of the economy, producing diverse range of 
products and services to meet deman ds of domestic as well as global markets. MSMEs are
