Post Covid-19 Pandemic Lockdown Scenario 
 
78. The outbreak of Corona virus Pandemic world over took many countries viz., 
China, Italy, Spain, France, Germany, United Kingdom, Un ited States, Brazil etc under 
its grip and India has been no exception. Like other countries, India too imposed 
nationwide lockdown commencing from 25 th March, 2020 to curtail the spread of the 
Covid-19 infection, followed by extensions with calibrated ope ning easing the 
restrictions.  However, the National lockdown led to a total shut down of all Automotive 
Plants that further pushed down the Indian Automotive Sector which was already reeling 
under a prolonged slump with sales down nearly to 18% in 2019-20.   As informed by the 

29 
 
Automobile Industry Associations, the production stoppage at the automotive OEM and 
component supplier due to Covid-19 pandemic and subsequent lockdowns led to a loss of 
approximately Rs.2300 crore per day to the automotive sector.  But the actual magnitude 
of the impact depends on the duration of lockdown period, the intensity and extent of 
spread of the Covid -19 outbreak. Considering the crisis, it is predicted that the 
automobile industry is likely to go through at least two consec utive years of severe 
contraction, leading to low levels of capacity utilization, lack of future CAPEX 
investment, high risk of bankruptcy and job losses across the entire automotive value 
chain. 
79. Further, the Auto Industry Associations have highlighted  that the impact of 
Covid-19 would be felt on both the demand as well as the supply aspects of the 
automobile industry. Dried up source due to shutdown of domestic and international 
supplier operations, logistics logjam, insufficient workforce due to delay  in return of 
migrant labour and financial insecurity caused by lack of sales and delayed payments, 
shortage in component parts  which is mostly imported from China, re -allocation of 
production parts to Indian suppliers due to bottlenecks in global chain, decrease in export 
orders due to shutdown in Europe/USA, liquidity crunch for suppliers due to increased 
inventory as no production by OEMs are the major factors haunting the supply side of the  
automobile industry. On the other hand, demand would be impac ted mainly due to 
negative consumer sentiments and liquidity crunch due to loss of income resulting from 
job lay -off estimated to be 24% since the implementation of national lockdown. But 
demand for individual passenger cars may increase slightly. 
 
80. Given the characteristics of the Covid -19 pandemic world over, the 
Committee understands that this disease is expected to exist for more time. The 
Committee appreciates the Government‟s decision of graded opening of the 
lockdown and restarting the economic ac tivity for life to move -on along with the 
Corona virus side by side.  The Committee however recommends that with a view to 
protect life and livelihood, the economy needs to be opened up gradually ensuring 
the safety to life.  Therefore, the Committee, with  regard to Automobile Sector, 

30 
 
recommends that the Government should issue guidelines and Standard 
Operational Procedures (SOP) that all the concerned stakeholders should prioritize 
employee protection and safety, regularly monitor and track health status o f the 
employees, follow disease control protocols, define travel guidelines, ensure 
quarantine facility, schedule for flexible working hours etc. 
 
81. The Committee notes the recent announcement of relief package by the 
Government to reboot the economy to tide over the crisis and extend support to the 
various stakeholders, like infusion of liquidity through Collateral Free Automatic 
Loans, Subordinate Debt Scheme, financial support to NBFCs etc. which will 
encourage new investments, promoting growth across the supply chain, including 
Automobile Dealers, and safeguarding employment.  Although the package has 
infused  a fresh lease of life amid the gloom, but at the same time, the Committee 
however feels that this stimulus package in particular, falls short of  addressing the 
issues of the Automotive Industry as the measures taken by the Government is 
targeted to boost only the supply side of the economy.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the government should focus on announcing a stimulus package 
for demand generation for the automotive sector where the government spending 
could boost a faster revival of the economy.   
 
82. Further, in order to help the ailing Automobile Industries financially, t he 
Committee after taking into consideration the inputs g iven by some of the 
Automobile Associations, recommends the following additional proposals for 
consideration of the Government: 
 the expenditure incurred by companies for making payments to temporary 
and contract labour during the lockdown period  should be eligible as CSR 
expense; 
 
 the condition to avail ITC (Input Tax Credit) requiring payment of invoice to 
the supplier within 180 days of invoice to be done away with till situation 
returns to normal or at least provide waiver of interest which is charged 
from date of invoice of supplier, as most payments to the vendors will be 
deferred in the present scenario; 
 

31 
 
 provision for acceptance of self certification by OEMs, instead of testing and 
approval by Gov ernment agencies for meeting regulatory requirements, 
prioritized attention to new approvals of alternate materials/parts identified 
for testing for compliance and validation purpose and fast trac k approvals 
by testing agencies; 
 
 instead of 50%, 100% waiver on demurrage charges to be provided at the 
Airports/Seaports and rail yards until 1 month post resumptio n of full 
commercial production; 
 
 to make up the lost sales in March 2020, vehicles purchased till 30.05.2020 be 
permitted to enjoy 6 months depreciation in FY 2019 -2020 which will help in 
stimulating sales; and 
 
 Temporary exemption of import/export taxes on R&D/testing vehicles  and 
50% discount in testing prices in NATRIP facilities. 
 
 
83. Since the physical distancing is one of the pre -requisites to tackle the corona 
virus spread, it is expected that a la rge number of people would switch over to 
personal mobility from public transport to commute for safety reasons to avoid 
jostling with others on crowded buses and trains.  As most of these people would be 
first time buyers, the Committee expects an immedia te surge in the purchase of 
affordable two -wheeler or small and mid -sized cars. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that the Government should capitalize this trend for promoting sale of 
small and midsized cars by ensuring availability of finance through e asy vehicle 
loans at low interest rates to the prospective customers to create demand in the 
Automobile Sector. 
 
84. The Indian Auto Industry is highly dependent on automotive spare parts 
imported (around 27%) from China.  However, due to the outbreak of c orona virus, 
the component manufacturing units were shuttered down in China stalling the 
imports and subsequently affecting the whole value chain in India.  Keeping in view  
the programme of “Make in India” and localized production, the Committee 
recommends that the Government should encourage and promote setting up of new 

32 
 
automotive component manufacturing units/MSMEs to strengthen the economy and 
become a self-reliant country. 
85. In the current Global scenario, the Committee observes that many of the 
countries are planning to pull out their manufacturing units from China and are 
looking for alternate lucrative and prospective countries for re-location.  Since India 
could be a preferred destination for foreign investment due to its sustained GDP 
growth, ex panded robust market, enabling environment and transparent open 
policy regime, the Committee desires that the Government should take all out 
efforts to seize this opportunity and turn the present adversity to a blessing in 
disguise . 
 
86. Further, to attra ct the foreign Companies to set shop pertaining to the 
Automotive Sector in the Indian soil, the prevalent land and labour laws of the 
country may need an overhauling, so as to make it more investor friendly. The 
Committee, accordingly, recommends that DHI  may take up the issue with the 
appropriate Departments of the Government of India to facilitate the same. 

33 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS — AT A GLANCE 
 
 The Committee was informed by the Auto Industry Associations that the n on-
availability of finance to consumers due to tightening of norms for retail financing by the 
Banks across the board in rural as well as urban areas has affected the growth of the Auto 
Industry Sector.  This approach by banks  has reduced the availability of finance to 
customers to go in for new vehicle purchase. Further, Banks are following CIBIL ratings 
in a very rigorous manner as a result of which  the customers are finding it difficult to get  
automobile loans. Most of the two  wheeler customers are first time use rs and they don‟t 
have any CIBIL ratings or credit ratings. Moreover, the markets are shifting towards rural 
markets, where potential customers find in difficult for getting loans as they do not have 
any record of financial security, since  they do not pay income tax. So with incr easing 
stringent compliance measures, the rural customers find it difficult to avail finance from 
the banks for purchasing new vehicles. Earlier financing of about 85 -90 percent was 
available but now it is limited to only 60 -70%.  As per the submission of Department 
of Heavy Industry, amongst all the sectoral loans, NPAs are the least at 1.5 - 2% for 
Auto Loans. The Committee notes that majority of vehicle purchases are made 
through loans. The Auto loan is a secured loan as the vehicle itself is collateral.  The 
Committee, therefore, finds no reason why the banks should be refusing auto loans 
to prospective consumers. The Committee, therefore, recommends that D epartment 
of Heavy Industry should take up the matter with D epartment of Financial Services 
for issu ing required instructions to all banks throughout the country to adopt a 
liberal policy in sanctioning of vehicle loans subject to minimum regulation s of 
fulfilling the eligibility condition. 
(Para 17 ) 
 
 
2. The M inistry of Finance  in their written submiss ion has stated that funds 
worth `70,000 crore have been released for PSU banks recapitalization to improve 
liquidity situation. The Committee is pleased to note the action taken by the 
Government to strengthen the bank liquidity and believes that such a move will help 
PSU Banks to boost lending and improve liquidity situation.  Further, the NBFCs 

34 
 
will be allowed to use Aadhar authenticated KYCs to take up credit which would 
further help them to lend more Auto Loans. The Committee hopes that this move by 
the Ministry of Finance would bring some respite to the Auto buyers  in the country 
and help improve the downturn in the Automobile Sector. 
(Para 19 ) 
 
3. The Committee notes that in the year 2019, repo r ate has come down by 
about 1.1% and reduction in the repo rate means the consumers may be able to get 
loans at cheaper interest rates from the Banks. Therefore, t here is likelihood of 
commodities becoming cheaper due to lower interest cost, benefitting the end 
consumers. However, banks have not passed on the re duced rates to customers. 
Instead many retail auto loan rates have increased by 0.05% to 0.4%. In this regard, 
the Auto Association have highlighted that even 1% reduction in rates would 
motivate small car buyer s to go in for the purchase  of a new vehicle . The 
Department of Expenditure in its written reply has stated that the Government has 
recently announced linking of repo rate to interest rates charges for vehicle 
purchase, to provide impetus to the local manufacturing including automotive 
industry. The Committee however, has been informed that on ground, the reduction 
in repo rate by RBI has not been transferred to the customers by reducing interest 
rates.  Therefore, the Committee is of the view that D epartment of Heavy Industry  
should take up the matte r with M inistry of Finance and the Reserve Bank of India 
for issuing strict guidelines to all banks for linking repo rate to interest rates on 
loans to the consumers, to help revival of the Auto Industry Sector.  
 (Para 20 ) 
4. The Committee is therefore of the considered opinion that as far as the  
working capital requirement of Auto Dealers  is concerned,  collateral norms for 
regular loan products should be moderate for availing required finance . The 
Committee is of the view  that though banks have been faci ng various challenges 
because of bad loans, however, they should not look at all financial lendings with the 
same eye as the recovery rate is very high in the auto sector. Therefore, all measures 

35 
 
needs to be taken to ease the availability of finance to the  stakeholders in order to 
help them contribute substantially for the revival of auto sector. 
(Para 23 ) 
 
5. The Automobile Sector, due to its strong forward and backward linkages 
with several key segments of the economy, occupies a prominent place in the f abric 
of Indian Economy. Since the number of vehicles exported in various segments is 
nowhere near the potential, exporting vehicles in a large scale would significantly 
contribute to employment generation, trade balance and economic growth of the 
country. The Committee therefore recommends that constructive steps should be 
taken by the Government to promote export of vehicles in various segments, 
particularly the BS-VI compliant vehicles, and their engine & spare parts to various 
countries across the globe , especially to Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia and 
West Asia where there is still huge potential for the global automobile companies 
operating from India. The Committee also recommends that the Government in 
coordination with the automobile companie s should take appropriate steps to 
explore the rural markets, particularly in Two Wheeler and Three Wheeler 
segments that would contribute substantially for the growth of the Auto Sector. 
(Para 30 ) 
 
6. Further, t he Committee feels that as a respite to the  already stressed 
Automobile Sector, the DHI in collaboration with other concerned Ministries may 
work out some measure s to ensure that the surplus stock of non-BS-VI compliant 
vehicles left unsold, if any, is disposed off. Through a Review Petition, the H on‟ble 
Supreme Court may be convinced to consider the extension of period for disposal of 
surplus stock of BS -IV compliant vehicle particularly taking into account  the 
unexpected national lockdown imposed due to Covid -19 Pandemic. The Committee 
is of the o pinion that this would provide the much needed leeway of considerable 
time over and above the mandated date of 1 st April, 2020 to the dealers to dispose 
off their buffer stock of vehicles. Besides, the recent Coronavirus outbreak has 
taken its toll on the Indian Auto Industry, which is dependent on its component 

36 
 
supplies from China. However, the Committee feels that even in the pervading 
gloom of the Coronavirus scare, there is a silver lining owing to the fact that the 
supply disruption may force manufactu rers to look within and source their 
component parts locally. The Committee feels that such a de -risking plan is 
expected to boost the Auto Components Industry. Further, the Committee is also of 
the opinion that the disruption in the supply chain should al so be counted as a 
reason to extend the deadline of 1 st April 2020, as in the absence of a robust and 
consistent supply chain of Auto Components, there is bound to be a lesser capacity 
utilisation in the manufacture of BS-VI vehicles. To fill in this temporary shortfall of 
BS-VI vehicles, the inventory stock of BS IV vehicles, lying unsold with dealers can 
be utilised. 
(Para 35) 
 
7. The Committee is of the view  that while migrating to E lectric Mobility, the 
whole system of manufacturing needs to be overhauled. Hence it would be advisable 
for adopting phased manufacturing Programme rather than putting all the eggs in 
one basket and in case if the new technology does not yield the desired outcome, the 
existing established Auto Industry should be incentivised for better performance. 
(Para 38 ) 
 
8. The Committee also notes that the current state of EV infrastructure in the 
country is not encouraging for switching over to Electric Mobility on a large scale . 
The Committee therefore expresses its concern over the proposal of the Government 
to move to 30% EV by 203 0 which is seemingly a big challenge amid lack of 
charging infrastructure and therefore a clear roadmap  may be drawn up for 
achieving parity in term s of cost with fuel based engines to start going electric, so 
that demands for EV is generated among the people. 
(Para 39 ) 
 
 

37 
 
9. With regard to charging station infrastructure, the Committee recommends 
that specific Rules/guidelines should be formulated, wherein it is ensured that both, 
foreign companies as well a s indigenous ones, desiring to set shop in the country, 
should adhere to the proposed stipulated guidelines. The Committee also desires 
that the proposed guidelines invariably, should specify inter alia, the designated 
places, such as parks, housing Societ y Complexes etc, wherein charging stations can 
be set up. The Committee also deserves that it be apprised of the targets set in terms 
of members, for setting up of such charging stations. 
(Para 40 ) 
 
10. The Committee also recommends that the fee to be cha rged from the 
clientele, by the service provider should invariably be regulated and they should be 
allowed to charge as per laid down norms. 
(Para 41) 
 
11. The Committee notes that the over impetus and aggressive targeting by the 
Government on EV and its h igh cost price, have created confusion in the minds of 
the consumer whether to go in for purchase of EV or ICE vehicle, who were already 
in the wait and watch mode in the wake of mandated transition from BS -IV to BS -
VI w.e.f. 1st April, 2020. The Committee recommends that the MoRTH should come 
out with clear picture on the future of ICE technology and adoption of Electric 
Mobility for a synergised co-existence. 
(Para 42) 
 
12. The Committee is of the view that the Government should conduct a 
thorough study a nd incorporate necessary provision for eco -friendly 
management/disposal of used LIBs so that E -waste does not turn out to be 
environment hazard. 
(Para 44) 
 

38 
 
13. The Committee also recommends that DHI should take initiatives to foray 
into new and emerging te chnological areas instead of concentrating solely on the 
expensive lithium ion based battery operated electric vehicles. The Committee feels 
that other avenues such as hydrogen based fuel cell technology etc. may be tapped 
and explored. By adopting such mu lti-pronged approach, the Committee is of the 
opinion that the EV industry would not be constrained to depend on its survival 
solely on the imported lithium based ion cell battery. 
(Para 45) 
14. The Committee is , however,  not willing to buy th e argument that the new 
trend of shared mobility through aggregator services like Uber, Ola etc. has to some 
extent reduced the purchase demand of new vehicles as these aggregator services 
are available only in major cities and they also need to buy vehicles to run the ir 
business.  Moreover, most of the users are already owners of personal vehicles, but 
they prefer to avail Uber , Ola etc. service to avoid irritant driving on heavy traffic 
roads and also to disengage themselves from the parking hassles. The Committee 
while appreciating carpooling /shared mobility recommends for better Public 
Transport Services which would provide larger benefits in terms of emission 
reduction as well as increase in the demand for new heavy vehicles. 
(Para 47) 
 
15.     The Committee notes t hat the GST rate s on ICE based vehicles are at the 
highest slab of 28%.  GST on all electrically operated vehicles is fixed at 5% to 
promote electric mobility.  The Committee, therefore, feels that if GST rebates for 
EVs could be given for creating Public demand, there is scope for reducing GST on 
ICE Vehicles also to spur its demand to overcome the present slump in the 
Automobile Sector.  The cost of BS -VI vehicles is expected to be higher by 10 -15% 
due to upgraded technology.  To mitigate this cost increa se, the Committee is of the 
view that a reduced GST rate to 18% will bring down a sizeable amount in vehicle 
price creating more demand  for newer vehicles . The increased sale due to the 
reduction in GST rate, will cover up the loss in GST revenue. 
(Para 49) 

39

prices, which can prove to be advantageous to the Government as the expected loss 
to the exchequer, due to the proposed reduction in GST slab in the Auto Sector, can

benefitting the industries that are dependent on crude oil and its derivatives.

REPORT 
 
The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Sector has emerged as a highly 
vibrant and dynamic sector of the Indian economy over the last five decades. It contributes 
significantly in the economic and social development of the country by fostering 
entrepreneurship and generating large-scale employment opportunities at comparatively lower 
capital cost, next only to agriculture. MSME Sector has strong linka ges to large indu stries as 
ancillary units and contributes significantly in the inclusive industrial development of the 
country. MSME Sector is also  helping in establishment of industries in economically backward 
regions and removing regional  inequalities, promising justifiable dispersion of national income 
and wealth. MSMEs are now widening their domain across various sectors of the economy, 
producing diverse range of products and services to meet demands of domestic as well as global 
markets and also proving to be a boon for aspiring entrepreneurs in India. 
1. As per the 73rd round of National Sample Survey (2015-16), t he MSME Sector is 
providing livelihood to around 11.10 crore people . Around 6.34 crore MSMEs contributed 
approximately 30 per cent to the G ross Domestic Product. Its share in total manufacturing and 
export is 33 per cent and 49 per cent respectively.  The primary responsibility of promotion and 
development of MSMEs is with the State  Government. Nevertheless, the role of the Ministry of 
MSME and its organizations is to assist the States in their  efforts to encourage entrepreneurship, 
employment generation, and livelihood  opportunities and enhance the competitiveness of 
MSMEs in the changed economic scenario. 
The major Schemes of the Ministry of MSME are as under: 
 Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP); 
 Modified Market Development Assistance (MMDA); 
 Interest Subsidy and Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme; 
 Strengthening of Infrastructure of Existing Weak Khadi Institutions and Assistance 
for Marketing Infrastructure; 
 Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE); 
 Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS); 
 Scheme for Technology Upgradation and Competitiveness; 
 A Scheme for Promoting Innovation and Rural Entrepreneurship (ASPIRE); 
 Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI); 

2 
 
 Micro and Small Enterprises–Cluster Development Programme (MSE-CDP); 
 Science & Technology (S&T); 
 Mission Solar Charkha  
 Honey Mission;  
 Kumbhar Shashaktikaran Programme; 
 The National Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe Hub; and 
 Scheme for Promotion of MSMEs in NE Region and Sikkim. 
 
 
New Definition for MSME 
 
2. The Committee was informed by the Ministry that since the  economy has undergone 
significant changes, a revision in MSME criteria of classification was  necessary to establish an 
objective system of classification and to provide ease of doing  business. Accordingly t he new 
classification became effective from 1 stJuly, 2020. The earlier criterion of classification under 
MSMED Act, 2006 was based on investment in plant and machinery/equipment. However, the 
revised definition remove d the distinction between Manufacturing and Service enterprises. 
Besides, a new criterion of turnover has been added and it expected to bring about many benefits 
that will aid MSMEs to grow in size. It was decided that the turnover with respect to exports will 
not be counted in the limits of turnover for any category of MSME s whether Micro, Small or 
Medium. It will help in attracting investments and creating more jobs in the MSME Sector. 
Besides, the classification of MSMEs  has also removed the difference between manufacturing 
and services. The Ministry also apprised the Commi ttee that this was also the demand of 
the stakeholders for a long time and that it is a paradigmatic and significant change. 
 
 The new definition of MSMEs is as under: 
      (Rs. in crore) 
 Category Investment Turnover 
Micro 1 5 
Small 10 50 
Medium 50 250 
 
Now the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) are classified as below: 

3 
 
(i) A micro enterprise, where the investment in plant and machinery or equipment does 
not exceed one crore rupees and turnover does not exceed five crore rupees; 
(ii) A small enterprise, where the investment in  plant and machinery or equipment does 
not exceed ten crore rupees and turnover does not exceed fifty crore rupees; and 
(iii) A medium enterprise, where the investment in plant and machinery or equipment 
does not exceed fifty crore rupees and turnover does not exceed two hundred and fifty 
crore rupees. 
 
3. The Committee hopes that th e new classification of MSMEs would  bring 
about positive changes in the MSME Sector. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that a study needs to be conducted to know the exact impact of 
COVID-19 Pandemic on the MSME Sector and to ascertain what benefits have 
accrued to the MSME Sector by change of criteria for classification of MSMEs  and 
introduction of various Sche mes. The Committee may also be apprised about the 
findings of the study for perusal. 
4. The Committee reiterates its recommendation contained in its 297 th Report that the 
growth of MSMEs is concentrated mostly in a few States only which induces the people to 
migrate to those areas in search of employment and livelihood. Therefore, the Ministry 
should work in the direction of removing all the existing geographical imbalances and 
ensure that equitable presence of MSMEs is there in all the States so that there is 
horizontal industrialization and adequate employment generation to tide over the situation 
created particularly due to COVID-19 Pandemic.  
 
Demand for Grants (2021-22) 
5. While making presentation on the DFG (202 1-22), the Ministry o f MSME 
informed the Committee  that the MSME Sector is providing livelihood to around 11.10 
crore people.  Further t he Committee was apprised that the MSME Sector is providing 
ample entrepreneurship opportunities to the aspiring entrepreneurs at a lower cost  and 
during the FY 2020-21, approximately 44,097 micro enterprises were assisted, generating 
employment opportunities for about 3.53 lakh people. 
6. Regarding the details of the Action Plan set for the Ministry for the year  2021-22, 
the Committee was infor med by the Ministry that an amount of Rs. 15699.65 crore has

been allocated to the Ministry of MSME for the year 2021 -22. The Action Plan of the 
Ministry focuses on strengthening the overall ecosystem of MSMEs by providing 
infrastructural support, marketin g avenues, proper access to finance,  technical support 
and capacity building etc. This action plan is broadly reflected in the Output -Outcome 
Monitoring Framework Document of the Ministry for FY 2021-22.

Ministry of MSME in the BE of 2021 -22 under ‘Guarantee for Emergency Credit Line 
for MSME Borrowers’ and the details regarding utilization of the proposed

Views/Suggestions of the MSME Associations 
 
18. The Committee also invited the views/suggestions of some of the prominent 
Associations in writing from MSME Sector like FICCI, FISME, CII, ASSOCHAM etc. 
The MSME Associations appreciated the recent initiatives viz. putting in place financial 

11 
 
support mechan ism through Fund of Funds, collateral free credit facility, broadening 
definition of MSMEs, introducing IT -based CHAMPIONS Portal for grievance redressal 
of MSMEs, encouraging entrepreneurship amongst Khadi & Village Industries and 
promotion of self-employment etc., taken by the Government of India for strengthening 
the MSME Sector. The Committee takes note of the valuable views/suggestions of the 
MSME Associations, which are as detailed below: 
 
(i) Introduction of Special framework for MSMEs under NCLT framework to increase 
the ease of doing business for MSMEs.  
 
(ii) Reduction in the time -limit for re -opening of income tax assessment from 6 years 
to 3 years to facilitate the ease of doing business for MSMEs. 
 
(iii) Increasing the annual turnover limit from  Rs. 5 crore to Rs. 10 crore for eligibility 
of exemption of audit to reduce the burden on MSMEs and encourage them to go 
for digital transaction which, in turn, would create transparency and develop trust 
amongst lenders. 
 
(iv) Soft loans at interest rate  of 3 -4% with a minimum tenure of 9 -10 years for 
repayment, easy land acquisition, less compliances could help in developing 
import substitution in the country. 
 
(v) Special Economic Zones (SEZs) to facilitate import substitution should be 
developed and sp ecial benefits should be provided to MSMEs for establishing 
units in such SEZs. 
 
(vi) Necessary steps should be taken by the Government towards settlement of delayed 
payments of MSMEs as early as possible which would help the MSMEs in 
meeting their working capital requirements. 
(vii) Steps should be taken towards reducing the logistics cost for MSMEs. 
 
(viii) For promoting exports, MSMEs need to meet a certain required international or 
regional specific standard for which adequate facilities are not availab le in the 
country. Besides, available testing facilities are costly which MSMEs cannot 
afford. Therefore, Testing & Certifications should be made convenient and 
cheaper for MSMEs. Besides, the MSMEs should be given subsidies for testing 
facilities and the Indian Testing Certificates should have global acceptance.

(ix) International Alliances for Technology Transfer with various developed and 
developing countries that give high priority to innovation and technology should 
be established. 
(x) Indian Missions  should play a proactive role in promoting MSME products in 
overseas market. 
 
 
(xi) Necessary Steps should be taken encourage and promote entrepreneurship 
amongst women to further employment generation in the country. 
 
 
(xii) NBFCs are an important source of organised credit to facilitate MSMEs and it

(xiii) As the current budget has no specific allocation/announcement for the MSMEs

Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan,  technologically updated and upgraded for adoption

Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP)  
 
32. PMEGP is a bank appraised and financed credit linked subsidy programme for generation 
of employment opportunities through establishment of non -farm based microenterprises for self-
employment in rural as well as urban areas of the country. KVIC is the single nodal agency at the 
national level to implement the scheme across the country and at State/District level the 
implementing agencies are the KVIC and State Khadi and Village Industries Boards (State  
KVIBs) in rural areas, and District Industries Centers (DICs) in both rural and urban areas , and 
Coir Board for coir related activities.

NER/Hill areas). Around 6.53 lakh micro units have been assisted so far with a total subsidy of 
Rs. 15,300 crore with estimated employment to 53.7 lakh persons.

Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme 
44. The Committee was informed by the Ministry that the Interest Subsidy Eligibility 
Certificate (ISEC) Scheme is one of the components of Khadi Vikas Yojana. It was introduced to 
mobilize the funds from banking institutions in order to cater to the additional  fund requirement 
of Khadi and Village Industries Institutions. For this, an Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate is 
issued to Khadi Institutions (KIs). The off take of the ISEC depends upon the production and 
sales capacity of Khadi Institutions and the nature of production i.e., Silk, Cotton, Woolen Khadi 
and Polyvastra. It strengthens the KIs to avail the bank finance for the shortfall in working 
capital. Under the Scheme 4% of the interest is to be borne by the KIs and the interest 
differential betw een the actual lending rate and 4% is provided by the Government of India  
through Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC) to the lending Banks. The funds for 
this purpose are provided to KVIC under the Khadi Vikas Yojana Grant.

disbursed to 1289 Khadi Institutions under the ISEC to Khadi & Polyvastra. During FY 2020 -21 
(up to 31-12-2020), Rs. 24.96 crore was disbursed to 1,002 Khadi Institutions and the anticipated 
disbursement under ISEC is Rs. 40.00 crore to 1370 Khadi Institutions (up to 31 - 03 - 2021).

Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI)  
50. The Committee was informed by the Ministry that Government of India has launched 
the Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) with an aim to 
organize the traditional artisan s into clusters and to make the Traditional Industries more 
productive, profitable and capable for generating sustained employment. Under the scheme, the 
clusters are provided with assistance in setting up Common Facility Centers, Raw Material 
Banks, procurement of machines, training, exposure visits, branding etc. Maximum support from 
Government of India under the scheme is up to Rs. 5 crore for a cluster of more than 500 artisans 
and up to Rs. 2.5 crore for up to 500 artisans.  
51. It was also informed that the Ministry of MSME have approved 335 proposals for 
setting up clusters under the scheme benefitting around 1.98 lakh artisans and approved an 
amount of Rs.784.85 crores as Government of India grant for implementation of clusters  since 
2015-16 to 2020-21 (till 31.12.2020). 79 clusters have become functional till 31.12.2020. These 
clusters are in Khadi, Coir, Handicraft, Handloom, Agro -processing, honey sector etc.  In 2020 -
21, 37 clusters have been approved till 31.12.2020 assisti ng 21,226 artisans. Ministry has 
released an amount of Rs. 127.41 cr. during the year 2020-21 (till 31.12.2020) for implementing 
the activities prescribed in the DPRs such as setting up of Common Facility Centres (CFC), 
procurement of machineries, conducti ng Soft Interventions activities such as marketing 
initiatives, awareness programmes etc.  

24 
 
52. Further, the Committee was informed that 371 clusters have been approved till now and 
only 82 clusters are operational under SFURTI Scheme. The Ministry submitte d that SFURTI is 
an excellent scheme targeted at the welfare of artisans across the farthest areas of the country and 
assured to give prominence to this Scheme.  Besides, the Ministry informed that normally setting 
up of clusters was taking around three years but now it is taking around one plus year. 
53. The Committee notes that the BE for SFURTI Scheme for FY 2020-21 i.e. Rs. 464.85 
crore was reduced at the RE Stage to Rs. 300 crore and the Actual Expenditure was only 
Rs. 192.54 crores till 31 st January, 2021. The Committee also notes that against a projected 
Budget Estimate of Rs. 500 crore for the SFRUTI Scheme for FY 2021 -2022, an allocation 
of only Rs. 170 crore has been made. The Committee expresses its concern over the low 
utilization pattern and red uction in allocations for an important Scheme of the Ministry, 
which is capable of generating employment in a large scale in the rural areas for the 
artisans, particularly during the Covid Pandemic. The Committee recommends that a 
holistic evaluation study of the Scheme may be conducted and based on the said study more 
allocations should be projected by the Ministry at the RE Stage for effective 
implementation of SFURTI Scheme for benefit of the traditional artisans. 
54. The Committee is constrained to note that out of 371 clusters which have been 
approved, only 82 clusters are operational so far. The Committee recommends that the 
process of setting up of SFURTI clusters should be expedited; targets should be set and 
ensure that the approved clusters are completed and become operational within the 
stipulated timeframe for benefit of artisans.   
55. The Committee was apprised by the Ministry that besides 219 Districts, 56 
Aspirational Districts have also been covered under S FURTI. The Committee recommends 
that more attention should be paid to target more and more Aspirational Districts across 
the country as this can immensely improve the socio-economic conditions of the inhabitants 
in those districts and improve the human dev elopment index. The Ministry may coordinate 
with the state governments and with concerted efforts desired results may be achieved.  
56. During the Covid Pandemic induced lockdowns, scores of migrant workers were 
forced to return to their native places and had to stay back for months without any 
livelihood/ employment.  SFURTI is one such Scheme which has the potential to generate 
employment in rural areas with less investment for the artisans. The Committee 

25 
 
recommends that Ministry should endeavour to set u p more SFURTI clusters and ensure 
that each and every district of the country has SFURTI clusters on the lines of one -district 
one-product to solve the problem of unemployment in rural areas.

91. The COVID -19 spread very fast to almost all the countries of the world  and on  11th 
March, 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared it as a Pandemic. In India, the first 
COVID-19 case was reported from Kerala on 30th January, 2020, and subsequently the Pandemic 
spread to almost all the States/UTs. In order to contain the spread of COVID -19 Pandemic, the 
Government of India took various steps such as enforcing social distancing norms, self -isolation 
measures, travel ban, border closure and lockdown of the entire country. 
92. The Pandemic has significantly hampered economic activity all across the world. The 
restricted movement due to lockdown had severe effect on all the sectors of the economy 
especially on the MSMEs  in India . Most of them did not have the capacity to deal with 
something so unexpected and unprecedented. Consequently MSMEs, which rely m ostly on the 
cash availability and informal employment , had to face problems such as sudden dip in or ders 
and cash flows, uncertainty in demand, labour related issues , supply chain disruption etc. 
Particularly the Micro E enterprises that comprised the majority of MSME s suffered massive 
losses due to the lockdowns because they had to run their businesses with only limited resources. 

36 
 
A large number of MSMEs comprising manufacturing and service/retail firms had to shut down 
their business es during nationwide lockdowns due to the disruptions in the supply chain as 
procurement of raw materials at affordable rates became very difficult.  
 
Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan 
93. Taking cognizance of the gravity of the situation, the Government announced a series of 
measures under the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan  for ameliorating the MSME s. The 
announcements were focused on various important aspects such as availability of credit, demand 
generation, grievance redressal and handholding of MSMEs etc. The steps inter-alia includes: 
 
(i) The Government has notified composite criteria of classification of MSMEs based on 
Investment in plant & machinery or equipment and Turnover of MSMEs as structural 
change to facilitate both existing as well as new entrepreneurs.  
 
(ii) Earlier process of filing  of Udyog Aaadhar  Memorandum has been replaced by 
Udyam Registration  on a Portal developed by the Ministry of MSME, which  is 
expected to bring about many benefits for the MSMEs to grow in size.  
 
(iii) Financial support to the stressed MSMEs with infusion of Rs. 20,000 crore equity 
support through Subordinate Debt which is likely to benefit more than 2 lakh 
MSMEs. 
 
(iv) Fund of Funds created to infuse equity worth Rs.50,  000 crore in the MSME Sector.  
A Rs.10, 000 crore Corpus Fund to be set up which  would provide equity funding to 
growth potential and viable MSMEs. 
 
(v) Regarding e nsuring timely payment to the MSMEs, the Government of India and 
CPSEs have to clear all receivables of MSMEs within 45 days under the Public 
Procurement Policy which will ease  the liquidity problem of MSMEs.  Besides, 
initiatives have been taken for monitoring settlement of dues of MSMEs by larger 
units (Public and Private) through online SAMADHAN and SAMBANDH Portals. 
 
(vi) Rs. 3 lakh crore collateral free automatic loans for business, including MSMEs. 
 
(vii) Global tender to be disallowed in Government procurement Tenders up  to Rs 200 
crores which will provide more market opportunities to domestic entities. 
 
94. Further, to streamline and ensure better outcome from the various Schemes implemented 
by the Ministry, a few Ministerial Task Forces (MTF) were set up with the following objectives: 
 

37 
 
(i) Make India a global leader in Industry 4.0; 
(ii) Make India a Global Manufacturing Hub and Leading Exporter; 
(iii) Create world class Industrial/MSME Clusters; 
(iv) Establish effective Industry-Institute linkages and make Globally Benchmarked  
         MSME Institutes and;  
(v) To make Indian MSMEs/Industry lean, modern, eco -friendly and Globally  
Competitive. 
95. Based on the findings of these Task Forces requisi te changes/modifications are being 
made in various Schemes. Also t he CHAMPIONS Portal acts as a platform for receiving 
suggestions/ideas from general public for improving the Schemes and to cover many aspects of 
e-governance including grievance redressal a nd handholding of MSMEs . Several e -initiatives 
like setting up of Business  to Customer (B2C) official online e -Commerce Portal and an online 
payment portal by Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), online Portal to connect 
Suppliers, Showrooms and Franchisee network by Coir Board have been taken. Regular analysis 
of data and continuous interaction with Nodal Agencies and Implementing Agencies are being 
undertaken for these Schemes.  
 96. In response to a query regarding the new initiatives/schemes the Ministry proposes 
to implement during 2021-22, the Committee was informed that the Government of India has 
taken a series of measures under Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan. Some of these measures  are 
being implemented through the Ministry of MSME for revival and development of the 
stressed MSMEs which inter -alia include financial, technological, administrative measures 
etc. in revival and development  of the MSMEs . From the credit side, Government has 
announced the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Subordinate Debt (CGSSD) for Stressed 
MSMEs which is being implemented by the Ministry of MSME.  
 97. Further, the Committee was informed that the CGSSD Scheme was launched on 
24thJune, 2020. As on 03.02.2021, a total number of 34 Banks have registered as Member 
Lending Institutions under this Scheme and have extended 272 guarantees amounting to Rs. 
30.84 crore. The objective of the scheme is to provide personal loan through banks to the 
promoters of stressed MSMEs for infusion as equity/quasi equity in the business and provides 
Sub-Debt support in respect of restructuring of MSMEs. The salient features of the Scheme 
are as under: 
(i)   it provides for Rs. 20.000 crore as subordinate debt for Stressed MSMEs. 
(ii) MSME entrepreneurs of such stressed units find it difficult to bring in this additional 
equity and that in turn severely constrains the survival of these units. 

38 
 
(iii) Infusion of capital in such units in the form of equity or sub-debt will be of substantial 
help in sustaining and reviving the MSMEs which have either become NPA or are on the 
brink of becoming NPA. 
(iv)  Promoter(s) of the MSMEs will be given credit equal to 15% of their stake (equity plus 
debt) or Rs. 75 lakh whichever is lower, Promoter(s) in turn will infuse this amount in the 
MSME unit as equity and thereby enhance the liquidity and maintain debt-equity ratio. 
(v)  90% guarantee coverage for this sub-debt will be given under the scheme and 10% would 
come from the concerned Promoters. 
(vi)  There will be a moratorium of 7 years on payment of principal whereas maximum tenure 
for repayment will be 10 years. 
(vii)  Till date, 34 Banks including all PSU Banks have come on-board by signing MoU with 
CGTMSE for becoming the Member Lending Institution (MLI) of the Scheme. 
 98. As far as Rs. 50,000 crore Equity Infusion throug h MSME Fund of Funds (SRI Fund) 
is concerned, NSIC Venture Capital Fund Ltd. (NVCFL) has been incorporated to anchor the 
Mother Fund as SPV. In addition to this, Department of Financial Services is implementing Rs. 3 
lakh crore collateral free automatic loans for business, including MSMEs. Under this scheme, 
around 91 lakh guarantees have been issued till 25.01.2021.  
99. Further, u nder the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme  (ECLGS) which was 
introduced as an emergency measure to combat the unprecedented crisis caused due to the 
Covid-19 Pandemic, credit from Scheduled Commercial Banks, Financial Institutions, Non -
Banking Financial Companies is provided to eligible MSMEs, bus iness enterprises and 
individual loans for business purposes up  to 20% of their outstanding credit as on 29.02.2020. 
This additional credit is fully covered by a credit guarantee provided by National Credit 
Guarantee Trustee Company Ltd. (NCGTC). Loans pro vided under ECLGS have a 12 -month 
moratorium on repayment of principal. ECLGS is also available to eligible non -MSME 
enterprises. However, in FY 2021 -22, an allocation of Rs.10,  000 crore has been made by the 
Ministry of Finance to the Ministry of M SME under the Guaranteed Emergency Credit Line 
(GECL) facility for MSMEs . However, t he other modalities regarding utilization of allocated 
funds are being worked out in consultation with Ministry of Finance. 
100. Under the t echnological initiatives, the CHAMPIONS Portal has been launched by the 
Ministry of MSME which covers many aspect of e-governance including grievance redressal and 
handholding of MSMEs. It is a unified, empowered, robust, and a technology driven platform 
designed for helping and promoting the MSMEs with the following basic objectives: 

39 
 
● To help the MSMEs in th e present  situation in terms of finance, raw materials, labour, 
permissions etc. 
● To help the MSMEs capture new opportunities including manufacturing of medical items 
& accessories. 
● To identify the sparks, i.e., the bright MSMEs who can withstand at present and become 
national and international champions.

Departments and 24 State Governments, 54 Banks/Financial Institutions/Regional Rural Banks 
including 19 Private Sector Banks, have already been on -boarded on the portal to address the 
queries related to Credit in a fast track manner. 52 CPSEs have appointed their respective nodal

number of 27, 237 grievances were received and 98.33 % i.e. 26,783 has been replied.

DIs are working with State Governments in helping the MSME units for procuring raw materials

w.e.f. 1stJune, 2020 and again by 0.50% per annum on 1 st October, 2020 to provide cheaper 
financial assistance to MSME units has been t aken by the Ministry for development of MSME 
Sector. 
103. The Committee notes that Ministry has launched CHAMPIONS Portal for 
grievance redressal of MSME units but many small units are not aware about this 
portal and its functions. The Committee recommends  that adequate steps should be 
taken by the Ministry to create awareness about this portal and more budgetary 
allocations be made for publicity purposes. The use of the Portal may be made as 
simple as possible and also the portal should have an option for Hindi language as 
well as the Regional languages for ease of understanding. 

40 
 
104. As a consequence of COVID -19 Pandemic and subsequent lockdowns, numerous 
MSMEs became stressed and could not sustain their businesses due to u navailability of 
working capital, raw material and manpower. Accordingly the CGSSD Scheme has been 
designed to infuse capital in the form of subordinate debt to the MSMEs, which have either 
become NPA or are on the verge of becoming NPA,  to help them incre ase their liquidity. 
The Committee is of the view that the CGSSD Scheme has the capability of providing much 
desired liquidity to the MSMEs who are desperately in need of capital to sustain their 
business. The Committee therefore, recommends that all the p rocedures and technicalities 
for availing the benefits of the Scheme should be simplified;  irreducible minimum interest 
should be charged; repayment tenure of the loan should be kept at the maximum and; a 
friendly and favourable approach should be adopted  by the banks to help revive the 
MSMEs.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE – AT A GLANCE 
 
1. The Committee hopes that the new classification of MSMEs would bring about 
positive changes in the MSME Sector. The Committee therefore, recommends that a study 
needs to be conducted to know the exact impact of COVID -19 Pandemic on the MSME 
Sector and to ascertain what benefits have accrued to the MSME Sector by change of 
criteria for classification of MSMEs and introduction of various Schemes. The Committee 
may also be apprised about the findings of the study for perusal. 
                   (Para 3) 
 
2. The Committee reiterates its recommendation contained in its 297 th Report that the 
growth of MSMEs is concentrated mostly in a few States only which induces the people to 
migrate to those areas  in search of employment and livelihood. Therefore, the Ministry 
should work in the direction of removing all the existing geographical imbalances and 
ensure that equitable presence of MSMEs is there in all the States so that there is 
horizontal industrialization and adequate employment generation to tide over the situation 
created particularly due to COVID-19 Pandemic.  
                   (Para 4) 
 
3. The Committee observes that the allocations of the Ministry were either reduced or 
enhanced at the R.E. stage, but the actual expenditure incurred most of the time is less than 
the Revised Estimate. The Committee is therefore, of the opinion that proper es timation 
should be done by the Ministry beforehand to ensure that budget is utilized optimally as 
far as possible. The Ministry should also monitor the output of its various Schemes, 
including individual components so that the output targets are achieved timely.   
(Para 11) 
 
4. The Budget Estimate for FY 2021-22 is Rs. 15699.65 crore, which seems a significant 
increase vis-à-vis FY 2020-21. However, out of this amount an allocation of Rs. 10,000 crore 
has been earmarked for the Guaranteed Emergency Credit L ine Scheme (GECL) and in 
effect Rs. 5699.65 crore is the actual allocation, which is a reduction from the BE of FY 
202021. The Committee is worried that in absence of adequate funds how the Ministry is 
planning to implement its various schemes effectively in the present scenario of COVID -19 
Pandemic when MSME Sector is starved of funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may ask for an enhanced allocation at the RE Stage for proper 
implementation of its flagship Schemes and strengthening of the MSME Sector.   
(Para 12) 
 
5. The Committee is also of the opinion that the details of the action plan regarding the 
utilization of funds allocated under GECL Scheme should be worked out and furnished to 
the Committee for perusal. 
(Para 13) 
 
6. The Committee observes that the Ministry could utilize only 66% of the RE for the 
FY 2020-21 (up to January, 2021), which is a cause of concern. However, the Ministry cited 
COVID-19 Pandemic as the main reason for the underutilization of allocated funds. On th e 

43 
 
other hand, the Committee is of the opinion that the budget utilization should have been 
more because of the demand created due to COVID -19 Pandemic in the MSME Sector.  
The Committee is of the opinion that MSME Sector presently is in desperate need of fu nds. 
Therefore, the Ministry must ensure that the allocated budget is utilized optimally so that 
MSME Sector may thrive. 
(Para 15) 
 
7. The Committee notes that up to the end of 3 rd quarter of FY 2020 -21, the Ministry 
could utilize only 54% of the actual budget allocation i.e. Rs. 5664.22 crore. The Committee 
is constrained to note the underutilization of allocated funds and  would like to know the 
reasons for continuously projecting inflated demands and thereafter underutilizing the 
funds. The Committee therefore, recommends that proper assessment and planning should 
be made beforehand in respect of utilization of funds quarter -wise so that there is no rush 
to spend more in the last quarters of the year. 
(Para 17) 
 
8. The Committee is of the view that KVIC should concentrate more on its technology 
improvement and products upgradation aspect in this age of stiff competition with big 
market players. The Committee, therefore, recommends that latest training programmes 
by experienced and experts having expertise  in the field should be imparted to the artisans 
through its network of training institutions for product design and quality improvement in 
order to promote export of Khadi products. Further, the Committee recommends that the 
process of revamping and reori entation of KVIs should also be done wherever required so 
that it helps in productivity development of Khadi and Village Industries. 
(Para 23) 
 
9. The Committee raised concern over difference in BE i.e. Rs. 905 crore for FY 2021 -
22 vis-à-vis BE for FY 2020 -21 i.e. Rs. 1525 crore for Khadi Sector as this being an 
important sector which generates large scale employment for rural people. The Committee 
recommends that considering the importance of Khadi Sector and its employment 
generating potential, an increased budget allocation should be asked for at RE stage by the 
Ministry.  
(Para 24) 
 
10. Recently Khadi Prakritik Paint  has been developed and launched by Khadi and Village 
Industries Commission. The paint is said to be cow dung based, eco -friendly, non-toxic product 
with anti -fungal, anti -bacterial properties. It is claimed that the paint is cost -effective and 
odorless and has been certified by Bureau of Indian Standards. The Committee appreciates the 
efforts made by the KVIC and recommends tha t such type of initiatives and innovations 
take place regularly with the combination of innovative ideas and latest technology. The  
Committee therefore, recommends that adequate funds should be allocated for R&D and 
Technology related support facilities in order to improve the quality of Khadi products vis-
a-vis international products. 
(Para 25) 
 

44

market linkages for strengthening the MSME Sector and recommends that the Ministry 
should analyze the marketing system of MSMEs of developed countries and their system of 
newer technology adoption for their development and adopt the best practices followed 
internationally for advancement and development of indigenous MSMEs.  
(Para 28) 
 
12. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry in providing financial 
help to Khadi artisans during Covid Pandemic through Artisan Welfare Fund Trust.  The 
Committee recommends that some kind of contingent fund or financial provision should be 
put in place by the Ministry keeping in view the welfare of the artisans associated with 
MSME Sector for the unforeseen situations like Covid P andemic as a social security 
measure so that some kind of monetary help can be provided to artisans in times of distress 
in future.  
(Para 31)

45

33. The Committee desired that delay in payments by CPSEs and Government 
Departments affects MSMEs adversely as they need cash flow to run their businesses. The 
Committee however, recommends that delayed payments of MSMEs from CPSEs be 
monitored through the SA MBANDH and SAMADHAAN Portals regularly and the 
pending payments of MSMEs may be cleared by CPSEs and other Government agencies at 
the earliest for strengthening the liquidity of MSMEs. 
(Para 78) 
 
34. The Committee notes that TReDS is a new initiative by th e Ministry of MSME for 
resolving the problem of delayed payments to MSMEs by CPSEs/Government Agencies. 
Making penal provision of 1% per month for erring buyers will definitely prove to be a 
deterrent for defaulting buyers. The Committee expects that the p enal provision is 
enforced in letter and spirit. The Committee hopes that TReDS will able to solve the 
problem of delayed payments and improve the liquidity position of the MSMEs. The 
Committee recommends that TReDS should be implemented strictly and monit ored 
regularly and the MSMEs may be exempted from paying charges for on -boarding this 
platform beyond 31st March 2021. 
(Para 79) 
 
35. The Committee observes that NSIC through its Vendor Development Programmes 
sensitize and facilitate MSEs, including SC/ST enterprises, to become qualified vendors to 
public sector enterprises and other Government Departments as per the provision of 25% 
mandatory procurement under Public Procurement Policy. Of this, 4% should be from 
SC/ST MSEs. However, during its visit to Ko lkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in January, 

49 
 
2020, the Committee found that while the PSUs and Government procurement from MSEs 
has been gradually improving, procurement from SC/ST units is negligible. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that there should be mo re Vendor Development Programmes 
organized to popularize Public Procurement Policy among MSEs especially SC/ST and 
Women entrepreneurs. 
(Para 83) 
 
36. The Committee notes that the pace of expenditure under the NSCST Hub Scheme is 
not at all encouraging and that the allocation of Rs. 150 crore in the BE 2020-2021 has been 
reduced to Rs. 120 crore at the RE Stage. Further, the allocation for FY 2021 -2022 has also 
been kept at Rs. 120 crore at the BE Stage. The Committee fails to understand the reasons 
for such slow pace of expending in respect of such an important Scheme, which has been 
specially formulated for the marginalized section of the society. The C ommittee 
recommends that the Ministry should take adequate steps to speed up the spending 
process, so that allocated amount gets utilized to the optimum.  
(Para 84) 
 
37. The Committee observes that under National SC/ST Hub, the Actual Expenditure 
has always been less than the BE. The Committee is concerned about the under -utilization 
of allocated funds meant for the marginalized communities of the society. The Committee 
recommends that Ministry should endeavor to improve the situation by ensuring that the 
budget earmarked for SC/ST Hub Scheme is utilized fully for the benefit of the 
communities. Creating awareness among SC/ST entrepreneurs, ground level support and 
handholding of SC/ST entrepreneurs may work well in improving the performance of this 
scheme. Underutilization of funds is a serious cause of concern for the Committee; 
therefore, Ministry is advised to ensure full utilization of funds. 
(Para 85) 
 
38. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should create an All India Database 
of SC/ST entrepreneurs’ locations and vocations and share the same with CPSEs so that 
CPSEs can locate SC/ST units easily for availing their services. Also, the SC/ST Hub 
should run NSQF compliant skill development programmes for SC/ST technicians who 
could take contract jobs and services that CPSEs outsource. 
(Para 86) 
 
39. The trend under Public Procurement Policy has not been encouraging over the 
years. The Committee therefore, recommends that the trend should be reversed and 
adequate steps should be taken by the Ministry to ensure fair participation of SC/ST MSEs 
in Public Procurement Policy.  The Committee also recommends that more special VDPs 
should be organized for SC/ST entrepreneurs for improving their participation in Public 
Procurement Policy. The Ministry  should also adopt handholding approach while 
promoting SC/ST entrepreneurs.   
(Para 87) 
 
40. The Committee observes that many schemes of the Ministry are not working 
satisfactorily in North Eastern Region and has a very negligible presence in these areas.   

50 
 
Even the number of ISEC issued under Khadi and Polyvastra are also not impressive. The 
Committee recommends that serious efforts should be made by the Ministry to benefit the 
people of NER through its various schemes with the help of State Governments 
particularly potential women and SC/ST entrepreneurs be encouraged to participate in the 
growth process. 
(Para 88) 
 
41. The Committee recommends that Testing & Certifications should be made 
convenient and cheaper for MSMEs and they should be provided some sort of subsidy for 
availing such testing facilities. It is also required that a mechanism should be developed so 
that testing can be done at Indian Centres whereas certificates for the same test could be 
issued from various global testing centres, which are acceptable in respective 
countries/regions.  
(Para 90) 
 
42. The Committee notes that Ministry has launched CHAMPIONS Portal for grievance 
redressal of MSME units but many small units are not aware about this portal and its 
functions. The Committee recommends that adequate steps should be taken by the 
Ministry to create awareness about this portal and more budgetary alloc ations be made for 
publicity purposes. The use of the Portal may be made as simple as possible and also the 
portal should have an option for Hindi language as well as the Regional languages for ease 
of understanding. 
(Para 103) 
 
43. As a consequence of COV ID-19 Pandemic and subsequent lockdowns, numerous 
MSMEs became stressed and could not sustain their businesses due to unavailability of 
working capital, raw material and manpower. Accordingly the CGSSD Scheme has been 
designed to infuse capital in the form of subordinate debt to the MSMEs, which have either 
become NPA or are on the verge of becoming NPA,  to help them increase their liquidity. 
The Committee is of the view that the CGSSD Scheme has the capability of providing much 
desired liquidity to the MSMEs who are desperately in need of capital to sustain their 
business. The Committee therefore, recommends that all the procedures and technicalities 
for availing the benefits of the Scheme should be simplified;  irreducible minimum interest 
should be cha rged; repayment tenure of the loan should be kept at the maximum and; a 
friendly and favourable approach should be adopted by the banks to help revive the 
MSMEs. 
    (Para 104)

REPORT 
The Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) are rightly hailed as „the temples of modern India.‟ 
They were conceived to be a critical component of our mixed economy and were put into 
operation for transforming the independent India into a modern and industrially advanced nation. 
Primacy given to the CPSEs arose out of the fact that the private enterprises were not adequately 
equipped to undertake the mammoth task of creating infrastructure and other facilities which 
were indispensable for nation -building. The contribution of PSEs towards the growth of Indian 
economy through measures such as generation of income, capital formation, generation of 
employment, development of infrastructure facilities, building a strong industrial base, export 
promotion and impor t substitution, contribution to central exchequer, removal of regional 
disparities, checking concentration of income & wealth etc. is really commendable. 
 The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) in India 
2. The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSE s) comprise enterprises established by the 
Government of India (GOI) as Government companies under Section 617 of the Companies Act, 
and wherein the equity holding of the GOI is more than 50 per cent. It also includes statutory 
corporations constituted und er specific statutes of the Parliament. The CPSEs do not, however, 
include departmental undertakings, banking institutions and enterprises where equity holding of 
the GOI is 50% or less.  
3. The number of CPSEs has increased from 5 during the first five ye ar plan to 366 as on 
31.3.2020. The cumulative investment (paid up capital plus long term loans), which was Rs. 29 
crore in 5 enterprises as on 31.03.1951, has gone up to Rs.  20.62 lakh crore in 366 CPSEs.  Out 
of these 366 CPSEs, 256 are in Operation, 96 CPSEs have yet to commence business and 14 are 
under liquidation or approved for closure. Out of 256 operating CPSEs as many as 171 CPSEs 
showed profit during 2019 -20, 83 CPSEs incurred losses during the year, and 1 CPSE had no 
profit no loss. The Central Public Sector Enterprises are under the administrative control of 
various Ministries/ Departments and decision with regard to major investments, expansion, 
diversification, joint ventures, modernisation, technology upgradation, etc. are taken by the 
CPSEs in consultation with their respective administrative Ministries/Departments. 
 Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) 
4.      In their 52nd Report, the Estimates Committee of 3rd Lok Sabha (1962 -67) stressed the 
need for setting up a centralized coordinatin g unit, which could also make continuous appraisal 
of the performance of public enterprises. This led to the setting up of the Bureau of Public 
Enterprises (BPE) in 1965 in the Ministry of Finance. Subsequently, as a result of the 
reorganization of the Ministries/Departments of the Union Government in September, 1985, BPE 
was made part of the Ministry of Industry. In May, 1990, BPE was made a full fledged 
Department known as the DPE. Presently, it is part of the Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public 
Enterprises (Mo HI &PE).                            
 

2 
 
5.      The DPE is the nodal department for all the CPSEs and formulates policy pertaining to 
them. It lays down, in particular, policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, 
autonomy and financi al delegation and personnel management in CPSEs. It further collects and 
maintains information in the form of a Public Enterprises Survey on several areas in respect of 
CPSEs.        
6.      In fulfilling its role, the Department coordinates with other Min istries, CPSEs and 
concerned organizations. As per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government, the 
following subjects have been allocated to the DPE: 
 Coordination of matters of general policy affecting all Public-Sector Enterprises.  
 Residual work relating to erstwhile Bureau of Public Enterprises including Industrial 
Management Pool. 
 Evaluation and monitoring the performance of Public Sector Enterprises, including the 
Memorandum of Understanding mechanism. 
 Matters relating to Permanent Machinery of  Arbitration for the Public -Sector 
Enterprises.  
 Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central Public Sector 
Undertakings under Voluntary Retirement Scheme. 
 Review of capital projects and expenditure in Central Public Sector Enterprises. 
 Measures aimed at improving performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises and other 
capacity building initiatives of Public Sector Enterprises. 
 Rendering advice relating to revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector Enterprises 
including the mechanisms therefore. 
 Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises. 
 Matters relating to International Center for Public Enterprises. 
 Categorization of Central Public Sector Enterprises including conferring „Ratna‟ status. 
 Survey of Public Enterprises. 
7.      According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public 
Enterprises the Vision and Mission statements of DPE are as follows: 
 Vision 
 “Effective, Profitable and Globally Competitive Central Public Sector Enterprises” 
 Mission 
  “To continuously improve management and performance of CPSEs through Corporate 
Governance, Performance Evaluation, Human Resource Management, Research & Development 
so as to enhance their global competitiveness” 
 
 
 

3 
 
 Impact of Covid-19 and the Lockdown on CPSEs 
8. The impact of Coid -19 pandemic on India has been largely disruptive in terms of 
economic activity and loss of human lives.  CPSEs have been no exception to the adverse impact 
of the pandemic & subsequent lockdowns.  CPSEs being the maj or thread in the socio-economic 
fabric of the country, it has to witness unprecedented challenges like temporary shutdown, 
reduced scale of operation and production, manpower shortage, supply chain disruptions, 
restricted logistics and transportation etc.,  posed by the ongoing Covid -19 pandemic, on the 
operations and production capacity of the CPSEs.

10. The Committee is deeply concerned about the adverse impact of Covid -19 pandemic 
on CPSEs and the huge losses suffered by almost all the af oresaid CPSEs in the 1 st  and 2nd  
quarter of the financial year 2020 -2021 as compared to that of the previous financial year.

11. The information submitted by DPE regarding categorization and autonomy of CPSEs is 
as under:-  
Categorization of CPSEs 
12.  CPSEs are categorized into four schedules  namely „A‟, „B‟, „C‟ & „D‟ based on criteria 
such as quantitative parameters, i.e., Investment, Capital Employed, Net Sales, Profit before Tax, 
Number of employees and units, Capacity Addition, Revenue per employee, Sales/Capital 
Employed, Capacity Utiliz ation, Value added per employee as well as qua litative  parameters, 

4 
 
i.e., National importance, Complexities of the problems being faced by the company, Level of 
technology, Prospects of expansion and diversification and competition from other sectors are t o 
be considered while examining such proposals. In addition, critical/strategic importance of the 
concerned CPSE as well as factors such as Share price, MoU ratings, Ratna status, ISO 
certification are also taken into consideration. 
13.        The present procedure of categorization of CPSEs involves consideration of the 
proposals in the administrative Ministry concerned and the Department of Public Enterprises 
which consults the Public Enterprises Selection Board. The categorization of CPSEs has 
implications mainly for organizational structure and salary of Board level incumbents of the 
concerned CPSE. It also plays a role in grant of autonomy to the Board s of CPSEs under „Ratna‟ 
scheme. A s informed by DPE, at present there are 66 Schedule „A‟, 65 Schedule „B‟, 44 
Schedule „C‟ and 5 Schedule „D‟ CPSEs. The schedule -wise list of CPSEs is given in 
Annexure-I.                                                                                          
   Autonomy of CPSEs 
14.     The endeavor of the Government is t o make Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) 
autonomous board managed companies. Under Articles of Association, the Board of Directors of 
CPSEs enjoys autonomy in respect of recruitment, promotion and other service conditions of 
below board level emplo yees. The Board of Directors of a CPSE exercises delegated powers 
subject to broad policy guidelines issued by Government from time to time. The Government has 
granted enhanced powers to the Boards of the profit -making enterprises under various schemes 
like Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna by delegating powers in the areas of (i) capital 
expenditure, (ii) investment in joint ventures/subsidiaries, (iii) mergers & acquisitions, (iv) 
human resources management, etc.  
15. The main objective of the Maharatna s cheme which was introduced in 2010 is to 
empower mega CPSEs to expand their operations and emerge as global giants. The Maharatna 
Scheme empowers big sized CPSEs to expand their operations and emerge as global giants.The 
Government had introduced the Navra tna scheme, in 1997, to identify Central Public Sector 
Enterprises (CPSEs) that had comparative advantages and to support them in their drive to 
become global giants.  In October 1997, the Government had decided to grant enhanced 
autonomy and delegation of financial powers to some other profit making companies subject to 
certain eligibility conditions and guidelines to make them efficient and competitive. These 
companies, called Miniratna, are in two categories, namely, Category - I and Category -II. As 
informed by DPE, p resently there are 10 Maharatna CPSEs, 14 Navratna CPSEs and 73 
Miniratna CPSEs (61 Miniratna category-I and 12 Miniratna category-II) (Annexure-II). 
16.      Responding to a query of the Committee regarding the operational conditions of all th e 
CPSEs as of December 2020, DPE, in a written submission has informed that the Public

Scheme of  Research, Development and Consultancy (RDC) on Generic issues related to 
Public Sector Enterprises : 
31.    The Scheme of RDC on Generic issues of Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) was 
introduced in the year 2007 -08 and is being implemented since 2008 -09. In view of instructions 
issued by the Ministry of Finance (MoF) with regard to rationalization of Schemes, the  Scheme 
for Skill Development/Training programme to executives/employees of State Level Public 
Enterprises (SLPEs) was merged with the Scheme of RDC on Generic issues of Public Sector 
Enterprises (PSEs) during the year 2016-17. 

10 
 
32.    RDC scheme was modified so that activities could be spread round the year and its scope 
was expanded and diversified to include more activities. Some of the features of revised scheme 
are elaborated as under: 
        i.          Thematic studies and consultancies on generic is sues like corporate governance, 
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) system, professionalization, project management, risk 
management, human resource management, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) etc. related 
to Public Sector Enterprises are undertaken. I n addition, benchmarking studies on selected 
sectors are also undertaken to enable enterprises to move towards achieving those benchmarks 
and become nationally /internationally competitive. 
      ii.          With objective to gain experience in many ways of learning and to keep engaged 
through learning activities seminars, workshops, conferences, etc. on various generic issues are 
organized. After coming into force of the provisions of Companies Act, 2013 on Corporate 
Social Responsibility (CSR), frequent meets are held. 
    iii.          Under RDC Scheme, MoU is very important instrument towards improving the 
performance of the CPSEs. Some modifications and improvements made in MoU mechanism 
since 2016 -17 include (i) proposed result oriented parameters (ii ) Parameter included for 
monitoring CAPEX contracts/projects running/completed without time/cost overrun (iii) CAPEX 
parameter weightage has been increased; and (iv) Procurement policy issued by Ministry of 
MSME has been given importance. Efforts are being  made for online system based on a single 
window concept for all MoU related matters for all stakeholders. Task force system has been 
dispensed with and now, Inter- Ministerial Committee of MoU has taken place. 
    iv.          DPE supplements the efforts of CPSEs/ SLPEs in improving / upgrading the skills of 
managers / executives / employees through capacity building Skill Development / Training 
Programmes for upgrading the skills and knowledge of their executives. To supplement the 
efforts of SLPEs/CPSEs,  DPE conducts training programmes in collaboration with some of the 
premier management / training institutes IITs, IIMs, ASCI, IIPA etc. This enables wider 
exposure and sharing of experience on pertinent issues. 
      v.          The guidelines on Corporate Governance for CPSEs issued by DPE stipulate training to 
newly inducted Non Official Directors (NODs) in the business model of the company. Besides 
induction training by CPSEs with a view to familiarize with the rules and regulations, business 
module, risk profile etc., DPE also in collaboration with respective CPSEs, from time to time, 
organizes general short term training for NODs, official directors and other Directors on the 
boards of CPSEs on relevant areas including model code of business ethics and  conduct of the 
company. This enriches the board in suggesting the best solution for short/long term viability/ 
profitability of the enterprises. 
    vi.          The objective of International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE) Ljubljana, 
Slovenia is to promote and support enterprise development in developing countries in both 
private and public sector. ICPE is an intergovernmental organization. Being a founder member 
of ICPE, India has been taking active part in its activities by way of attending Council/Assembly 
Sessions regularly at the level of Secretary.

Counselling, Retraining and Redeployment (CRR) Scheme for Separated Employees of 
CPSEs:  
43. The CRR sch eme is being implemented by DPE since 2001 -02. The scheme has been 
regularly reviewed to keep it abreast with the requisite needs to meet  its desired objectives. The 
scheme was modified in November, 2007 and again in February, 2016 in order to widen its scope 
and coverage and to standardize methodology of training design and delivery in line with 
National Skill Qualification Framework. Further, based on internal review, DPE has approached 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) to include the  skill training through 
its Tool Room/ Technology Centres that are in demand.   The evaluation of the CRR scheme was 
done by Indian Institute of Public Administration (IIPA) in 2019 for FYs 2016 -17 & 2017 -18. 
The findings as pointed out by IIPA with respect  to job fairs, monitoring of the scheme have 
been shared with NSDC and incorporated in the scheme. The objectives of the CRR scheme are 
as under: 
  i.        Separated employees of CPSEs to be brought into the mainstream economy and thereby   
 contribute to national income.  
 ii.     Reorientation of VRS / VSS optees / dependents to enable them to adjust to new 
 environment and adopt new vocations.  
  iii.      Skill development for VRS optees/dependents for their redeployment.  
  iv.      Exposure to various industry associations, which is also a component of the CRR   
 scheme, to help the trainees in product / service selection.  
 v.        Awareness of various Central and State Government loan assistance/ subsidized schemes.
