ANNEXURES 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
47 
 
ANNEXURE- I 
Measures taken so far to support MSMEs 
 
A. Atmanirbhar Bharat  
1. ₹ 3 lakh crores Collateral -free Automatic Loans for Businesses, including 
MSMEs: The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) has been 
formulated as a relief measure to MSMEs by providing them additional funding 
of up to ₹ 3 lakh crore in the form of a fully guaranteed emergency credit line. 
Borrowers with up to ₹ 25 crore outstanding and ₹ 100 crore turnover are 
eligible. This scheme provides 100 per cent credit guarantee cover to Banks and 
NBFCs on principal and interest. No guarantee fee, no fresh collateral is required.  
2. ₹20,000 crore Subordinate D ebt for Stressed MSMEs : Provision made for ₹ 
20,000 crore subordinate debt for MSMEs which are NPAs or are stressed. 
Government to support them with ₹ 4,000 crore to Credit Guarantee Trust for 
Micro and Small enterprises (CGTMSE). Banks are expected to pro vide the 
subordinate-debt to promoters of such MSMEs equal to 15 per cent of the 
existing stake in the unit subject to a maximum of ₹ 75 lakhs.  
3. ₹ 50,000 crores equity infusion through MSME Fund of Funds:  Government to 
set up a Fund of Funds with a corpus of ₹ 10,000 crore that will provide equity 
funding support for MSMEs. The Fund of Funds shall be operated through a 
mother and a few daughter funds. It will provide equity funding for viable 
MSMEs. This scheme will help MSMEs to expand its size and capacit y and will 
also encourages them to get listed on stock exchanges.  
4. New definition of MSME: Low threshold in MSME definition have created a fear 
among MSMEs of graduating out of the benefits. Hence, government has revised 
definition of MSME by raising the I nvestment limit. An additional criteria of 
turnover has been introduced and distinction between manufacturing and service 
sector stands removed.  
5. Global tenders to be disallowed upto ₹ 200 crores:  General Financial Rules 
(GFR) of the Government amended to disallow global tender enquiries in 
government procurement of goods and services of value of less than ₹ 200 crores. 
This is a step in support of the Make in India initiative and will promote MSMEs 
to grow.  
6. Other Measures for MSMEs: e-market linkage for M SMEs to act as a 
replacement for trade fairs and exhibitions. MSME receivables from Government 

 
 
48 
 
and CPSEs to be released in 45 days. This would help MSMEs to solve the 
problems of marketing and liquidity.  
7. Income Tax Refund:  Income tax refunds to nearly 8.2  lakh small businesses 
worth ₹ 5,204 crore has been issued with the objective to help MSMEs to carry 
on their business activities without pay cuts and layoffs in these challenging 
times. 
8. Relief of ₹ 1500 crores to MUDRA - Shishu loans: GoI to provide Intere st 
subvention of 2 per cent to prompt payees for a period of 12 months. Small 
business under MUDRA to be benefited. 
9. Ease of doing business for business including MSMEs : Government announced 
further enhancement of Ease of Doing business through Insolvency a nd 
Bankruptcy Code (IBC) related measures which include (a). raising of the 
minimum threshold to initiate insolvency proceedings to Rs. 1 crore from Rs. 1 
lakh (which largely insulates MSMEs), (b) special insolvency resolution 
framework for MSMEs under Sec tion 240A of the Code, (c) suspension of fresh 
initiation of insolvency proceedings up to one year depending upon the pandemic 
situation and (d) empowering Central Government to exclude COVID 19 related 
debt from the definition of “default” under the Code for the purpose of triggering 
insolvency proceedings.  
10. Credit Guarantee Scheme for Micro Finance Institutions:  Guarantee to be 
provided to Scheduled Commercial Banks for loans to new or existing NBFC -
MFIs or MFIs for on lending upto  Rs 1.25 lakh to approximately 25 lakh small 
borrowers. Loans from banks to be capped at Marginal Cost of Funds based 
Lending Rate (MCLR) plus 2%. Maximum loan tenure will be 3 years, and 80% 
of assistance to be used by MFI for incremental lending. Interest rates will be a t 
least 2% below maximum rate prescribed by RBI. Guarantee cover will be 
available for funding provided by MLIs to MFIs/NBFC -MFIs till March 31, 2022 
or till guarantees for an amount of Rs. 7,500 crore are issued, whichever is 
earlier. 
11. Udyam Registration P ortal-The Udyam registration Portal has facility through 
which an entrepreneur can opt for linking itself with Government e -market 
(GeM) place. With this facility, MSEs can link themselves with the 
Government’s procurement system and can participate in Gov ernment’s 
mandatory procurement program from MSEs. In addition to it, the portal has 
linkages with IT, GST and TReDs portals. In this regard, the Public Procurement 
Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSE) Order 2012  had mandated every 

 
 
49 
 
Central Ministry /Department/PSU to set an annual goal for procurement of 
minimum 25% from the MSE sector. In addition, the Public Preference (Make in 
India) Order 2017 has mandated manufacturing, production of goods and services 
in India, in which preference for local man ufacturers and service providers and 
local content requirement is supporting public procurement from local suppliers, 
especially by MSMEs. 
12. Government of India on 02.07.2021 decided to include Retail and Wholesale 
Trade as MSMEs and they are allowed to be registered on UDYAM registration 
portal. However, benefits to the MSMEs engaged in Retail and Wholesale Trade 
would be restricted to availin g credit under Priority Sector Lending only. This 
measure will benefit a large number of trading entities.  
13. The World Bank has approved a loan of $500 million to support Government of 
India’s programme “Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance (RAMP)” 
aimed at revitalizing the MSME sector, which has been heavily impacted by the 
COVID -19 pandemic. The Cabinet approval for the same is under process. 
RAMP is a part of the COVID Resilience and Recovery initiatives of the 
Government. The program aims at improv ing market access, access to credit, 
strengthening Institutions and governance at the Central and State level. The 
programme will support the ongoing support programmes of the Government, 
focusing on competitive aspect of MSMEs. It would enhance MSME 
performance through capacity building, handholding, skill development, quality 
enrichment, technological upgradation, digitization, outreach and marketing 
promotion through delivery of higher quality integrated services.  
14. Amendments to the Factoring Regulation A ct 2011 have been approved by 
Parliament which will enhance supply of credit to MSMEs from NBFCs.  
15. Government, on 23.10.2020, approved the Scheme for grant of ex -gratia payment 
of difference between compound interest and simple interest for six months, to 
borrowers in specified loan accounts. 
 
B. Union Budget for 2021-22 
1. To ensure faster resolution of cases, NCLT framework to be strengthened,             
e-Courts system shall be implemented and alternate methods of debt resolution 
and special framework for MSMEs shall be introduced.    
2. Budgetary allocation for MSMEs  of Rs. 15,700 crores provided in 2021 -22, 
which is more than double of BE for 2020-21.    

 
 
50 
 
3. Customs duty have been reduced uniformly  to 7.5% on semis, flat, and long 
products of non -alloy, alloy, and s tainless steels to provide relief to metal re -
cyclers, mostly MSMEs, Duty on steel scrap has been exempted for a period up 
to 31st March, 2022.  
4. Basic Customs Duty rates have been uniformly reduced  on caprolactam, nylon 
chips and nylon fiber & yarn to 5%. This will help the textile industry, MSMEs, 
and exports, too. 
5. Certain customs duty changes to benefit MSMEs have been made. Duty 
increased from 10% to 15% on steel screws and plastic builder wares. On prawn 
feed it is increased from  5%  to  15%.  Exemptio n  on  import  of  duty -free  
items  is rationalised as  an incentive  to  exporters  of 36 garments,  leather,  and  
handicraft  items.  Almost all these  items are made  domestically by MSMEs.  
Exemption  are withdrawn on imports  of certain  kind  of  lea thers  as  they  are  
domestically  produced  in  good  quantity and  quality,  mostly  by  MSMEs.  
Customs  duty  on  finished synthetic  gem  stones  is increased to  encourage  
their  domestic  processing. 
 
C. Announcements related to MSMEs in Relief Package announced on 28thJune 
2021 
1. 1.1 Lakh crore Loan Guarantee Scheme for COVID Affected Sectors which 
includes Rs. 50,000 crore for health sector to scale up medical infrastructure 
targeting under-served areas and Rs. 60,000 crore for other sectors. Interest  rate 
capped at 8.25% p.a. for other sectors and further decisions to be taken at later 
stage based on evolving needs. 
2. Additional 1.5 lakh crore for Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme 
(ECLGS) launched as part of AtmaNirbhar Bharat Package in May, 2020.  Limit 
of admissible guarantee and loan amount increased above existing level of 20% 
of outstanding on each loan. Overall cap of admissible guarantee raised from Rs. 
3 lakh crore to Rs. 4.5 lakh crore. 
3. Extension of Atmanirbhar Bharat RozgarYojana Launched on 1st Oct, 2020. 
Scheme extended from 30.6.2021 to 31.03.2022. Incentivizes employers for 
creation of new employment, restoration of loss of employment through EPFO. 
Approved outlay Rs. 22,810 crore for 58.50 lakh estimated beneficiaries. Last 
date for re gistration is 30.06.2021. Subsidy provided for two years from 
registration for new employees drawing monthly wages less than Rs. 15000 for:  

 
 
51 
 
(i) Both Employer’s and Employee’s share of contribution (total 24% of wages) 
for establishment strength upto 1000 employees. 
(ii) Only Employee’s share (12% of wages) in case of establishment strength of 
more than 1000. 
4. Rs. 88,000 crore  Boost to Export Insurance Cover  Export Credit Guarantee 
Corporation (ECGC) promotes exports by providing credit insurance services. 
Proposed to infuse equity in ECGC over 5 years to boost export insurance cover 
by Rs. 88,000 crore. 
 
D. Measures taken by Reserve Bank of India 
1. As credit facilities to MSME borrowers, extended under the emergency credit 
line guarantee scheme of GoI guaranteed by national credit guarantee trustee 
company (NCGTC), are backed by an unconditional and irrevocable guarantee 
provided by the GoI, member l ending institutions, viz., SCBs (including 
scheduled RRBs), NBFCs (including HFCs as eligible under the scheme) and 
AIFIs, permitted to assign  zero per cent risk weight on the credit facilities  
extended under the ECLGS scheme to the extent of guarantee cov erage. 
2. In view of the need to support viable MSME entities on account of the fallout of 
COVID-19, the scheme of one -time restructuring of loans to MSMEs without an 
asset classification downgrade, was extended where the borrower’s account was a 
‘standard as set’ as on March 1, 2020 and the aggregate exposure of banks and 
NBFCs was not more than Rs.25 crore. The restructuring had to be implemented 
by March 31, 2021, subject to certain conditions. 
3. Scheduled Commercial Banks allowed to deduct credit disbursed to new MSME 
borrowers from their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) for calculation of 
the cash reserve ratio. To further incentivize the inclusion of the MSMEs into the 
banking system, this  exemption, available for exposures up to Rs 25 lakh and 
credit disbursed up to October 1, is being allowed until December 31, 2021.  
4. Special liquidity facility of Rs 16,000 crore to Small Industries Development 
Bank of India (SIDBI) for on -lending/refinancing - To meet the funding 
requirements of small industries including MSMEs and to kick start the 
investment cycle with additional focus on smaller MSMEs and businesses 
including those in credit deficient and aspirational districts, the Reserve Bank 
extended to SIDBI refinance facilities of ₹15,000 crore in April 2020, ₹15,000 
crore in April 2021 and ₹16,000 crore in June 2021 at the repo rate.  
5. Restructuring of MSME Accounts under Resolution Framework 2.0: Individual 

 
 
52 
 
borrowers, small businesses and MSMEs hav ing aggregate exposure of up to Rs 
25 crore and classified as ‘Standard’ as of March 31, 2021, are eligible for the 
latest framework. They, however, shouldn’t have availed restructuring under any 
of the earlier frameworks (including the August 2020 resolut ion). Restructuring 
under the latest framework needs to be invoked up to September 30, 2021 and 
shall have to be implemented within 90 days after invocation.  
6. In February 2020, scheduled commercial banks were allowed to deduct the 
equivalent of incremental credit disbursed by them up to the fortnight ending July 
31, 2020 as retail loans for automobiles, residential housing and loans to micro, 
small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), over and above the outstanding level of 
credit to these segments as at the end of the fortnight ending on January 31, 2020 
from their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) for maintenance of cash 
reserve ratio (CRR). This exemption is available for a period of five years from 
the date of origination of the loan or the tenure of the loan, whichever is earlier. 
7. To provide support to small business units, micro and small industries, and other 
unorganised sector entities adversely affected during the pandemic, the Reserve 
Bank announced in May 2021 special three -year long -term repo opera tions 
(SLTRO) of ₹10,000 crore at repo rate for the Small Finance Banks (SFBs), to be 
deployed for fresh lending of up to ₹10 lakh per borrower.  
  

 
 
53

taxpayers have to furnish annual return along with quarterly payment of taxes.

THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
   
Recommendation/ Observation 
1. The Automobile Sector, due to its strong forward and backward linkages with 
several key segments of   the economy, occupies   a  prominent  place in   the fabric of 
Indian Economy. Since the number of vehicles exported in various segments is nowhere 
near the potential, exporting vehicles in a large scale would significantly contribute to 
employment generation, trade balance and economic growth of the country. The 
Committee therefore recommends that constructive steps should be taken by the 
Government to pro mote export of vehicles in various segments, particularly the BS -VI 
compliant vehicles, and their engine & spare parts to various countries across the globe, 
especially to Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia and West Asia where there is still 
huge potential for the global automobile companies operating from India. The Committee 
also recommends that the Government in coordination with the automobile companies 
should take appropriate steps   to explore the rural markets, particularly in Two Wheeler 
and Three  Wheeler segments that would contribute substantially for the growth of the 
Auto Sector. 
        (Para 30) 
Action Taken Replies 
 With regards to providing support to auto industry for enhancing exports , the 
following steps have been taken in this direction. 
i)          PLI scheme for the auto sector has been notified with an outlay of Rs 25,938 
crore to enhance the competitiveness of the industry and will help it attain higher 
foothold in exports.  
A number of schemes such as Mahatma Gandhi National Rural E mployment 
Guarantee Act (MNREGA), PradhanMantri Gram SadakYojana (PMGSY), and National 
Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) have been launched for the development of rural 
markets.  It is imperative to recognise that infrastructure is a major driver of growt h for 
auto industry. Consistent allocation of enhanced budget greatly emphasised on the rural 
population, the underprivileged, infrastructure development and development of National 
Highways is significant to give boost to economy especially  with 
focus on rural infrastructure creating a robust business environment an d thus, helping 
auto industry to contribute positively towards National GDP.  
The Two wheeler companies (2W) have already traced the r ural sector, becoming 
the major contributor of automobile sales in this area, Apart from OEMs, Federation of 
Automobile Dealers‟ Association(FADA) may increase their rural penetration  and 
Automotive Skill Development Council need to made rural people   aware of the job 

 3 
opportunities that they might land into after training and show them the path from skill to 
entrepreneurship. 
In a way, COVID-19 has  also contributed in growth of automobile in rural areas as the 
migrants who have gone back duringCOVID-19 to their native villages require an 
alternative source of income enabling pickups, 3-wheelers and LCVs to sell faster in rural 
markets. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2. The Committee is of the view that in addition to setting of Automotive Vehicle 
Scrapping Facility (AVSF) centres across the country, the government sho uld make 
provisions for upfront financial incentives in the Scrappage Policy to boost demand for 
purchase of new vehicles. The proposed financial incentives would encourage end users 
to discard their old and polluting vehicles and go in for purchase of the  new BS VI 
compliant vehicles.                (Para 68)                                                                                                                       
 
3. Further, the Committee also recommends that adequate transparency should be 
maintained while selecting the proposed AVSF centre, which should be based on 
adherence to pre decided parameters that have to be met by such centres. 
        (Para 69) 
Action Taken Replies For Para 3 & 4 
MoRT&H has undertaken following initiatives to phase out old and unfit vehicles:-  
1.Draft GSR Notification 190(E )dt 15.03.2021 -The Draft Notification provides Motor 
Vehicles (Registration and Functions of Vehicle Scrapping Facility) Rules, 2021 for 
establishment of Registered Vehicles Scrapping Facility (RVSF) to ensure transparency in 
the selection of RVSF.  
2.Draft GSR Notification 177(E) dt 12.03.2021 - The Draft Notification provides that 
Certificate of Registration of Government -owned Vehicles would be non -renewable on

3.Draft GSR N otification 191 (E) dt 15.03.2021 - The Draft Notification provides for 
revision of registration fee, fitness testing fee and fitness certification fee of vehicles. The

4.Draft GSR Notification 220 (E) dt26.03.2021 - The Draft Notification provides for 
concession in the motor vehicle tax for the vehicle registered against submission of

5.Draft GSR Notification 278(E ) dt 08.04.2021 - The Draft Notification provides for 
recognition, regulation and control of Automated Testing Stations.  
All the above initiatives are to ensure transparency in the vehicle scrapping process.

to propel the Indian Automobile Industry to be the engine of the "Make in  India"

dealership groups internationally, without compro mising their ownership. FADA also

 The Government of India encourages foreign investment in the automobile sector 
and has allowed 100% foreign direct investment (FDI) under the automatic route except 
Note 3 of FDI Policy wherein GOI mandates that FDI would b e allowed from all 
neighbouring countries to India (with whom India shares a land border) only after 
obtaining approval of the GOI, even in sectors where “automatic” clearances were

Recommendation/ Observation 
5. Given the characte ristic of the Covid -19 pandemic world over, the Committee 
understands that this disease is expected to exist for more time. The Committee 
appreciates the Government's decision of graded opening of the lockdown and restarting 
the economic activity for life to  move-on  along with  the Corona virus side by side. The 
Committee however recommends that with a view to protect life and livelihood, the 
economy  needs  to  be opened  up gradually  ensuring : the   safety  to life.    Therefore, 
the Committee, with re gard to Automobile Se ctor, recommends that the Government 
should issue guidelines and Standard Operational Procedures (SOP) that all the 
concerned stakeholders should prioritize employee protection and safety, regularly 
monitor and track health status of t he employees, follow disease control protocols, define 
travel guidelines, ensure quarantine facility, schedule for flexible working hours etc. 
        (Para 80)

 Various government & autonomous bodies strictly followed the guidelines a nd 
Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) issued by Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry 
of Health & Family Welfare  to ensure safety of employees for resuming work post 
COVID-19 lockdown.  Various employee and customers‟ safety control measures were 
being taken. Some of them are as following:- 
 Social distancing at workplace 
 Sanitization of vehicles & premises, status of Aarogya Setu App 
 Mandatory wearing of face mask, contribution to PM care relief fund, working in 
shifts to ensure social distancing

 Invested in safety initiatives, procurements of sanitizers, thermal scanners, 
oximeters etc.

6. The Committee notes the recent announcement of relief package by the 
Government to reboot the economy to tide over the crisis and extend supp ort to the 
various stakeholders, like infusion of liquidity through Collateral Free Automatic Loans, 
Subordinate Debt Scheme, financial support to NBFCs etc. which will encourage new 
investments, promoting growth across the supply chain, including Automobi le Dealers, 
and safeguarding employment. Although the package has infused a fresh lease of life 
amid the gloom, but at the same time, the Committee however feels that this stimulus 
package in particularly, falls short of addressing the issues of the Automo tive Industry as

economy. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the government should focus on 
announcing a stimulus package  for demand generation for the automotive sector where

Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee notes that in the year 2019, repo rate has come down by about 
1.1% and reduction in the repo rate means the consumers may be able to get loans at 
cheaper interest rates from the Banks. Therefore, there is likelihood of commodities 
becoming cheaper due to lower interest cost, benefitting the end consumers. However, 
banks have not passed on the reduced rates to customers. Instead many retail auto loan  
rates have increased by 0.05% to 0.4%. In this regard, the Auto Association have 
highlighted that even 1% reduction in rates would motivate small car buyers to go in for 
the purchase of a new vehicle. The Department of Expenditure in its written reply has  
stated that the Government has recently announced linking of repo rate to interest rates 
charges for vehicle purchase, to provide impetus to the local manufacturing including 
automotive industry. The Committee however, has been informed that on ground, th e 
reduction in repo rate by RBI has not been transferred to the customers by reducing 
interest rates. Therefore, the Committee is of the view that Department of heavy Industry 
should take up the matter with Ministry of Finance and the Reserve Bank of India  for 
issuing strict guidelines to all banks for linking repo rate to interest rates on loans to the 
consumers, to help revival of the Auto Industry Sector. 
(Para 20) 
Action Taken Replies 
It has been intimated that RBI has deregulated the interest rates on advances including 
housing loans sanctioned by scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs) subject to 
the regulatory instructions contained in Master Direction on interest Rates on Advances 
dated March 03, 2016. The interest rates are decided by banks as p er their Board 
approved policy.  
However, with a view to improve monetary policy transmission, banks have been advised 
to link floating -rate retail loans and loans to Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) to an 
external benchmark such as RBI policy rate from October 01, 2019. Similar instructions 
have been issued for linking floating rate loans to Medium enterprises to external 
benchmarks w.e.f. April 1, 2020.

9. Further, the Committee feels that as a respite to the   already  stressed Automobile 
Sector, the DHI in collaboration with other concerned   Ministries may work out some 
measures to ensure that the surplus stock of non -BS-VI compliant vehicles left unsold, if 
any, is disposed off. Through a Review Petition, the Hon'ble Su preme Court may be 
convinced to consider the extension of period for disposal of surplus stock of BS -IV 
compliant vehicle particularly taking into account the unexpected national   lockdown  
imposed  due to Covid-19  Pandemic. The  Committee is of  the opinion  that this would   
provide the much needed   leeway of considerable time over and   above the mandated   
date of 1st   April, 2020 to   the  dealers  to dispose off their buffer stock of   vehicles.  
Besides,  the  recent  Coronavirus  outbreak  has taken its  toll on the Indian Auto 
Industry, which is dependent on its component supplies from China. However, the 
Committee feels that even in the pervading gloom of the Coronavirus scare, there is a 
silver lining owing to the fact that the supply disruption may fo rce manufacturers to look 
within and source their component parts locally. The Committee feels that such a de -
risking plan is expected to boost the Auto Components Industry. Further, the Committee 
is also of the opinion that the disruption in the supply chain should also be counted as a 
reason to extend the deadline of 1st April 2020, as in the absence of a robust and 
consistent supply chain of Auto Components, there is bound to be a lesser capacity 
utilisation in the manufacture of BS -VI vehicles. To fill in this temporary shortfall of BS -
VI vehicles, the inventory stock of BS IV vehicles, lying unsold with dealers can be 
utilised.

CHAPTER – I 
 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.  The Committee takes note of the data furnished by DPE regarding production by 
CPSEs and recognizes the severity of operational disruptions i n CPSEs due to complete 
lockdown. The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that a detailed study needs to be 
conducted to comprehend at micro -level; the actual impact of COVID -19 Pandemic and 
consequent lockdowns on the performance of the CPSEs so that necessary timely 
intervention by the Government can be made to mitigate the economic fallout.  
(Para 10) 
 Action Taken Replies 
 The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) has informed that they collect 
information on performance  relating to all the CPSEs a nnually and brings out  a 
comprehensive Public Enterprises Survey which is laid on the table of  both the House of 
the Parliament. The recommendation of the Hon‟ble Committee would be duly 
considered while preparing the Public Enterprises Survey for the year  2020-21 to include 
a chapter on impact of COVID -19 pandemic and consequent lockdowns on the 
performance of CPSEs. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.  The Committee notes that BHEL in collaboration with NTPC & IGCAR, with 
funding support from DHI is developing  Advanced Ultra Super Critical Technology for 
thermal power generation, which is an indigenous technology being developed for the 
first time in India. Since the R&D phase of the said project is in the final stages, as 
informed by DHI, the Committee is of t he view that initiatives may be taken for exploring 
the domestic power market using the new technology to supplement the Make in India 
initiative. 
(Para 35.14) 
Action Taken Replies 
All the envisaged seven (07) major technical milestones pertaining to the “ R&D 
Project for Development of Advanced Ultra Super -critical (AUSC) Technology for 
Thermal Power Plants” (Phase-1) were completed / achieved by December 2020, and the 
financial closure of R&D Phase-1 was accomplished in March 2021. 
  The next intended footstep, i.e. Phase-2, involves setting up of a 1x800 MW coal -
fired AUSC technology demonstration plant (TDP) under the aegis of Ministry of Power 
(MoP). In this regard, NTPC Ltd. and BHEL have signed a MoU (Memorandum of 
Understanding) in July 2019 for forma tion of Joint Venture (JV) company for setting up 

 3 
of 1x800 MW AUSC TDP at Sipat site of NTPC Ltd. The approval for Phase -2, which 
encompasses financial support from Government of India, is under purview of NTPC 
Ltd. and Ministry of Power. The technical spe cifications of the TDP are under process of 
finalisation. Further steps shall be taken after the successful implementation of the AUSC 
technology in the TDP. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.  The Committee notes that 40% of the component required for HMT Machines viz. 
CNC Controllers & Drivers, Spindle Bearings, Linear Motion Guides etc were imported. 
However, disruptions in import due to lockdowns and closure of ports have 
adversely affected the productions. Efforts have been made by HMT to provide technical  
support to Domestic Manufactures and utilize its infrastructure facilities for production 
of import substitutions. The Committee observes that the turnover and profit/loss for the 
2nd quarter have been poorer than that of 1st quarter of the current FY 202 0-21. The 
Committee recommends that new avenues may be explored for alternate manufacturing 
hubs for import substitution and technology transfer from other countries to meet the 
requirements of HMT so that the production process is back on track. 
(Para 41.10) 
Action Taken Replies 
HMT Limited has been looking for alternate sources and is encouraging domestic 
manufactures to take up manufacturing of the items which were hitherto imported. With 
the easing of disruptions due to lockdown and opening of ports, th e production process 
has been on track in the third and fourth quarters of financial year 2020-21. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.         The Committee recommends that DHI should make concerted efforts to uplift the 
company from its dependency on Chinese r aw materials and co -ordinate with concerned 
Indian stakeholders, who would be able to provide the Company with the requisite raw -
materials, so as to facilitate the Company to realise the vision of an ‘Atmanirbhar 
Bharat’. 
     (Para 43.10) 
Action Taken Replies 
REIL has partially arranged few items such as solar cell from other sources which 
were procured from China. However, continuous efforts are being made for procurement 
of other components/items such as semiconductors, thermal printer, LCD etc.  from 
indigenous sources /  other countries, which may result into positive output in terms of 
having independency from Chinese market and the initiatives taken by the Company will 
provide impetus in achieving its goal of „Atmanibhar Bharat‟. 
 

 4 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee observes that under the Public Procurement Policy (PPP), the 
MSEs are promoted to improve their market accessibility and competitiveness through 
increased participation in Government procurements and encouraging development of 
linkages between MSEs and PSEs. As per the mandate of the Public Procurement Policy 
for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) Order 2012, every Central Ministries/PSEs 
should set an annual target of minimum 25% procurement of goods & services from MSE 
Sector. Out of 25% annual procurement, a sub -target of 4% & 3% should be from MSEs 
owned by SC/ST and Women entrepreneurs, respectively. Keeping in view the 
extraordinary situation, the Committee is of the view that the Central Ministries and 
PSUs may procure more than  the prescribed limits laid down under the PPP for MSES 
Order 2012, so as to give further boost to the localized production. 
 (Para 56)   
Action Taken Replies 
Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises has informed that they have 
taken various initiativ es to improve the market accessibility and competitiveness of 
MSEs through increased participation in Government procurement and encouraging 
development of linkages between MSEs and CPSEs. In FY 2020 -21, 141 CPSEs had 
procured Rs.39,557.34 crore (31.69%) o f goods and services from MSEs (including 
SCs/STs), which is more than the mandated target 25%. Furthermore, the 
recommendation of the Committee has been forwarded to all the Ministries/Departments 
and also to CPSEs by DPE to take note of it for consideration and compliance. 
Recommendations rece ived from the Committee has been conveyed to CPSEs for 
compliance.  
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee takes note of the new initiative taken by DHI for constitution of 
Project Development Cell (PDC) for attracting investments and development of investible 
projects in India in coordination with various other Ministries/Departments and State 
Governments. The Committee desires that the details of the roadmap formulated by PDC 
for providing support to investors for investing in India in the automobile and auto 
components sector, capital goods sector etc. may be furnished for information of the 
Committee.  
(Para 58.1.2) 
Action Taken Replies 
Project Development Cell (PDC) was constituted and operationalized in  June 
2020 in this Ministry . Strategy to attract investments fall under the following 4 
categories: 
 

 5 
 One-to-one investor engagement: 
  MHI has been interacting with multiple individual investors in the automotive, 
auto components, electric mobility and capital  goods sectors. The purpose of these calls 
is to understand and facilitate the India investment plans of companies, through extension 
of support at the Central and State Government level. 
 Investment focused webinars: 
  In the post -COVID19 era, virtual inv estment-focused webinars are the primary 
means of reaching a wider investor audience. MHI has been participating in various 
industry consultations and investment promotion webinars, coordinated with the support 
of other entities including industry association. 
 Production Linked Incentive schemes: 
With an aim to Enhance India‟s Manufacturing Capabilities and Enhancing 
Exports – in automobile and automobile components sector, PLI Scheme for the 
automobile and automobile components sector has been notified in  September 2021.  
 
To enhance India‟s Manufacturing Capabilities and Enhancing Exports – for 
manufacture of Advance Chemistry Cell (ACC) in India, a Production -Linked Incentive 
(PLI) scheme for manufacture of Advance Chemistry Cell (ACC) in India is approve d by 
the Union Cabinet on  12th May, 2021  under Aatmanirbhar Bharat with a total outlay of 
Rs. 18,100 crores over a period of 5 years.  The Scheme has been notified on  9th June, 
2021. The PLI scheme for ACC battery envisages to incentivize large domestic and  
international players in establishing a competitive ACC battery set -up in the country. It 
represents one of the largest economic opportunities of the twenty -first century for 
several global growth sectors, such as consumer electronics, electric vehicles, and 
renewable energy. 
Regional Investment Dialogues: 
  MHI PDC has participated in multiple Regional Investment Dialogues, 
coordinated by DPIIT. These dialogues establish synergies and facilitate information 
exchange between internal stakeholders for investor promotion. 
An Empowered Group of Secretaries has been Constituted by DPIIT to provide 
support and facilitation to investors for investing in India and to boost growth in the key 
sectors of the economy. Project Development Cells (PDCs) within relevant 
Ministries/Departments of GoI have also been envisioned to ensure a faster mechanism to 
facilitate investments through integrated efforts by Central ministries and the State. In 
furtherance of above, MHI has constituted a PDC  with the  Joint Secretary (Auto)  as 
Nodal Officer with following focus areas of PDC has been mentioned:

Recommendation/Observation  
7.  The Committee notes that the Capital Goods Sector is the backbone of the 
manufacturing sector as it produces machines required for industrial production. Due to 
technology gaps in Capital Goods being manufactured in India, this sector is importing 
high-end machines required for manufacturing. The Committee is of the view that there is 
an urgent need to address the gaps in technology needs, skill and infrastructure 
development for Capital Goods Sector. The Committee recommends that more webinars 
with prospective/potential investors be organized in collaboration with Indian Mi ssions 
abroad to promote industrial investments for the development of high -end technology, 
skill and infrastructure. The Committee is hopeful that DHI would work to make India 
investment-ready and investor friendly. The Committee also suggests that DHI ma y 
prepare a list of potential clusters, potential sectors and potential investments with 
several state governments, so as to facilitate the grounding of investments and creation of 
investible projects. 
(Para 58.2.2) 
Action Taken Replies 
In order to address  the skill  gaps and  infrastructure development and 
technology needs for the Capital Goods Sector, Phase I of the Capital Goods scheme was 
rolled out by the Department in 2014. Phase I of the scheme fostered partnerships 

 7 
between Academia and Industry for en gendering technology development with 
Government support. The outcomes of the Scheme have proved the efficacy of the 
strategies deployed for technology and industrial infrastructure 
development.  Nine Common Engineering Facility Centres (CEFCs) including fo ur 
Industry 4.0 SAMARTH centres, Eight Centres of Excellence (COEs) for Technology 
Development, A 500 acres world class Machine Tool Park in Tumakuru, Karnataka in 
partnership with the Government of Karnataka have been established under the scheme. 
25 new technologies in the field of machine tools, textile machinery, earth moving 
machinery, nano and sensor technologies, are being developed at national research 
institutes of eminence such as IITs, IISc, CMTI, etc. and are undergoing 
commercialization. 
Further, six Web -based open manufacturing technology innovation platforms 
have been  developed by IIT Madras,  Central Manufacturing Technology Institute 
(CMTI), International Centre for Automotive Technology (iCAT), Automotive Research   
 Association of India(ARAI ), BHEL and HMT  under the phase I of the Capital Goods 
scheme. These Platforms will bring all India‟s technical resources and the concerned 
Industry on to one network to kick start and facilitate identification of technology 
problems faced by Industry and crowd source solutions for the same in a systematic 
manner. These platforms will identify technological solutions to the problems and 
challenges posed by the Industry. The identified technologies shall subsequently be 
developed with the help of the industr y and premier academic institutions in the existing 
Centres of Excellence (CoEs) established under Phase I and new  CoEs to be developed 
by the Department under Phase II of the Capital Goods scheme. 
The Ministry is also planning to promote skilling in Capit al Goods Sector 
by creation of skilling packages for skill levels 6 and above, in association with Skill 
Councils and imparting of skill training in the Samarth Udyog and Skill Centres 
developed under Phase -I of the Capital Goods Scheme and other identifie d institutions. 
The same would also be done for the technologies identified through the Technology and 
Innovation platforms in association with Skill Councils, CPSEs, Autonomous bodies. 
Embassy of India, Tokyo, the Ministry and the Government of Japan orga nized a 
webinar on Investment Opportunities in India in Capital Goods sector with 150 
prospective companies from India and Japan on June 24 2020.   The Secretary (Heavy 
Industry) and Hon‟ble Ambassador, Embassy of India, Tokyo co -chaired the said 
webinar. At the end of the webinar, one to one contacts session was held between Indian 
and Japanese participants.  State Governments also participated. B2B followed. Now 
individual one to one meetings are being held by the Department and the Mission with 
investors.  
This webinar generated a large number of leads besides awareness in the 
catchment area about opportunities in India. Positive long terms impact is expected.  The 
Ministry also plans to organize participate in similar webinars  in  collaboration  
with Indian Missions abroad to promote industrial investments  for the development of 
high-end technology skill and infrastructure.

Recommendation/Observation 
8.  The Committee appreciates the efforts undertaken by the DHI regarding 
promotion of technological development and innovation and suggests that a master list of 
all the imported items used by CPSEs in assembly of their products should be prepared 
and shared with all the national research centres and educational institutions indulged in 
R&D activities, design  and scientific innovations. Further the Committee desires that 
such research institutions should be provided financial assistance to support R&D 
activities for creation of a healthy manufacturing ecosystem. India is importing high -end 
technology machines since the domestic industry does not presently have the 
technological capabilities to manufacture the same. The Committee is of the view that 
concerted efforts involving technology driven innovations have to be made to create an 
environment congenial for R&D and innovation for achieving the goal of self-reliance. 
(Para 58.4.2) 
 
Action Taken Replies  
As advised by the Committee, a master  list of all the imported 
items used by CPSEs in assembly of their products will be prepared. In order to address 
the technology needs for the Capital Goods Sector, Phase I of the Capital Goods scheme 
was rolled out by the Department in 2014. Phase I of the scheme, fostered partnerships 
between Academia and Industry for engendering technology development with 
Government suppor t. The outcomes of the Scheme have proved the efficacy of the 
strategies deployed for technology and industrial infrastructure 
development.  Nine Common Engineering Facility Centres (CEFCs) including four 
Industry 4.0 SAMARTH centres, Eight Centres of Excel lence (COEs) for Technology 
Development, a 500 acres world class Machine Tool Park in Tumakuru, Karnataka in 
partnership with the Government of Karnataka have been established under the scheme. 
25 new technologies in the field of machine tools, textile mac hinery, earth moving 
machinery, nano and sensor technologies, are being developed at national research 
institutes of eminence such as IITs, IISc, CMTI, etc. and are undergoing 
commercialization.  Alongside, six Web -based open manufacturing technology 
innovation platforms have been  developed by IIT Madras,  Central Manufacturing 
Technology Institute (CMTI), International Centre for Automotive Technology (iCAT), 
Automotive Research   Association of India(ARAI), BHEL and HMT  under the phase I 
of the Capital Goods scheme.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
9.  The Committee has been told that DHI is developing web -based open 
manufacturing Technology Innovation Platforms under the ongoing Capital Goods 
Scheme for enhancing India’s technological capabilities. The Committ ee hopes that this 
initiative would facilitate more start -ups and angel funding of innovations in India as 
well as development of mother manufacturing technologies indigenously through Grand 
Challengers on the Platform. The Committee recommends that the si x Technology 
Platforms which are presently under trial runs may be formally launched on priority to 

 9 
promote industrial investments. Further, the Committee recommends that DHI should 
take all out efforts to promote the development of Technical Platforms und er the Capital 
Goods Scheme in order to ensure their optimum utilization by experts including 
academia, technology students, manufacturing experts, etc.  
(Para 58.4.3) 
Action Taken Replies 
 
 Ministry has embarked on innovative path to engender R&D in manuf acturing by 
developing six Technology Innovation Platforms which shall be  accelerators for making 
India self -reliant in various fields of the Capital Goods Sector with focus on bridging 
technology gap. The Ministry has developed web based open manufacturin g technology 
innovation platforms under the ongoing Capital Goods Scheme. These platforms will 
help in bringing all India‟s technical resources and the concerned Industry on to one 
platform to kick start and facilitate identification of technology problems  faced by Indian 
Industry and crowd source solutions for the same in a systematic manner so as to 
facilitate start-ups and angel funding of India innovations. This includes the development 
of the key „mother‟ manufacturing technologies' indigenously throug h „Grand 
Challenges‟ on the Platforms to help achieve the vision of an  Aatmanirbhar Bharat and a 
globally competitive manufacturing sector in India. 
Six Technology Platforms have been developed by IIT Madras,  Central 
Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMT I), International Centre for Automotive 
Technology (iCAT), Automotive Research    Association of India (ARAI), BHEL and 
HMT. These platforms will focus on development of technologies for the globally 
competitive manufacturing in India.  
So far, the technolo gy and innovation platforms have developed a strong user 
base of about 40,000 users from industry, academia, R&D institutes, and retired industry 
experts. Around 23 grand challenges have been posted on these portals for seeking 
technological solutions. 58 webinars have been conducted in order to enhance the 
outreach of the initiative. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
10.  The Committee is of the view that CPSEs have a very pivotal role in giving a 
push to the growth of Indian economy and are regarded as one of the key generators of 
remunerative employment in the formal sector. Further, the Capital Expenditure has a 
high multiplier effect to increase the country’s GDP. The Committee recommends that 
the CPSEs should take extraordinary efforts at extraordinary time s to achieve targets of 
Capital Expenditure and to ensure that the capital outlay provided to them for the FY 
2020-21 is utilized properly within the targeted period. 
  (Para 61) 
 
 

 10 
Action Taken Replies 
As recommended by the Hon‟ble committee, DPE has been continuously 
monitoring and reviewing the Capital expenditure activities of the select CPSEs (having 
annual CAPEX target of more than Rs. 500 crore) during the FY 2020-21.  
For FY 2020-21, CPSEs under the CAPEX review have been able to achieve Rs. 
2,04,243 crores of CAPEX i.e. 92.73% of the planned targets. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. The Committee observes that from a measly Rs.24,738 crore in June 2020, the 
CAPEX achievement of CPSEs have risen to a whopping Rs.84,824 crore by September, 
2020. This is  a promising scenario. However, the Committee is of the opinion that it 
should be ensured that CPSEs are encouraged to maintain the pace of escalation in 
CAPEX. Any help/intervention needed by CPSEs on this front should be extended to 
them. DHI may strive to make concerted efforts on this front and impress upon the 
respective Administrative Ministries of other CPSEs, through DPE, to provide necessary 
hand-holding to any CPSE, who is in need of it, to keep up the achieved momentum of 
CAPEX. 
(Para 62) 
Action Taken Replies 
DPE has informed that they will continue to review the CAPEX performance of 
CPSEs on regular basis to escalate the CAPEX by CPSEs to achieve their planned 
targets. Further, the CAPEX has been prescribed as Parameter for CPSEs in the revised 
MoU Guidelines for the year 2021-22 and onwards. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
12.  The Committee notes the efforts being made by DHI as well as CPSEs under its 
administrative control to achieve the goal of Atmanirbhar Bharat in manufacturing 
sector by adopti ng various innovative measures for indigenous production/manufacture 
of items, including items which were imported earlier. However, the Committee is of the 
view that a lot more needs to be done to make India actually self reliant. Besides, 
indigenous capa bilities available for R&D, design, prototyping, manufacturing and 
testing in many of the CPSEs may be made available to all stakeholders for seamless co -
operation between the public and private sectors. In this direction, the Committee hopes 
that with the  public-private partnership and development of Technology Platforms, the 
vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat can become a reality. 
 (Para 63) 
 
 
 

 11 
Action Taken Replies 
Apart from the initiatives taken by this Ministry under the Phase -I of the Capital 
Goods Scheme including the development of the technology and innovation platforms as 
explained to the ATR of the Recommendation No. 29, MHI is preparing the proposal for 
the Phase -II of the Capital Goods Scheme which will, to a great extant, enhance the

and Innovation Platforms will identify technological solutions to the problems and 
challenges pos ed by the Industry. The identified technologies shall subsequently be 
developed with the help of existing CoEs developed under Phase I and new CoEs to be 
set up by the Ministry under Phase II of the scheme, industry and premier academic 
institutions, CPSEs under MHI.  This will enable seamless co - operation between public 
and private sectors to fulfill vision of ATAMNIRBHAR BHARAT. 
The NATRIP centers are giving preference to the Indian vendors/ manufacturers 
and promoting the Make in India initiative. Moreo ver, centers facilities are supporting 
Automobile OEM‟s and suppliers to develop their product indigenously and trying to 
achieving the goal of Atmanirbhar Bharat.

 (Para 37.11)

the operations of the company have been clo sed and all the employees have been given 
VRS. The other formalities like settlement of other dues, delisting of shares, disposal of 
assets, transfer of land, etc. is under progress. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
30. The Committee notes the efforts being mad e by SIL to promote e -mobility mission 
of Government of India with all components sourced from Indian suppliers thereby 
fulfilling the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat. Since BEL, with which SIL has tied up, is in 
advanced stage of developing/manufacturing all  critical equipments/components, 
including Lithium Ion battery packs required for electrical vehicles and supplying the 

 26 
same to SIL shortly, the Committee may be apprised about the progress made in this 
regard. 
 (Para 37.12) 
Action Taken Replies 
The Union Cabinet has approved the closure of SIL on 20.01.2021. Accordingly, 
the operations of the company have been closed and all the employees have been given 
VRS. The other formalities like settlement of other dues, delisting of shares, disposal of 
assets, transfer of land, etc. is under progress. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation (Para 37.9, 37.10, 37.11 and 37.12) 
 
 The Committee expresses concern over the closure of one more CPSE  i.e. 
SIL under MHI .  The Committee desires that MHI periodically review the 
performance of CPSEs under their administrative control and take all preventive 
measures to arrest the early signs of weakness in CPSEs and improve their financial 
performance. The Committee  also impresses upon the Ministry to expedite 
settlement of dues of employees at the earliest.  The Committee would also like to be 
apprised of the fate of : (i) ‘Type Approval’ of new model of Electric Vehicl e from 
ICAT and also whether the E-Rickshaw variant has been submitted to ICAT for 
obtaining ‘Type Approval’  and (i i) ti e up of SIL with BEL for 
developing/manufacturing all critical equipments/components etc. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
31. The Committee recommends that regular Vendor Development Programmes 
should be conducted by the CPSEs to give wide publicity on th e Public Procurement 
Policy so that MSEs are provided with business opportunities to expand their market 
base. The Committee desires that DHI may ensure conduct of such VDP regularly by the 
CPSEs under their administrative control. 
(Para 57) 
Action Taken Replies 
Vendor Development Programmes (VDP) are being organized regularly by the 
CPSEs in their premises which serves as a platform for identification of needs and for 
mutual benefits. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee appreciates the efforts  made by MHI to organise regular 
Vendor Development Programme (VDP) for MSEs. The Committee desires that the 
list of all such VDP organised by MHI in the last two years may be furnished to the 
Committee. The Committee would also like to know the outcome of  these VDPs on 
increasing the publicity of Public Procurement Policy and enhancing the business 
opportunities  for the MSEs. 

 27

FINAL REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY ARE STILL AWAITED 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
32. The Committee notes that in October, 2018 the Government had approved the 
Revival and Mill Development Plan (RMDP) of NEPA Ltd. which was slated to be 
completed in December, 2019 with a total financial package of Rs.469.41 crores. 
However, the RMDP missed its first deadline and, as intimated by DHI, was likely to be 
completed in September, 2020 as it has been designed to boost production and 
support/generate local employment. On completion of RMDP, NEPA is expected to 
produce 1,00,000 MT p. a. of Writing & Printing Paper and Newsprint paper which will 
help minimize imports and increase exports. Since the lockdown has been eased almost 
completely, the manpower and other facilities are available for carrying out RMDP 
works in full swing. DHI had apprised the Committee that a Monitoring Committee under 
the Chairmanship of AS&FA, DHI has been constituted to regularly review the progress 
of the implementation of the RMDP. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts 
should be made on a priorit y basis to complete the RMDP of NEPA expeditiously. A 
compliance report on this aspect may be furnished to the Committee. 
(Para 44.6) 
Action Taken Replies 
  The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), on 3.10.2018, approved 
the proposal for providing  additional budgetary support of Rs.469.41 crores to NEPA 
Ltd. to meet the revised cost estimates of the RMDP, payment of pending salary/wage 
and statutory dues and for funding VRS of about 400 employees of NEPA Ltd. 
As directed by CCEA, a monitoring commi ttee under the chairmanship of 
AS&FA of this Ministry was constituted to periodically review the progress of the 
implementation of RMDP of NEPA Ltd. A technical committee comprising of the field 
experts from other CPSEs and CPPRI under this Ministry was al so constituted to assist 
the monitoring Committee. 
Till date, 21 meetings of the monitoring committee have been held and efforts are 
being made to complete the RMDP at the earliest despite impediments like delayed / 
insufficient supplies of the paper machi nes and rewinders etc. by foreign supplier who 
had gone into insolvency proceedings and countrywide lockdown due to Covid – 19 
pandemic which resulted into unavailability of sufficient skilled manpower and NEPA 
site to execute the project activities. 
 

 28

33.  The Committee notes the efforts taken by B&R to secure its employees by 
providing them with health insurance coverage and desires that the DHI may take 
necessary initiatives in this direction so that other CPSEs follow the sam e to cover major 
unexpected health care costs thereby protecting their staff against unforeseen health 
issues.

The recommendation made by the Committee have been well taken. The 
feasibility of making other CPSEs to adopt s uch or similar health coverage scheme, will

1 
 
REPORT 
 
 India‟s Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Sector has emerged as a 
vibrant, dynamic and progressive sector of the Indian economy over the last five decades. 
MSME Sector not  only play crucial role in providing large -scale employment 
opportunities at comparatively lower capital cost than large industries but also help 
industrialization of rural and backward areas of the country, thereby, reducing regional 
imbalances, assuring more equitable distribution of national income and resources.  
MSME Sector has  strong linkages to large indu stries as ancillary units and contributes 
significantly in the inclusive industrial development of the country . MSME Sector is also 
nurturing a culture of entrepreneurship among the people of the country, especially the 
youth thereby mitigating the problem of unemployment effectively. 
 
2. MSMEs are widely spread across the country in almost all the sectors. MSMEs are 
now widening their domain across various sectors of the economy, producing diverse 
range of products and services to meet demands of domestic as well as Global markets 
and also proving to be a boon for aspiring entrepreneurs in India.  As informed by the       
M/o of MSME, the MSME Sector is providing livelihood to around 11.10 crore people of 
the country. There are a round 6.34 crore MSMEs , which contributed 27 per cent to the 
Gross Domestic Product in the year Financial Year 2020 -21.The MSME Sector has the 
huge potential to generate employment and livelihood in the rural hinterlands  of the 
country. It also has the capacity to earn foreign exchange for the exchequer through larger 
exports. 
 
3. COVID-19 pandemic had an enormous adverse impact on almost all sectors of the 
Indian economy including the MSME Sector, due to factors such as lack of funds, supply 
chain disruptions, lower productivity, non -availability of workforce etc. However, t he 
Government has adopted a multi -pronged approach covering the six pillars such as (i) 
New Enterprise Development and Employment Generation (ii) Credit Assistance and 
Capital Infusion (iii) Technological U pgradation (iv) Infrastructure & Capacity Building 
(v) Skill Development & Entrepreneurship Development T raining and (vi) Procurement 
and Marketing Support, in order to help the MSMEs to revive and regain their               
pre-pandemic growth trajectory as well as improve their economic growth. 

2 
 
Ministry of MSME  
 
4. The Ministry of MSME was formed on 9 th May, 2007 merging the erstwhile 
Ministry of Small Scale Industries and the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries.  The 
Ministry designs policies, promotes/facilitates programmes/projects/schemes and 
monitors their implementation, with a view to assisting MSMEs and helping them to scale 
up.  
 
The major Schemes of the Ministry of MSME are mentioned as under:- 
 Prime Minister‟s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP); 
 Modified Market Development Assistance (MMDA); 
 Interest Subsidy and Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme; 
 Strengthening of Infrastructure of Existing Weak Khadi Institutions and Assistance 
for Marketing Infrastructure; 
 Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE); 
 A Scheme for Promoting Innovation and Rural Entrepreneurship (ASPIRE); 
 Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI); 
 Micro and Small Enterprises–Cluster Development Programme (MSE-CDP); 
 Science & Technology (S&T); 
 Honey Mission;  
 Kumbhar Shashaktikaran Programme; 
 The National Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe Hub;  
 Scheme for Promotion of MSMEs in NE Region and Sikkim; and 
 Guaranteed Emergency Credit Line (GECL). 
 
New Definition of MSMEs 
 
5. The Committee was informed that the revision in the definition of MSMEs  which 
was brought in w.e.f. 1stJuly, 2020 as part of the AtmaNirbhar Bharat package introduced 
a composite  criteria of investment and annual turnover and identical limits for 
manufacturing and services sector ( table below). The resulting economies of scale can 
enhance productivity without the MSMEs losing out on several Government incentives 
including market support, export promotion, preferential procurement in the public sector 
and incentives through the Micro Small  Enterprises-Cluster Development Programme 
(MSE-CDP), Prime Minister Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) and Scheme 
of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) and enabling of IT 

3 
 
ecosystems. This enabling environment will promote compet ition among MSMEs .The 
new definition of MSMEs is as under:- 
 
                                                              (Rs. In crore) 
Category Investment Turnover 
Micro 1 5 
Small 10 50 
Medium 50 250 
 
6. The Committee understands that the modified definition of MSMEs will 
facilitate expansion and growth of MSME enterprises , increasing the investment 
limit under the new definition allows MSMEs to invest in plant an d machinery for 
growth without the fear of losing the status.  Further, the increased limit also enables 
MSMEs to invest in new technologies to enhance their productivity.  It also removes 
the distinction between MSMEs in the manufacturing as well as services sector and 
increases the country’s exports through MSMEs. The Committee appreciates the 
Government’s decision to modify the definition of M icro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises as detailed above at para no.  5, as per the long -standing demand of 
Industry Associations.  The Committee also welcomes the decision to include retail 
and wholesale trade under the purview of MSME, thereby enabling them to get 
priority sector lending.  
 
Demands for Grants (2022-23) 
 
7. Regarding the details of the Action Plan set for the Ministry for the year2022 -23, 
the Committee was informed by the Ministry that an amount of Rs. 21,422crore has been 
allocated to the Ministry of MSME for the year 2022 -23. The Action Plan of the Ministry 
focuses on strengthening the overall ecosyst em of MSMEs by providing infrastructural 
support, marketing avenues, proper access to finance,  technical support and capacity 
building etc. This action plan is broadly reflected in the Output -Outcome Monitoring 
Framework Document of the Ministry for FY 2022-23.  
9. During the course of the presentation in connection with DFG (2022 -23), the 
Ministry of MSME apprised the Committee about the main highlights of the Union 
Budget 2022-23 for MSME Sector, which is as under :- 
 
 Udyam, e-shram, NCS and ASEEM portals to be interlinked; 
 ECLGS to be extended up to March 2023; 

4 
 
 Guarantee cover under ECLGS to be expanded by Rs. 50,000 crores , total cover of 
Rs. 5 lakh crores for hospitality and related activities; 
 Rs. 2 lakh crores additional credit for Micro and Small Enterprises facilitated under 
the Credit Guarantee Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE); and 
 Raising and Accelerating MSME performance (RAMP) programme with outlay of 
Rs. 6,000 crores to be rolled out.

took note of the Proposed as well as Budgetary Allocations to the Ministry of MSME for

12. The Committee notes that for financial year 2021 -22, the Ministry was 
allocated Rs. 15699.65 crore as BE and RE and the AE upto 31 st January, 2022 
stands at Rs. 12071.84 crore which is only 76.89% of the allocated BE/RE.  
Therefore, the Committee expects the Ministry to utilize the balance amount of 
23.11% during the remaining two months.  Further, the Ministry should henceforth 
rationalize the expenditure spreading all through the year to avoid uneven spending 
 
13. The Committee further observes that for the FY 2022 -23, the Ministry has 
been allocated Rs. 21,422 crore as BE,  which apparently appears to be a significant 
increase from the previous year's BE of Rs. 15 ,699.65 crore .  However, out of Rs. 
21,422 crore, Rs. 15,000 crore  has been  earmarked for Guaranteed Emergency 
Credit Line scheme (GECL) leaving behind Rs. 6,422 crore only, which is the actual 
allocation for development of other schemes/projects of the Ministry . BE allocation 
of Rs. 6422 crore for FY 2022 -23  as mentioned at paragraph number 1 0 above  is 
the lowest allocation as compared to past several years’ i.e. BE 2017 -18, 2018 -19, 
2019-20 and 2020 -21.  The Committee expresses concern on such poor allocation of 
BE 2022 -23 to the M/o MSME especially at this juncture when MSME sector is 
struggling to revive from the huge adverse impact of COVID -19 Pandemic and 
remain in operation due to liquidity crunch.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should address the issue by taking it up with the            
M/o Finance for an enhanced allocation at the RE stage to enable the Ministry to 
achieve its vision of a progressive MSME sector by promoting growth and 
development of the Sector, through support to existing enterprises, adopting cutting 
edge technologies, encouraging creation of new enterprises etc. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry should utilize the BE 2022 -23 of Rs. 21422.00 crore 
optimally for the development of MSME Sector. 
 
14. Further with regard to SME Division the RE 2021 -22 and AE upto  31st 
January, 2022, are Rs. 208.6 5 crore and Rs. 146.6 crore respectively , which shows

O/o DC-MSME has spent 83.32% of RE 2021 -22. The Committee suggests that the 
Ministry of MSME should strive hard to utilize the remaining amount of RE

allocated to all the three aforesaid wings of the Ministry optimally so that the  
schemes/projects do not suffer for lack of funds.

Views/Suggestions of the Stakeholders 
 
 
16. As part of examination of the DFG (2022 -23), t he Committee had sought the 
views/suggestions of the Associations (FICCI, FISME, CII and ASSOCHAM) on the 
Government‟s target of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises contributing $2 trillion to 
the country‟s target of becoming $5 trillion economy by 2024 . The Associations apprised 
the Committee that although the Covid pandemic had adversely affected the MSME 
Sector but they are very optimistic that MSME Sector will revive quickly but it is very 
important that the blueprint laid down by the Government materializes in a time -bound 
manner. The important suggestions put forth by the Associations in this regard along with 
the recommendations of the Committee are as under:- 
 
SEPARATE POLICY FOR MEDIUM ENTERPRISES 
17. Issues of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises are different from each other and  
unified policy would not be able to treat them well as per their actual requirements.  The 
schemes need to be segregated and modified as per each of the category so that  every 
category has specific solutions. It will help enterprises to identify schemes, which are 
relevant for them. Medium sector enterprises have the potential to grow to become large 
enterprises and subsequently, these enterprises could support many other Micro & Small 
enterprises in cascading effect. If only 10% of medium enterprises could be  transformed 
into large enterprises, there would be a significant cascading effect for Micro and Small 
enterprises. Therefore, separate policy should be formulated  for Medium enterprises. At 
present, no significant scheme is  available for Medium Enterprises and given that new 

11 
 
definition is into effect, announcing special schemes for medium -sized enterprises would 
benefit numerous enterprises who have joined MSME spectre due to new definition. 
 
18. The Committee recommends that based on the divergent needs of the Medium 
Enterprises vis-à-vis Small and Micro Enterprises, it is in interest of both the 
categories to have separate and dedicated policies for better targeted development 
and growth. 
 
SETTING UP OF SME FINANCE COMPANIES 
 
19. At present, no SME Finance Companies exist in the country. Therefore, as in the 
case of infrastructure finance companies or micro-finance companies that are not engaged 
in real economic activity  but in the financing of it, SME finance  companies may  be 
established in the country. 
 
20. The Committee suggest s that SME finance companies may be established in 
the country on the lines of infrastructure finance companies or micro -finance 
companies that are not engaged in real economic activity but in financing of it. 
 
CONSULTATION WITH STAKEHOLDERS 
 
21. There is an absence of a structured need assessment  exercise before proposing and 
designing any of the major schemes. Due to weak stakeholder discussions on proposed 
schemes, the design flaws come to light too late and  also discourage potential 
implementing agencies. There is a special need for the involvement of stakeholders at the 
design stage of the  scheme to make the schemes demand driven, especially the schemes 
that are based  on SPV/consortium approach. Process of structured need assessment will 
help generate „content‟ having clarity on objectives, beneficiaries; scope and coverage of  
schemes; role and function of implementing agency. 
22. The Committee is of the view that Emphasis should be made on involvement 
of stakeholders at design stage of schemes, especially the schemes that are based on 
SPV/Consortium approach. 
GST REGIME 
 
23. The GST regime was meant to be a digitized system; however, department 
authorities still insist that separate hard copies are also provided to claim refund. This 
defeats the  purpose of digitizing process. The time involved by the MSMEs in finally 

12 
 
getting the  refund sanctioned causes a tremendous strain on the cash flows of the 
MSMEs, which in turn restricts the possibility of increasing exports. 
 
24. The Committee recommends that the GST regime should be a digitized 
system, without the requirement o f separate hard copies to be provided the 
concerned Dep artment to claim refund. This not only defeats the purpose of 
digitizing process, bu t also eases inordinate delay in getting the refund sanctioned , 
thereby resulting in tremendous strain on cash flows of the MSMEs. 
 
EMERGENCY CREDIT LINE GUARANTEE SCHEME (ECLGS) 
 
25. The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme mandated for providing collateral 
free loans to MSMEs has been a very effective financial measure to restore their liquidity 
and financial health. The said emergency credit line has greatly helped MSMEs to restart 
operations by giving them additional working capital support. It is a welcome step of the 
Government in the Budget 2022 -23 to increase the corpus of ECLGS to Rs. 5 lakh crore 
by adding  Rs. 50 thousand crore for hospitality & related enterprises and extend the 
validity of scheme till 31st March, 2023. However, some more concerns have been raised 
by MSME, which are not able to avail the scheme. Repayment period of 3 -4 years 
including moratorium period under the scheme is very little time for MSMEs which are 
struggling to survive through second wave of Covid -19. As the cash  flow has dried, it 
would take a longer period to come back to normal liquidity and hence it is suggested that  
repayment period should be extended up to 7 – 8 years with at least 2 years of moratorium 
on principal amount. With respect to the interest, moratorium for interest from 01.03.2020 
onwards should be announced by the RBI. This accumulative interest  should be made part 
of term loan/principal amount. No interest on interest should be charged from MSMEs 
while amalgamating the interest in principal amount. 
 
26. The Committee finds that under Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme, 
repayment period of 3 -4 years including moratorium period is a very short period 
for MSMEs, which are struggling to survive from the second wave of Covid -19. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the repayment period should be extended 
upto 7 -8 years with at least 2 years of moratorium on principal amount. With 

13 
 
respect to the interest, moratorium for interest from 01.03.2020 onwards should be 
announced by RBI. 
 
 
 
CREDIT GUARANTEE FUND TRUST FOR MICRO AND SMALL 
ENTERPRISES (CGTMSE) 
 
27. During the budget 2022-23, it was announced by the Hon‟ble Finance Minister that 
the CGTMSE Scheme shall be revamped and Rs. 2 lakh crore will also be infused in the  
scheme. It is indeed a welcome step in the direction to make this scheme more viable  and 
convenient for its stakeholders including MSEs. As the scheme is to be revamped,  it has 
been requested that the limit of collateral free loans under this scheme, either term loan or 
working capital loan, should be increased from existing Rs. 2 crore to upto Rs. 5 crores, 
irrespective of the constitution (Private Ltd ., LLP, Partnership and/or proprietorship) of 
applicant MSEs provided all other criteria are fulfilled. 
 
28. The Committee is in consonance with the suggestion of Associations and 
recommends that while revamping the CGTMSE scheme, the limit of collateral free 
loans under this scheme, either term loan or working capital loan should be 
increased from the existing R s. 2 crore upto Rs. 5 crores, irrespective of the 
Constitution (Private Ltd., LLP, Partnership and/or Proprietorship) of applicant 
MSE’s provided all other criteria are fulfilled. 
 
AATMANIRBHAR BHARAT 
 
29. Government is focusing upon Make in India, which is entirely appreciable effort as 
it helps MSMEs to grow. It is a fact that India is importing MSME oriented products in  
huge quantity, which can be manufactured in India. One of the reasons behind this  could 
be explained as lack of awareness amongs t MSMEs about the products that are  being 
imported in the country. Feedback has been received from the industry that  Government 
should put out a list of such products along with their production  specifications so that 
enterprises become excited about getting into the production of such products. Such 
imported products should also carry the information about their  market potential in the 
country. This would be beneficial for a large number of potential entrepreneurs who wish 
to set up new manufacturing enterprises. A Central Market  Intelligence Center for import 

14 
 
related products and components would be of great  help to MSMEs to achieve the goal of 
Aatmanirbhar Bharat. Soft loans at minimal  interest rate of 3 -4% with a minimum tenure 
of 9-10 years for repayment period, Easy land acquisition, less compliances could be key 
factors in developing domestic manufacturing with MSMEs. Till the domestic 
manufacturing is strengthened, high  import restrictions should be avoided and only, if 
necessary, it should be applied in phased manner. 
 
30. The Committee understands that a number of MSME oriented products are 
presently being imported , which can be manufactured in India. The Committee , 
therefore, recommends that a Central Market Intelligence Centre for import related 
products and components be set up in the country. The said Centre may be 
entrusted with the task of putting out a list of products , which are being imported 
alongwith their specificat ions and spreading awareness of the same through 
electronic, print and social media to attract interested entrepreneurs to set up new 
manufacturing enterprises in MSME Sector, thereby fulfilling the Government ’s 
vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat. 
 
TESTING AND CERTIFICATION FACILITIES IN TECHNOLOGY CENTRES  
31. For any business to flourish, it is important that products are of certain standards 
and excel in quality. For exports, MSMEs need to meet a certain required international or  
regional specific standard for which adequate facilities are not available in the country. 
Besides, available testing facilities are costly , which MSMEs cannot afford. Testing &  
Certifications should be made convenient and cheaper for MSMEs. The country has 
arobust infrastructure of  technology centers that are supporting MSMEs in many ways.  
The Associations have received very positive feedback about these technology centers 
and Ministry of MSME must be congratulated for running this facility across the country. 
Keeping this network i n view, suggestion s have also been received that Technology 
Centers could also be utilised to facilitate subsidised testing for regional  MSMEs. A 
mechanism/tie-up should be developed that testing can be done in India at these 
technology Centers whereas cer tificates for the same test could be issued from  various 
global testing centers , which are acceptable in respective countries/regions.  Ministry of 
MSME could do tie-ups with various global agencies through its technology centers.  
 
32. The Committee recommends that the existing Technology Centres should also 
be used to facilitate subsidi sed testing and certification of regional MSMEs. Further 

15 
 
a mechanism should be devised by the Ministry to tie up with global Testing Centres 
whose certificates are acceptable in respective countries/regions. The Committee 
hopes that this new arrangement will not only ease the testing process and reduce 
the cost, but also encourage new entrepreneurs to come up with more innovations.

Certificate (ISEC) Scheme is one of the components of Khadi  Vikas Yojana. It was 
introduced to mobilize the funds from banking institutions in order to cater to the 
additional fund requirement of Khadi and Village Industries Institutions. For this, an
